text: The year 1866 was marked by an extraordinary occurrence, an enigmatic and baffling event, which surely remains fresh in everyone’s memory. Beyond the whispers that stirred those who lived by the sea and inflamed the thoughts of the general populace, even deep within the heart of landmasses, mariners were especially stirred. Traders, ordinary deckhands, ship captains, skippers, hailing from both Europe and America, military officers from every nation, and the administrations of various countries across both continents, were profoundly concerned with the situation.
For a while, ships had encountered “an enormous thing,” a lengthy, spindle-shaped entity that was sometimes luminous and possessed a size and velocity far exceeding that of a whale.

The details concerning this phantom (recorded in numerous logs) were largely consistent regarding the form of the entity or beast, the relentless speed of its travel, its astonishing capacity for movement, and the singular vitality it appeared to possess. Should it be a whale, it exceeded in magnitude every specimen previously categorized by science. By averaging the sightings gathered on various occasions—discounting the cautious guesses of individuals who limited the creature to two hundred feet, just as we dismissed the inflated claims that measured it at a mile wide and three long—we could reasonably infer that this enigmatic creature far exceeded any proportions recognized by modern ichthyologists, provided it was real. And that it was real remained an indisputable truth; given the inclination of the human spirit toward the wondrous, it is easy to grasp the global agitation sparked by this otherworldly phenomenon. As for dismissing it as mere folklore, such a notion was impossible.

Five miles from the Australian eastern shoreline, the Governor Ashby, a steamer belonging to the Calcutta and Burnach Steam Navigation Company, encountered this shifting entity on the 20th of July, 1866. Initially, Captain Baker supposed he had come upon a previously uncharted sandbank; he was readying himself to calculate its precise coordinates when the mysterious body propelled two jets of water one hundred and fifty feet into the atmosphere with a whistling sound. Unless that sandbank was being subjected to the periodic outbursts of a geyser, the Governor Ashby was clearly dealing with a marine creature, previously undocumented, that expelled jets of water, air, and mist through its blow-holes.

On the 23rd of July of that same year, the Columbus, a vessel belonging to the West India and Pacific Steam Navigation Company, noted comparable phenomena within the Pacific Ocean. Yet, this remarkable whale-like animal possessed the ability to travel between locations at an astonishing speed; for, within a span of three days, the Governor Ashby and the Columbus had sighted it at two distinct positions on the map, which were over seven hundred nautical leagues apart.

A fortnight and a day afterward, at a distance of two thousand miles, the Albion, belonging to the Compagnie-Nationale, and the Tamar, of the Royal Mail Steamship Company, while navigating to windward within the stretch of the Atlantic situated between Europe and the United States, each reported the creature to the other at 42° 15′ N. lat. and 60° 35′ W. long. Based on these concurrent sightings, they felt it reasonable to calculate that the beast’s length was at least three hundred and fifty feet, given that the Albion and the Tamar were both surpassed in size by the animal, despite their own total measurements of three hundred feet.

At present, the most massive whales, specifically the ones inhabiting the ocean regions near the Aleutian, Kulammak, and Umgullich islands, have not surpassed sixty yards in length, assuming they reach that size at all.

Public opinion was significantly swayed by these accounts coming in succession, including new findings recorded on the transatlantic vessel Pereire, a crash involving the Inman line’s Etna and the creature, an official report filed by the crew of the French frigate Normandie, and a precise examination conducted by Commodore Fitz-James’s team aboard the Lord Clyde. While those of a frivolous nature made light of the occurrence, serious and pragmatic nations like England, America, and Germany viewed the situation with greater gravity.

The monster became a trend wherever crowds gathered. It was the subject of café songs, newspaper mockery, and theatrical performances. Various tales about it spread everywhere. The press featured cartoons of every colossal and fictitious beast, ranging from the white whale, the fearsome “Moby Dick” of the northern zones, to the massive kraken with tentacles capable of ensnaring a five-hundred-ton vessel and dragging it down into the oceanic depths. Ancient myths were brought back to life, and the theories of Aristotle and Pliny were revisited, both of whom acknowledged that such creatures existed, alongside the Norwegian folklore of Bishop Pontoppidan, the narratives of Paul Heggede, and finally, the testimonies of Mr. Harrington (whose integrity remained unquestioned), who maintained that while aboard the Castillan in 1857, he had witnessed this giant serpent, which prior to that moment had only ever appeared in the waters of the old “Constitutionnel.”

Next erupted the endless debate dividing the gullible from the skeptical within scholarly circles and academic publications. “The question of the monster” ignited every intellect. Publishers of scientific periodicals, feuding with those who accepted the supernatural, wasted vast quantities of ink throughout this notable crusade, with a few individuals even resorting to violence; because, moving past the sea-serpent, they transitioned into personal attacks.

For half a year, conflict fluctuated within the editorials of the Geographical Institution of Brazil, the Royal Academy of Science of Berlin, the British Association, the Smithsonian Institution of Washington, as well as the debates found in the “Indian Archipelago,” the Cosmos of the Abbé Moigno, Petermann’s Mittheilungen, and the scholarly reports of major newspapers throughout France and elsewhere. Less expensive publications retorted sharply and with boundless energy. These humorists mocked a statement by Linnæus, cited by those opposing the creature, insisting “that nature did not make fools,” and urged their peers not to contradict nature by acknowledging the reality of krakens, sea-serpents, “Moby Dicks,” and additional fantasies of deranged mariners. Finally, a piece in a popular satirical periodical by a celebrated writer, the head of the staff, finished the monster, much like Hippolytus, delivering the fatal strike during a widespread roar of amusement. Humor had triumphed over knowledge.

Throughout the opening months of 1867, the matter appeared interred, destined never to resurface, until fresh evidence was presented to the populace. It ceased to be a mere academic puzzle requiring a solution and transformed into a genuine peril that demanded urgent evasion. The issue assumed an entirely different form. The creature morphed into a diminutive isle, a crag, or a shoal, yet a shoal of indeterminate and fluctuating dimensions.

On March 5th, 1867, the Laurentian, belonging to the Montreal Ocean Company, encountered a rock not indicated on any map for that maritime region while positioned at 27° 30′ lat. and 72° 15′ long. during the night, striking the obstacle with her starboard quarter. Propelled by the wind and her four hundred horse-power, the vessel was traveling at a speed of thirteen knots. If the hull of the Laurentian had not possessed such exceptional durability, the impact would have shattered the ship, causing it to sink along with the 237 passengers it was transporting back from Canada.

At approximately five in the morning, while dawn was beginning to break, the mishap occurred. The quarter-deck officers rushed toward the stern of the ship. With the utmost care, they scrutinized the ocean. Beyond a powerful whirlpool roughly three cables away, which appeared as though the water had been stirred with great force, they observed nothing. The precise coordinates of the location were recorded, and the Laurentian proceeded on its journey seemingly unscathed. Whether it had collided with a hidden reef or a massive piece of wreckage remained unknown; however, upon inspecting the hull during maintenance, it was discovered that a section of the keel had been fractured.

This occurrence, inherently so serious, could have faded from memory as numerous others have, had it not been repeated under comparable conditions twenty-one days later. Yet, owing to the citizenship of the individual impacted by the collision, and the renown of the firm owning the ship, the incident gained widespread attention.

On the 13th of April, 1867, with the ocean looking lovely and the wind proving helpful, the Caledon, belonging to the Cunard Company’s line, reached 15° 12′ long. and 45° 37′ lat. It was traveling at a rate of thirteen knots and a half.

At four-seventeen in the afternoon, during the time the passengers had gathered for lunch inside the great saloon, the Caledon experienced a minor jolt to her hull, located on the quarter slightly behind the port-paddle.

The Caledon had avoided a collision, yet she had sustained a blow, apparently from an object that was pointed and piercing rather than dull. Because the impact was so minor, nobody felt any concern until the carpenter’s watch ran onto the bridge, yelling, “We are sinking! we are sinking!” Initially, the passengers were quite terrified, though Captain Mercer hurried to calm them. The peril could not be pressing. The Caledon, separated into seven sections by sturdy bulkheads, was capable of enduring any breach without consequence. Captain Mercer descended into the hold without delay. He discovered that water was rushing into the fifth section; the speed of the inflow indicated that the water pressure was significant. Luckily, the boilers were not located in this section, otherwise the flames would have been put out instantly. Captain Mercer commanded that the engines be halted right away, and a crewman went below to determine the magnitude of the damage. A few minutes later, they identified a massive opening, measuring two yards across, in the hull of the vessel. A breach of this size could not be repaired; consequently, the Caledon, with her paddles partially underwater, had to proceed on her journey. At that time, she was three hundred miles away from Cape Clear, and following a three-day postponement, which provoked intense anxiety in Liverpool, she arrived at the company’s dock.

The Caledon, currently situated in dry dock, received a visit from the engineers. They found the situation almost beyond belief; a symmetrical triangular tear existed two and a half yards beneath the waterline. Because the fracture in the iron plating appeared so precise, it seemed as if a punch had fashioned it. It was evident that the tool responsible for the hole was unconventional; furthermore, after being propelled with immense force to penetrate an iron plate measuring 1-3/8 inches in thickness, it had retreated through a backward movement that defied explanation.

This final piece of information served to stir up the tide of popular sentiment yet again. From that point on, every unfortunate incident that lacked a different explanation was attributed to the monster. The burden for all these maritime disasters, which were regrettably numerous, was placed upon this fictitious beast; because out of the three thousand vessels reported lost each year at Lloyd’s, the total of steam and sailing ships presumed vanished due to a complete lack of intelligence reached at least two hundred!

At present, the “monster” stood accused, whether fairly or unfairly, of their vanishing, and because of it, travel between the various continents grew increasingly perilous. The citizenry insisted firmly that the oceans be cleared of this terrifying whale at any cost.

During the timeframe of these occurrences, I had recently come back from a scholarly investigation within the unpleasant region of Nebraska, located in the United States. Because of my position as Assistant Professor at the Museum of Natural History in Paris, the government of France had assigned me to this mission. Following a half-year stay in Nebraska, I reached New York near the conclusion of March, carrying a valuable assortment. My voyage back to France was scheduled for the start of May. In the interim, I was busy organizing my botanical, mineralogical, and zoological treasures, at the moment the mishap befell the Caledon.

I possessed complete mastery over the topic that served as the current day’s primary concern. In what other way could I have been? Having perused and studied every European and American journal repeatedly, I remained no closer to a final verdict. This enigma left me perplexed. Unable to establish a firm stance, I oscillated between opposing viewpoints. That a genuine phenomenon existed was beyond question, and those who doubted were encouraged to touch the very injury sustained by the Caledon.

When I reached New York, the issue had reached its peak. The theory regarding the drifting isle and the inaccessible sandbar, backed by individuals ill-equipped to reach a conclusion, was discarded. And, truly, if this reef did not contain a mechanism within its core, by what means could it alter its location with such remarkable speed?
The notion of a drifting shell belonging to a massive sunken vessel was abandoned for that identical reason.

Only two potential answers to the problem persisted, resulting in the formation of two separate factions: one group favored a beast of immense power, while the other supported a submersible craft possessing vast propulsive energy.

Yet this final theory, however reasonable it appeared, failed to survive investigations conducted in both spheres. It was improbable that a private individual would control such an apparatus. Where, when, and in what manner was it manufactured? And by what means could its assembly remain concealed? A government might, of course, own such a ruinous device. And during these calamitous eras, as human inventiveness has increased the potency of military armaments, it was conceivable that a nation might attempt to operate such an intimidating mechanism in total secrecy. Following the chassepots arrived the torpedoes, following the torpedoes the submarine rams, then—the counteraction. At least, I hope so.

Yet the theory of a war machine collapsed in the face of official statements from Governments. Since the matter concerned the public interest and transatlantic communications were being disrupted, the truthfulness of these reports seemed beyond question. Still, how could one accept that the building of this submarine boat had remained hidden from view? It would be a great challenge for a private individual to maintain such a secret in these conditions, and for a nation whose every move is constantly monitored by formidable adversaries, it would surely be impossible.
Following investigations conducted throughout England, France, Russia, Prussia, Spain, Italy, and America, and even in Turkey, the theory regarding a submarine monitor was conclusively dismissed.

When I reached New York, a number of individuals paid me the tribute of seeking my counsel regarding the event at hand. I had previously released a two-volume quarto study in France, which bore the title “Mysteries of the Great Submarine Grounds.” This publication, which received significant acclaim from the academic community, earned me a distinct standing within this somewhat shadowy field of Natural History. They requested my guidance. For as long as I was able to dispute the occurrence, I maintained a firm denial. However, once I was pushed into a tight spot, I felt compelled to provide a clear explanation. Consequently, “the Honourable Étienne Delorme, Professor in the Museum of Paris,” was summoned by the New York Herald to provide a concrete judgment. I acted. I spoke, because I lacked the ability to remain silent. I examined the matter from every angle, both political and scientific; and I provide here a selection from a thoroughly researched piece I printed in the issue dated the 30th of April. It stated the following:—
“Having scrutinized each of the various theories individually and discarded every alternative proposal, I am compelled to acknowledge that a sea creature of immense strength must exist.”

“The vast abysses of the sea remain completely hidden from our knowledge. Lead lines are unable to attain them. We can barely guess what occurs in those distant reaches—what creatures dwell, or might dwell, twelve or fifteen miles under the sea’s surface—or how these animals are structured. Nevertheless, addressing the issue presented to me might alter the nature of the predicament. We either possess full knowledge of every type of creature inhabiting our world, or we do not. If we lack total knowledge—if Nature still guards ichthyological mysteries from us, it is entirely logical to accept the possibility of fish, or different varieties of cetaceans, or even entirely new species, possessing a physiology designed for strata beyond the reach of soundings, which some sort of chance event, whether whimsical or strange, has occasionally forced to the ocean’s surface.”

“Conversely, if we are acquainted with every species of life, we are obligated to look for the creature in question among the sea animals that have been categorized; and, in that scenario, I would be inclined to accept that a colossal narwhal exists,” I said.

“The ordinary narwhal, known as the sea’s unicorn, frequently reaches sixty feet in length. Magnify its dimensions by five or ten times, grant it power matching that scale, extend its lethal armaments, and you possess the creature in question. It shall hold the measurements established by the Tamar’s crew, serve as the tool needed for the Caledon’s puncture, and exert the force essential to penetrate the steamer’s plating.”

“Truly, the narwhal carries a kind of ivory blade, or a halberd, as some naturalists describe it. Its main tusk possesses the strength of steel. A number of these tusks have been discovered embedded in whale carcasses, creatures the unicorn consistently defeats. Others have been extracted, with significant difficulty, from the hulls of vessels they had completely transfixed, much like a drill bores into a cask. The Museum of the Faculty of Medicine of Paris holds one such protective implement, measuring two and a quarter yards long and fifteen inches across at its base.”

“Agreed! assume this projectile possesses sixfold the force and the creature is ten times as robust; propel it at a velocity of twenty miles per hour, and you generate an impact sufficient to cause the necessary disaster. Pending additional data, I will persist in the belief that it is a sea-unicorn of immense proportions, equipped not with a halberd, but with a genuine spur, similar to the ironclad frigates, or ‘rams’ of war, which would combine both its weight and its capacity for propulsion. In this way, the baffling occurrence might be accounted for, provided there is nothing beyond everything that has been theorized, observed, noticed, or encountered; which remains a slight possibility.”
My final remarks were craven; however, I desired, to a degree, to protect my standing as Professor, while avoiding providing the Americans—who possess a hearty laugh—too many reasons to mock me.

I kept a means of retreat open for my own use. Yet, in practice, I acknowledged that the “monster” was real. My piece received enthusiastic debate, earning it significant acclaim. It gathered a specific group of supporters. The answer it offered allowed the imagination complete freedom. Mankind finds pleasure in magnificent ideas regarding otherworldly creatures. Furthermore, the ocean is exactly the ideal vessel for them, serving as the sole environment where these titans—compared to which land beasts like rhinoceroses or elephants are insignificant—might emerge or evolve.

From that perspective, the commercial and industrial journals primarily addressed the matter. Every publication focused on insurance firms—which were warning of increased premium costs—including the Shipping and Mercantile Gazette, the Lloyd’s List, the Packet-Boat, and the Maritime and Colonial Review, reached a consensus. The public had expressed its view. The United States led the effort, initiating plans in New York for an expedition intended to hunt the narwhal. The Evangeline, a high-speed frigate, was readied for service with all possible haste. Commander Hallett was granted access to the arsenals and hurried the outfitting of his vessel; yet, as is typical, once the decision to chase the creature was made, the beast vanished. For a period of two months, there was no mention of it. Not a single vessel encountered it. It appeared as though the unicorn were aware of the schemes being devised against it. It had been discussed so extensively, even via the Atlantic cable, that humorists claimed the tiny creature had intercepted a telegram and was exploiting the news.

Once the frigate was equipped for an extended voyage and outfitted with powerful angling gear, the direction to take remained unknown. As restlessness mounted, word arrived on the 2nd of July that a steamer belonging to the San Francisco line, traveling from California to Shanghai, had spotted the creature three weeks earlier within the North Pacific Ocean. This report triggered intense agitation. The vessel was resupplied with provisions and loaded with a full supply of coal.
I got a letter three hours prior to the Evangeline departing from the Brooklyn pier, which read:—
“For M. DELORME, instructor at the Paris Museum, staying at the Fifth Avenue Hotel, New York.”

“Sir—should you agree to become a part of the Evangeline on this voyage, the United States Government would be pleased to have France take part in the mission. A cabin has been reserved for you by Commander Hallett,” said I.
“With warmest regards, “J.B. PRUITT, “Secretary of Marine.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: A mere three seconds prior to the delivery of J. B. Pruitt’s correspondence, the notion of hunting the unicorn had crossed my mind no more than the idea of navigating the North Sea. Once I had finished perusing the missive from the honourable Secretary of Marine, however, I was seized by the conviction that my authentic calling and the singular purpose of my existence was to pursue this unsettling beast and rid the globe of it.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: However, I had only recently come back from an exhausting trip, tired and craving rest. I desired nothing beyond once more beholding my homeland, my companions, my modest room near the Jardin des Plantes, and my beloved, invaluable specimens. Yet, I was unable to be restrained! I abandoned everything—my weariness, my associates, and my items—and immediately agreed to the proposal from the American Government.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: “Furthermore,” I mused, “every path returns to Europe (for my own advantage), and I shall not rush my journey to the French shoreline. This noble creature might permit its capture within European waters (for my own advantage), and I am determined not to return without at least eighteen inches of its ivory weapon for the Museum of Natural History.” Yet, in the interim, I am required to pursue this narwhal across the North Pacific Ocean, which, in order to head back to France, was traveling toward the antipodes.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: “Baptiste,” I shouted, sounding impatient.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: My servant was Baptiste, a loyal and sincere Flemish lad who had traveled everywhere with me. I held him in high regard, and he reciprocated that affection. By temperament he was stolid, by conviction methodical, and by custom diligent; he showed minimal agitation amidst the various shocks of existence, possessed great manual dexterity, and was capable of performing any task requested of him; furthermore, notwithstanding his name, he offered no counsel—not even when I sought it.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: For the past decade, Baptiste accompanied me on every scientific pursuit. He never grumbled about the duration or exhaustion of our travels, nor did he ever protest when packing his suitcase for any destination, regardless of the distance, be it China or Congo. Furthermore, he possessed robust health that resisted all illness, sturdy muscles, and a complete lack of nerves; his upright character was a given. This young man was thirty, and his age compared to mine as fifteen to twenty. Might I be forgiven for mentioning that I was forty?

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: However, Baptiste possessed a single flaw; he was excessively formal, and he would only ever address me by using the third person, a habit that occasionally irritated me.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: “Baptiste,” I repeated, as I started to ready myself for leaving with trembling fingers.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: I felt no doubt regarding this loyal lad. Usually, I refrained from inquiring whether my journeys suited his schedule; however, on this occasion, the mission could prove lengthy, and the venture might involve significant danger while hunting a creature with the power to destroy a frigate as simply as one might crush a nutshell. Such a situation provided cause for contemplation for even the most indifferent person alive. “What would Baptiste say?” I wondered.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: “Baptiste,” I shouted for the third occasion.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: Baptiste emerged.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: “Did you call, sir?” he asked, as he walked in.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: “Indeed, lad; get everything ready for my departure and your own as well. We are departing in two hours,” I said.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: “Whatever you wish, sir,” answered Baptiste, in a low voice.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: “There is no time to waste;—pack every one of my travel items, jackets, undergarments, and socks into my trunk—do not bother counting, just grab as many as possible, and be quick.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: “What about your assortments, sir?” remarked Baptiste.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: “In time, we shall remember them.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: “What! the skins of the archiotherium, the hyracotherium, the oreodons, the cheropotamus, and the rest?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: “They are going to hold them at the hotel,” I said.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: “And your live Babiroussa, sir?” asked I.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: “It shall be fed while we are away; furthermore, I intend to command that our collection of animals be sent on to France,” I said.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: “So, we are not going back to Paris?” asked Baptiste.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: “Certainly,” I replied, with evasion, “by curving.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: “Would the arc be to your liking, sir?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: “Oh! it is going to be a trifle; merely not as straight a path, that is the whole of it. We are booking our travel aboard the Evangeline.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: “Whatever you deem appropriate, sir,” Baptiste answered with composure.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: “You understand, my companion, this concerns the beast—that renowned narwhal. We intend to rid the oceans of it. The writer of a two-volume quarto text regarding the ‘Mysteries of the Great Submarine Grounds’ is unable to resist joining Commander Hallett. It is a magnificent undertaking, yet a perilous one! Our destination remains uncertain; such creatures possess a highly fickle nature. Regardless, we shall proceed; our captain is quite alert.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: A credit account was established by me for Babiroussa, and after Baptiste trailed behind, I leaped inside a taxi. Our belongings were moved to the frigate’s deck without delay. I hurried onto the vessel and inquired about Commander Hallett. A sailor led me toward the poop, where I stood before a handsome officer, who extended his hand toward me.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: “Monsieur Étienne Delorme?” he inquired.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: “The man himself,” I answered; “Commander Hallett?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: “Professor, you are welcome; your quarters have been prepared for you,” I said.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: I inclined my head and requested that I be led to the quarters assigned to me.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: The Evangeline had been selected and outfitted appropriately for her upcoming journey. As a frigate capable of impressive velocity, she possessed high-pressure engines that allowed for seven atmospheres of pressure. With this power, the Evangeline reached an average speed of almost eighteen and one-third knots per hour—a notable pace, yet one that remained inadequate for confronting this massive cetacean.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: The ship’s internal layout matched its maritime performance. My quarters, situated in the rear section and leading into the gunroom, pleased me greatly.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: “This place will suit us,” I remarked to Baptiste.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: “Furthermore, with your honour’s permission, like a hermit-crab inside a whelk’s shell,” Baptiste stated.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: I climbed back onto the poop deck to observe the arrangements for our sailing, having left Baptiste behind to store our luggage in a suitable spot.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: Just then, Commander Hallett was commanding the final lines securing the Evangeline to the Brooklyn dock to be released. Thus, in fifteen minutes or possibly sooner, the frigate would have departed in my absence. I would have failed to join this remarkable, otherworldly, and unbelievable voyage, the account of which might very well be met with a degree of doubt.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: However, Commander Hallett refused to waste a single hour or day searching the waters where the creature had been observed. He summoned the engineer.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: “Are the boilers at maximum capacity?” he inquired.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: “Certainly, sir,” the engineer answered.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: “Proceed,” shouted Commander Hallett.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: A throng of onlookers packed the Brooklyn wharf and the entire section of New York adjacent to the East River. Five hundred thousand voices erupted in three consecutive cheers; a multitude of cloths fluttered over the dense crowd, bidding farewell to the Evangeline as she made her way to the Hudson’s currents, near the tip of the slender peninsula that constitutes New York City. Subsequently, the frigate navigated the New Jersey shoreline along the eastern edge of that picturesque river, lined with estates, and sailed between the fortifications, which greeted her with their most powerful artillery. The Evangeline replied by raising the American flag three times, its thirty-nine stars gleaming brilliantly from the mizzen-peak; then, adjusting her pace to navigate the restricted passage indicated by markers in the interior bay created by Sandy Hook Point, she skirted the extended sandy shore, where a few thousand observers offered a concluding shout. The flotilla of vessels and support craft continued to trail the frigate, only turning back once they were parallel to the lightship, whose pair of beacons signaled the mouth of New York Channel.

chapter_title: CHAPTER III I FORM MY RESOLUTION
text: At the tolling of six bells, the pilot boarded his vessel and returned to the small schooner that lay in wait to our leeward, the furnaces were stoked, the propeller churned the sea with increased speed, the frigate moved along the flat, golden shoreline of Long Island; and when eight bells sounded, having passed beyond the view of the Fire Island beacons to the north-west, she steamed at maximum velocity into the black depths of the Atlantic.

Captain Hallett proved a capable mariner, deserving of the frigate under his charge. The man and his ship functioned as a single entity. He served as its very spirit. Regarding the matter of the cetacean, he harbored no uncertainty, and he forbade any questioning of the creature’s reality while aboard. He maintained belief in it, much like pious women accept the leviathan—through conviction rather than logic. The beast was real, and he had taken an oath to purge the oceans of it. He acted as a sort of Knight of Rhodes, a modern Dieudonné de Gozon, setting out to confront the serpent that ravaged the island. Either Captain Hallett would slay the narwhal, or the narwhal would slay the captain. No other outcome existed.

The ship’s officers held the same view as their leader. Constant conversation, debate, and assessment of the likelihood of an encounter occupied them, while they kept a close eye on the expansive sea. Several men chose to station themselves in the cross-trees, a position they would have otherwise reviled. Throughout the sun’s journey across the sky, the rigging remained full of crewmen, despite the deck’s intense heat scorching their feet; nevertheless, the Evangeline had not reached the anticipated Pacific region. Regarding the crew, they wished for nothing more than to find the unicorn, strike it with a harpoon, lift it onto the deck, and finish it off. They kept a keen watch over the water.

Furthermore, Captain Hallett had mentioned a specific amount of two thousand dollars, reserved for the individual who would be the first to spot the beast, whether that person happened to be a cabin-boy, a common seaman, or an officer.
It is left to your discretion to determine the manner in which sight was employed aboard the Evangeline.

I, for my own part, did not lag behind the rest, nor did I yield to anyone my portion of the routine sightings. There were a hundred justifications for naming the frigate the Argus. Among our number, only Baptiste appeared to register a protest through his apathy regarding the matter that captivated us all, and he seemed disconnected from the widespread fervor aboard the vessel.

I mentioned previously that Captain Hallett had meticulously equipped his vessel with all the gear required to capture the massive whale. No whaling ship had ever been more thoroughly prepared. We carried every implement in existence, ranging from hand-hurled harpoons to the barbed bolts of a blunderbuss and the detonating spheres of a duck-gun. Positioned upon the forecastle was an ideal breech-loading firearm, featuring a remarkably heavy breech and a slender bore, a design that had appeared at the 1867 Exhibition. This valuable piece of American hardware was capable of launching a nine-pound conical shell to an average range of ten miles without difficulty.
The Evangeline therefore lacked no instruments of ruin; and, even more fortunately, Tom Harlan, the greatest of all harpooners, was aboard.

A Canadian, Tom Harlan possessed a rare swiftness of hand and remained unmatched in his perilous trade. He held a superlative command of audacity, coolness, skill, and cunning, and it would require an especially crafty whale or a uniquely “cute” cachalot to evade the blow of his harpoon.

At approximately forty years old, Tom Harlan stood as a tall individual exceeding six feet, possessing a robust frame, a somber and quiet demeanor, a penchant for sporadic outbursts of violence, and a fiery temper whenever he faced opposition. His physical presence drew notice, yet it was primarily the audacity in his gaze that lent his countenance a unique quality.

Anyone identifying as Canadian identifies as French; and, despite Tom Harlan being quite reserved, I have to concede that he grew fond of me. My origin surely attracted him. It provided a chance for him to speak, and for me to listen to, that ancient tongue of Rabelais, which remains spoken in certain Canadian provinces. The harpooner’s ancestors hailed from Quebec, and they were already a clan of robust fishermen back when this city was under French rule.

Gradually, Tom Harlan developed a fondness for conversation, and I delighted in listening to the accounts of his experiences in the arctic waters. He described his angling and his battles with an innate lyrical quality; his storytelling resembled a heroic verse, and it felt as though I were hearing a Canadian Homer chanting the Iliad of the northern territories.

I am depicting this resilient associate just as I truly understood him. We have become long-time companions, bound by that permanent bond forged and solidified during times of dire peril. “Ah, brave Tom!” I desire nothing beyond surviving another century, so that I might possess additional opportunity to reflect at greater length upon your legacy.

What, then, was the perspective of Tom Harlan regarding the sea beast? I have to confess that he remained a skeptic of the unicorn, standing alone among the crew in his refusal to accept the general consensus. He steered clear of the topic entirely, though I felt compelled to bring it up with him on one occasion. On a glorious night, the 30th of July—exactly three weeks since we had set sail—the frigate sat parallel to Cape Blanc, positioned thirty miles downwind from the Patagonian shoreline. We had passed the tropic of Capricorn, and the Straits of Magellan lay fewer than seven hundred miles to the south. In less than eight days, the Evangeline would be cutting through the Pacific.

Tom Harlan and I sat upon the poop deck, discussing various topics while observing this enigmatic ocean, the immense abysses of which had remained beyond human sight until now. I steered our talk toward the giant unicorn, weighing the potential for our mission’s triumph or defeat. However, noticing that Tom Harlan allowed me to do the talking while remaining largely silent, I questioned him with greater insistence.
“Is it possible, Tom,” I remarked, “that you remain unconvinced regarding the reality of this cetacean we are pursuing? Do you possess some specific motive for such disbelief?”

For a few moments, the harpooner stared steadily at me, then tapped his wide brow with his hand—a customary gesture—as though gathering his thoughts, and finally remarked, “Perhaps I have, M. Delorme.”

“However, Tom, being a whaler by trade and well-acquainted with every major marine mammal—you, whose mind could readily embrace the theory of gigantic cetaceans, should be the final person to express skepticism in a situation like this!”

“That is precisely what misleads you, Professor,” Tom answered. “It is understandable that the masses might credit the notion of unusual comets moving through the heavens, or the presence of prehistoric beasts deep within the Earth; yet, neither the man of science who studies the stars nor the one who examines the rocks holds any stock in such fantasies. In my time as a whaler, I have tracked many a whale, struck a large quantity with my harpoon, and put several to death; still, regardless of how powerful or formidable they were, neither their flukes nor their physical defenses could have managed to so much as mark the steel hull of a steamship.”
“However, Tom, there are accounts of vessels that have been completely transfixed by the tusks of the narwhal,” I said.

“It is feasible that vessels made of wood could be damaged in such a way,” the Canadian answered, “yet I have not witnessed this occur; and, pending additional evidence, I refuse to believe that whales, cetaceans, or sea-unicorns possess the capability to cause the result you mention.”

“Well, Tom, I reiterate this, my certainty anchored in factual deduction. I maintain that a robustly structured mammal exists, a member of the vertebrata phylum, akin to dolphins, cachalots, or whales, and equipped with a defensive horn capable of immense piercing force.”
“Hum!” the harpooner remarked, as he swayed his head like someone unwilling to be persuaded.

“Observe a detail, my esteemed Canadian,” I continued. “Should such a creature truly exist, should it dwell within the oceanic abyss, and should it inhabit the layers situated miles beneath the surface, it would of necessity be endowed with a constitution of unparalleled durability.”
“And for what reason does this influential group exist?” demanded Tom.

“For it demands immense power to remain within these layers and withstand their force. Hear me out. Suppose we grant that atmospheric pressure equals the weight of a water column thirty-two feet tall. Actually, that column would be less tall, given that we refer to sea water, which possesses greater density than fresh water. Very well, Tom, as you descend, for every thirty-two feet of water overhead, your frame sustains a pressure matching that of the atmosphere—namely, 15 lbs. per square inch of surface area. Consequently, at 320 feet, this pressure equals 10 atmospheres, 100 atmospheres at 3200 feet, and 1000 atmospheres at 32,000 feet, which is roughly 6 miles; this means that if you reached such an ocean depth, every three-eighths of an inch of your body’s surface would endure a pressure of 5600 lbs. Ah! my brave Tom, are you aware of how many square inches your body’s surface possesses?”
“I am completely unaware, M. Delorme.”
“Approximately 6500; and, since the actual atmospheric pressure measures about 15 lbs. per square inch, the 6500 square inches you possess are currently supporting a load of 97,500 lbs.”
“Unnoticed by me?”

“Unnoticed by you. And should you remain unflattened by that force, it is owing to the air entering your frame at a matching pressure. Consequently, there is an absolute balance between the inner and outer pressure, which renders them mutually ineffective, and which permits you to endure it comfortably. Yet, within the water, the situation differs.”
“I comprehend,” answered Tom, his focus sharpening; “for the ocean encircles my person, yet it fails to enter.”

“Exactly, Tom: meaning that at a depth of 32 feet under the ocean’s surface, you would be subjected to a force of 97,500 lbs.; at 320 feet, that force would be tenfold; at 3200 feet, it would be a hundred times greater; and finally, at 32,000 feet, a thousand times that pressure would equal 97,500,000 lbs.—which is to say, you would be crushed just as though you had been pulled between the plates of a hydraulic press!”
“The fiend!” cried Tom.

“All right, my capable harpooner, if a creature with a backbone, measuring hundreds of yards in length and sized accordingly, is able to exist at such profound depths—where the surface area equates to millions of square inches, meaning tens of millions of pounds, we are forced to calculate the pressure exerted upon them. Reflect, then, on the necessary durability of their skeletal frames and the power of their biological systems to endure that level of force!” said I.
“Why!” Tom Harlan cried out, “they have to be constructed from iron plating measuring eight inches in depth, similar to the armoured frigates.”
“Indeed, Tom. And consider the devastation that a body of that size would inflict, were it propelled at the velocity of a locomotive into the side of a ship.”
“Yes—certainly—perhaps,” the Canadian answered, rattled by these statistics, though still refusing to concede.
“So, am I persuasive enough for you?”
“One thing you have persuaded me of, sir, is that if creatures of that nature truly inhabit the ocean depths, they are bound to possess the immense strength you claim.”
“However, if they are not real, my stubborn harpooner, in what way do you account for the mishap involving the Caledon?”

For a significant duration, the journey of the Evangeline remained free of any notable occurrences. However, a single event took place that demonstrated the remarkable skill of Tom Harlan and verified the degree of trust we could invest in him.

On June 30th, our frigate communicated with several American whaling vessels, discovering that they possessed no information regarding the narwhal. However, the captain of the Monroe, aware that Tom Harlan was a crew member on the Evangeline, requested his assistance to pursue a whale they had spotted. Commander Hallett, eager to observe Tom Harlan’s skills, authorized him to board the Monroe. Our Canadian was favored by such fortune that he did not merely harpoon one whale, but struck two with a single double blow, piercing one directly through the heart and securing the second following a chase lasting several minutes.
Without a doubt, I would not wager on the creature’s success if it ever crossed paths with the harpoon belonging to Tom Harlan.

Moving at high speed, the frigate traveled along the south-eastern shoreline of America. On the 3rd of July, we arrived at the mouth of the Straits of Magellan, positioned even with Cape Vierges. Commander Hallett, however, refused to navigate the winding route, choosing instead to round Cape Horn.

The vessel’s company concurred with his assessment. It was indeed a prospect that they could encounter the narwhal within this constricted channel. Numerous mariners maintained that the creature was incapable of traversing the area, “that he was too big for that!”

At roughly three in the afternoon on the 6th of July, the Evangeline rounded the lonely isle fifteen miles to the south—a desolate crag at the edge of the American continent that Dutch mariners had christened Cape Horn after their own home city. Steering was adjusted to the north-west, and by the following day, the frigate’s propeller was finally churning the Pacific waves.
“Stay alert!” shouted the sailors.

And they were spread open broad. Both eyes and spectacles, slightly blinded, it is certain, by the vision of two thousand dollars, found not a moment of rest. Through the light and the dark they observed the face of the sea, and even those with night vision, whose ability to perceive in the gloom increases their odds a hundred times over, would have been sufficiently occupied to secure the reward.

I, who found no allure in wealth, remained the most vigilant person on the ship. Spending minimal time eating and only a few hours resting, regardless of whether it rained or the sun shone, I stayed on the vessel’s poop. Whether I leaned against the forecastle netting or the taffrail, I watched with intensity the gentle foam that turned the ocean white to the horizon; and how frequently I felt the same excitement as most of the crew whenever a fickle whale surfaced with its dark back above the swells! The ship’s poop filled instantly. From the cabins rushed a flood of officers and sailors, every one of them observing the whale’s path with anxious eyes and panting chests. I stared until my vision blurred, while Baptiste, remaining ever stoic, continued to say in a steady tone:
“You would see more clearly, sir, if you did not squint so!”
Yet, futile anticipation! The Evangeline slowed its pace and steered toward the creature indicated, a mere whale, or ordinary cachalot, which quickly vanished under a barrage of curses.

Yet the conditions were pleasant. The journey proceeded under the finest circumstances. Although it was the inclement time of year in Australia, with the July of that region matching our January in Europe, the ocean remained lovely and simple to observe across a wide perimeter.

On July 20th, we intersected the tropic of Capricorn at 105° longitude, and on the 27th of that month, we traversed the equator at the 110th meridian. Following this, the frigate steered a more definitive course toward the west, searching the middle of the Pacific. Commander Hallett reasoned, quite logically, that staying in the open ocean was preferable to nearing landmasses, which the creature appeared to avoid (possibly because the depth was insufficient for him! the majority of the crew proposed). The frigate sailed well clear of the Marquesas and the Sandwich Islands, traversed the tropic of Cancer, and headed toward the China Seas. We had arrived at the site of the beast’s most recent activities: and, in honesty, we were barely existing on the vessel. Our hearts hammered, bracing themselves for inevitable future aneurysms. The whole crew suffered from a nervous agitation that I cannot adequately describe: they found no appetite and no rest—twenty times daily, a mistake or a visual trick by some seaman perched on the taffrail would trigger cold sweats, and these repeated shocks maintained us in a condition of such intense tension that a collapse was inevitable.

And in fact, a response manifested before long. Throughout a three-month period, where every single day felt like an eternity, the Evangeline ploughed through the entirety of the Northern Pacific, chasing whales, executing abrupt changes in direction, swinging unexpectedly from one heading to another, halting abruptly, increasing her speed, and reversing time and again while jeopardizing the integrity of her engines, and not a single location along the American or Japanese shoreline remained unexamined.

Those who had most fervently championed the mission transformed into its fiercest critics. Opposition grew, spreading from the sailors up to the captain, and surely, were it not for the unwavering resolve of Captain Hallett, the vessel would have steered directly south. This futile hunt could not endure for much more time. The Evangeline possessed no cause for self-reproach, as she had exerted every effort to achieve success. Never had the crew of an American ship displayed greater dedication or endurance; the blame for this outcome could not be laid upon them—there was no alternative but to head back.

The commander received this report. Because the crew was unable to conceal their dissatisfaction, the work was negatively impacted. I shall not claim that a mutiny occurred on the vessel, yet following a fair duration of stubbornness, Captain Hallett requested three days of forbearance, much like Columbus. He stated, “If in three days the monster did not appear, the man at the helm should give three turns of the wheel, and the Evangeline would make for the European seas.”

On the 2nd of November, this vow was delivered. The ship’s crew found themselves galvanized by it. With fresh vigilance, the sea was observed. Every man desired a final look to encapsulate his memories. With frantic energy, the glasses were employed. It was a magnificent challenge issued to the giant narwhal, and he could hardly neglect to respond to the call and “appear.”

Forty-eight hours went by, and the steam remained at fifty percent capacity; countless plans were implemented to draw the notice and provoke the indifference of the creature, provided it were encountered in that region. Substantial amounts of bacon were dragged behind the vessel, much to the delight (I must admit) of the sharks. Tiny boats spread out in every direction from the Evangeline while she remained stationary, leaving no portion of the ocean unsearched. Yet the evening of the 4th of November came, and the underwater enigma remained concealed.

On the 5th of November, when the clock struck twelve, the period of waiting would (in a moral sense) reach its end; once that moment passed, Commander Hallett, true to his word, was scheduled to steer the vessel toward the south-east and leave the northern areas of the Pacific behind permanently.

At that moment, the frigate occupied the position of 31° 15′ north latitude and 136° 42′ east longitude. Less than two hundred miles to leeward, the Japanese coastline continued to persist. Evening drew near. Eight bells had recently been struck; the moon, currently in its first quarter, was obscured by massive clouds. Beneath the ship’s stern, the ocean rolled in a tranquil manner.

I was hunched over the starboard netting at that precise instant. Near me, Baptiste remained, his gaze fixed directly ahead. Perched within the ratlines, the crew studied the horizon as it gradually narrowed and grew dim. Officers swept the deepening gloom with their night glasses; occasionally, the sea shimmered beneath moonlight that pierced through a pair of clouds, before every vestige of illumination vanished into the shadows.

Observing Baptiste, I perceived that he was experiencing a fraction of the prevailing mood. Or so it seemed to me. It is possible that his nerves were responding to a feeling of inquisitiveness for the initial time.
“I said, “Baptiste, come, this is the final opportunity to secure the two thousand dollars.”

“I would like to ask, sir,” answered Baptiste, “if I might mention that I did not anticipate winning the reward; and, even if the Union government had proposed a hundred thousand dollars, they would not have lost a cent.”

“You are correct, Baptiste. It is, in the end, a senseless matter, and one that we began with too little consideration. How much time squandered, what pointless feelings! We ought to have returned to France half a year ago,” said I.

“Inside your small chamber, sir,” answered Baptiste, “and within your gallery, sir, and I ought to have finished organizing every one of your specimens, sir. And the Babiroussa would have been placed inside its enclosure at the Jardin des Plantes, and have attracted every inquisitive soul in the city!”
“Just as you state, Baptiste. I suspect we stand a decent possibility of becoming objects of ridicule for our efforts.”
“That is reasonably sure,” Baptiste answered, in a low voice; “I believe they shall mock you, sir. And, am I required to state it?”
“Proceed, my dear companion.”
“You shall receive nothing but what you merit, sir.”
“Certainly!”
“Should one possess the distinction of being a scholar like yourself, sir, it is unwise to place one’s self in——”
Baptiste lacked the opportunity to complete his praise. Amidst a widespread hush, a sound had suddenly emerged. It was the cry of Tom Harlan calling out—
“Observe that direction! The exact object of our search—positioned off our weather beam!”

Upon hearing this shout, the entire complement of the vessel rushed to the harpooner—the commander, the officers, the masters, the sailors, and the cabin boys; the engineers abandoned their machinery, and the stokers departed from their furnaces.

The command to halt her had been issued, so the frigate continued forward solely by her remaining inertia. The night was then absolute, and despite the excellence of the Canadian’s vision, I wondered how he had succeeded in sighting anything, or indeed what he had been able to discern. My pulse throbbed as though it might shatter. Yet Tom Harlan was correct, and we collectively spotted the entity he indicated. At a distance of two cables from the Evangeline, off the starboard quarter, the ocean appeared entirely lit up. It was no simple phosphorescent occurrence. The creature rose several fathoms above the surface, then emitted that highly vivid yet mysterious glow described in the accounts of various shipmasters. This splendid radiance had to be generated by a source of immense luminous intensity. The glowing area marked a vast, highly stretched oval upon the water, with a core that focused a scorching heat, the blinding brightness of which faded through gradual stages.
“It is merely a collection of phosphoric bits,” one of the officers shouted.

“Certainly not, sir, no,” I answered. “Pholades and salpæ could never generate a glow of such intensity. This radiance is fundamentally electrical in character. Furthermore, look, look! it is in motion; it shifts ahead, recedes; it is rushing in our direction!”
A collective shout erupted from the frigate.
“Quiet!” the Captain commanded; “turn the rudder, put the engines in reverse.”
The steam supply was cut, and the Evangeline, veering to the left, traced a half-circle.
“Turn the rudder to the right, move forward,” shouted the Captain.
The commands were carried out, and the frigate sped swiftly away from the blazing beacon.
My assessment was wrong. Although she attempted to veer away, the otherworldly creature drew near at a speed twice as fast as hers.

We struggled to inhale. It was bewilderment rather than terror that rendered us silent and paralyzed. The creature closed the distance, playing amidst the swells. It circled the frigate, which traveled at fourteen knots at the time, and swathed the ship in electric bands resembling glowing particles. Afterward, it retreated a distance of two or three miles, trailing a luminous wake, similar to the clouds of vapor cast off by high-speed locomotives. Abruptly, from the black edge of the horizon where it had withdrawn to gather speed, the beast darted toward the Evangeline with frightening haste, halted abruptly roughly twenty feet from the side, and vanished—not by submerging, as its glow remained undiminished—but instantly, as though the origin of its radiant light had been depleted. Then it emerged once more on the opposite flank of the ship, as if it had pivoted and glided beneath the keel. A crash that would have been our undoing could have happened at any second. Nevertheless, I was amazed by the way the frigate was handled. It retreated instead of engaging.
An expression of inexplicable surprise appeared upon the captain’s visage, which was ordinarily quite stoic.

“M. Delorme,” he remarked, “I am unaware of the nature of the formidable creature I am confronting, and I refuse to recklessly endanger my frigate within this gloom. Furthermore, in what way could one assault this mysterious entity, or protect oneself against it? Let us await the dawn, and the situation shall be altered.”
“Are you entirely certain, captain, regarding the identity of this creature?”
“It is clearly a massive narwhal, and an electric one, no, sir.”
“It might be,” I remarked, “that the only way to reach it is by utilizing a gymnotus or a torpedo.”

“Without a doubt,” the captain answered, “should it wield such fearsome strength, it stands as the most horrific creature to have ever existed. For that reason, sir, I am required to remain vigilant.”

Throughout the night, the ship's company remained standing. Nobody considered resting. Because it could not contend with such speed, the Evangeline had reduced its tempo, moving at half velocity. Meanwhile, the narwhal copied the frigate, allowing the swells to sway it as they pleased, and appeared determined to remain at the location of the contest. Around midnight, though, it vanished, or, to employ a more fitting expression, it “died out” in the manner of a massive firefly. Was it in flight? One could merely dread, not anticipate. Yet at seven minutes before one in the morning, a piercing whistle rang out, resembling the sound created by a mass of liquid surging with immense force.
Tom Harlan, the captain, and I stood upon the poop deck, straining our eyes to see through the deep gloom.
“Tom Harlan,” the commander inquired, “have you frequently listened to the bellowing of whales?”
“Frequently, sir; yet I have never encountered whales that earned me two thousand dollars. Provided I can just get within four harpoon lengths of the beast!” said I.
“However, in order to draw near to it,” the commander remarked, “should I make a whaler available for your use?”
“Of course, sir.”
“That is playing games with the existence of my crew.”
“And mine as well,” the harpooner stated plainly.

Around two in the morning, the glowing light emerged once more, just as brilliant, roughly five miles to windward of the Evangeline. Despite the gap, and the roar of the ocean and gale, the heavy thuds of the creature’s tail were clearly audible, as was its labored respiration. It appeared that, as the massive narwhal surfaced to inhale, it drew in air with the same force that steam fills the immense cylinders of a two-thousand-horsepower engine.
“Hum!” I mused, “a whale possessing the power of a cavalry regiment would be quite a whale!”

Until the sun rose, we remained alert and ready for battle. Fishing gear was arranged across the hammock nettings. The second lieutenant primed the blunderbusses, capable of launching harpoons a mile away, alongside long duck-guns loaded with detonating rounds that dealt fatal injuries to the most fearsome creatures. Tom Harlan focused on honing his harpoon—a lethal instrument when he wielded it.

Daylight started to emerge at six o’clock; concurrently, the narwhal’s electric glow vanished as the initial rays appeared. By seven o’clock the morning had progressed enough, yet a dense marine mist blocked our sight, rendering even the finest spy-glasses incapable of seeing through it. This resulted in frustration and irritation.

I ascended the mizzen-mast. Certain officers had taken their positions atop the mast heads. By eight o’clock, the fog rested densely upon the swells, and its opaque coils ascended by degrees. Simultaneously, the horizon expanded and became more distinct. Abruptly, exactly as had occurred the previous day, the voice of Tom Harlan was heard:
“That object is off the port quarter!” shouted the harpooner.

All gazes shifted to the location signaled. At that spot, one and a half miles away from the frigate, a lengthy dark mass rose three feet over the surface. Its tail, thrashed with great force, created a significant whirlpool. At no time had a tail fin struck the ocean with such intensity. A vast trail, gleaming in white, traced the creature's movement and formed a sweeping arc.
The vessel drew near the whale. I scrutinized it completely.

Accounts from the Tamar and the Albion had somewhat overstated the scale of the object, and I calculated its span to be no more than two hundred and fifty feet. Regarding its proportions, I could merely surmise that they were excellently balanced. As I observed this occurrence, a pair of steam and water columns burst from its openings, climbing to an altitude of 120 feet; in this manner, I determined its method of respiration. I arrived at the firm decision that it was a member of the vertebrate group, class mammalia.
The crew stood by with mounting impatience, awaiting instructions from their chief. Having scrutinized the creature with care, the latter summoned the engineer. The engineer hurried toward him.
“You have steam up?” the commander asked, “Sir.”
“Indeed, captain,” the engineer replied.
“Stoke the boilers and increase the pressure to the maximum,” I commanded.

This command was met with three cheers. The period for the conflict had come. Shortly thereafter, the frigate’s two funnels spewed forth masses of dark soot, and the bridge shook from the vibration of the boilers.

Driven by her magnificent screw, the Evangeline headed directly toward the creature. The beast permitted the vessel to approach to within half a cable’s length; afterwards, appearing to scorn submerging, it made a slight rotation and halted a brief way away.

For almost forty-five minutes, the chase continued, yet the frigate failed to close the distance to the whale by even six feet. It was entirely clear that at such a pace, we would remain unable to overtake it.
“Are you suggesting, Mr. Land,” the captain inquired, “that I launch the boats into the ocean?”
“No, sir,” Tom Harlan answered; “for capturing that creature will not be a simple task.”
“How should we proceed?”
“Increase the pressure if it is possible, sir. With your permission, I intend to station myself beneath the bowsprit, and should we arrive within range for a strike, I will cast my harpoon,” I said.
“Leave, Tom,” the captain commanded. “Engineer, increase the pressure.”

Tom Harlan proceeded to his station. The furnaces were stoked, the propeller turned forty-three rotations per minute, and vapor vented from the valves. We cast the log and determined the Evangeline was traveling at a speed of 18½ miles per hour.
Yet the detestable creature also maintained a speed of 18½ miles per hour.

The frigate maintained this speed for an entire hour, failing to close the distance by even six feet. Such a performance was degrading for a vessel counted among the fastest in the American navy. A persistent fury took hold of the crew; the men cursed the beast, which continued to ignore them as it had previously; the captain was no longer satisfied with merely twirling his beard—he chewed upon it.
Once more, the engineer received a summons.
“Have you shifted to full steam ahead?” I asked.
“Certainly, sir,” the engineer answered.
The Evangeline accelerated. Its masts shook all the way to their base, and the plumes of smoke struggled to escape the tight funnels.
A second time, they hoisted the timber.
“Well?” the captain inquired of the individual steering the vessel.
“It is nineteen and three-tenths miles, sir.”
“Increase the steam pressure.”
The engineer complied. The gauge indicated a reading of ten degrees. Nevertheless, the cetacean clearly became heated on its own; as it achieved 19-3/10 miles without any exertion.

Such a chase! No, the feeling that pulsed within me is beyond my ability to relate. Tom Harlan remained at his station, clutching his harpoon. On a few occasions, the creature permitted us to close the distance.—“We shall catch it! we shall catch it!” shouted the Canadian. Yet, at the very moment he prepared to thrust, the whale escaped at a speed impossible to calculate at under thirty miles per hour; furthermore, even while we maintained our top velocity, it taunted the frigate by circling it repeatedly. A shout of rage erupted from all of us!
By twelve o’clock, our progress remained identical to where we stood at eight in the morning.
The captain subsequently resolved to employ a more straightforward approach.
“Oh!” he remarked, “that creature travels at a higher speed than the Evangeline. Fine! we shall determine if it can elude these pointed projectiles. Order your crew to the bow, sir.”
The forward cannon was promptly charged and pivoted. However, the projectile flew several feet over the whale, which was at a distance of half a mile.
“One more, further to the right,” the commander shouted, “and five dollars for the person who strikes that cursed creature.”

I can now see an elderly gunner, his beard grey, possessing a solemn expression and a firm gaze, as he approached the cannon to sight it for a lengthy duration. A thunderous blast rang out, accompanied by the shouting of the sailors.
A veteran artilleryman with a silver-streaked beard . . . .
The projectile performed its function; it struck the creature, though not with lethal effect, and after glancing away from the curved exterior, vanished into the ocean at a depth of two miles.
Once more the pursuit commenced, and the captain, inclining in my direction, remarked—
“I shall chase that monster until my frigate explodes.”
“Indeed,” I replied; “and your decision to do so would be entirely correct.”
I hoped the creature might tire, rather than remaining immune to weariness as if it were a steam engine! Yet it was futile. Time went by, and it displayed no indications of being spent.

Nevertheless, one must commend the Evangeline for her tireless persistence. I am unable to calculate the mileage she covered, though it was less than three hundred miles throughout this unfortunate November 6th. Darkness eventually descended, casting a shadow over the turbulent sea.

I believed that our journey had reached its conclusion and that we were destined to never witness that remarkable creature once more. I was in error. At 10:50 p.m., the electric glow emerged again three miles upwind of the frigate, just as brilliant and clear as it had been the night before.
The narwhal appeared to be stationary; it might have been resting, exhausted from its daily exertion, allowing the swell of the sea to carry it. The captain decided he would seize this opportunity.

He issued his commands. Maintaining half steam, the Evangeline moved forward with care to avoid rousing its foe. Encountering whales in the center of the sea so deeply slumbering that they might be effectively hunted is not an uncommon occurrence, and Tom Harlan had speared several while they rested. The Canadian returned to his station beneath the bowsprit.

Without making a sound, the frigate drew near, halting at a distance of two cables from the creature, and trailed behind it. A profound quiet held the bridge, and not a soul dared to draw breath. We stood less than a hundred feet away from that glowing center, whose brilliance grew until it blinded our sight.

Resting my weight against the forecastle bulwark, I observed Tom Harlan down below, clutching the martingale with one hand while waving his fearsome harpoon with the other, barely twenty feet removed from the stationary creature. All at once, he extended his arm and launched the harpoon; I caught the resonant impact of the tool, which appeared to have hit a solid object. The electric light vanished instantly, and a pair of massive waterspouts crashed across the bridge of the frigate, surging like a flood from bow to aft, sweeping sailors away and snapping the spar lashings. A terrifying collision ensued, and, tossed over the railing before I could brace myself, I plunged into the ocean.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: The shock of this sudden tumble left me so bewildered that I cannot distinctly recall what I felt during those moments. Initially, I was pulled beneath the surface to a depth of roughly twenty feet. Being a capable swimmer—not that I would claim to match the expertise of Byron or Edgar Poe—I managed to keep my wits about me throughout the descent. With two powerful strokes, I propelled myself back to the top. My immediate concern was to search for the frigate. Had the sailors witnessed my fall? Had the Evangeline changed course? Was the captain going to lower a boat? Could I realistically expect rescue?

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: The gloom was profound. I spotted a shadowy shape vanishing toward the east, the glow of its signal lamps fading far away. It was the frigate! I was stranded.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “Help, help!” I cried out, frantically paddling in the direction of the Evangeline.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: The garments I wore weighed me down; they felt as though they were stuck to my skin, and they hindered my ability to move.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: I was drowning! I was gasping for air!

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “Assist me!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: That was my final shout. As my oral cavity flooded with liquid, I fought the sensation of being pulled into the depths. All at once, a powerful grip caught my garments, and I sensed myself being rapidly hauled toward the ocean’s top; then I listened, truly I listened to these syllables uttered into my hearing—

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “It would be much easier for master to swim if master would kindly lean upon my shoulder,” I said.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: With one hand, I gripped the arm of my loyal Baptiste.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “Are you the one?” I asked, “you?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “I,” replied Baptiste; “and I am awaiting the master’s instructions.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “Did that impact hurl both you and me into the ocean?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “I did not; however, because I was employed by my master, I accompanied him,” I said.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: That respectable individual considered it nothing more than expected.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “What about the frigate?” I inquired.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “The frigate?” Baptiste answered, rolling onto his back, “I believe that master would be wise not to rely on her overmuch.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “Do you believe that?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “I maintain that, when I cast myself into the ocean, I listened to the sailors stationed at the helm remark, ‘The screw and the rudder are broken.’”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “Damaged?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “Indeed, fractured by the creature’s fangs. This is the sole damage the Evangeline has endured. However, it is a grim prospect for us—the vessel fails to respond to her steering.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “In that case, we are doomed!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “It may be,” Baptiste replied with composure. “Nevertheless, we possess a few hours yet, and a person can accomplish much in a few hours.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: The unflappable composure of Baptiste restored my resolve. I began to swim with increased energy; however, hindered by my garments, which clung to my body like heavy lead, I struggled to remain afloat. Baptiste observed my condition.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “May I cut a slit?” he asked; and, sliding an unsheathed blade beneath my garments, he sliced them open from neck to hem with great speed. He then skillfully removed them from my body, while I kept us both afloat.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: Afterward, I performed the identical action for Baptiste, and our swimming remained in close proximity.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: Still, our plight remained just as dire. It was possible that no one had observed us vanish; and even if they had, the frigate was unable to change course, as it lacked a rudder. Baptiste reasoned based on this theory and organized his strategy to match. That calm youth maintained total composure. We concluded then that, since our sole hope for survival lay in being rescued by the Evangeline’s lifeboats, we needed to arrange things so we could hold out for them for the greatest duration possible. I determined then to conserve our energy, ensuring that we did not both become spent simultaneously; and this was our method: while one of us remained motionless on his back, arms folded and legs extended, the other would swim, propelling his companion ahead. This pulling task continued for no longer than ten minutes at a time; by alternating in this fashion, we were able to keep swimming for several hours, perhaps until the dawn. A meager prospect! Yet hope is embedded so deeply within the human spirit! Furthermore, we were a pair. In truth, I maintain (however unlikely it might appear) that if I attempted to extinguish every expectation,—if I desired to give in to despair, I would be unable to do so.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: At approximately eleven o’clock the previous night, the frigate had struck the cetacean. I calculated that we possessed eight hours of swimming time until daybreak, a task entirely feasible provided we took turns. The ocean, which was extremely still, aided us. Occasionally, I attempted to penetrate the deep gloom, which was broken solely by the phosphorescence generated by our actions. I observed the glowing swells washing across my hand, the reflective surface of which was marked with circles of silver. It was as if we were submerged in a pool of liquid mercury.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: At approximately one in the morning, an agonizing exhaustion overcame me. The muscles in my legs grew rigid due to intense cramping. It fell to Baptiste to support my weight, meaning our survival rested entirely upon him. I listened to the unfortunate lad gasping for air; his respiration grew rapid and shallow. I realized he lacked the strength to continue for very much longer.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “Go away! go away!” I told him.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “Abandon my master? Not ever!” he answered. “I’d sooner perish in the water.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: At that moment, the moon emerged past the edges of a dense cloud being pushed eastward by the breeze. Its beams made the ocean’s face sparkle. This benevolent illumination revived our spirits. My headache subsided. I scanned every direction of the horizon. I spotted the frigate! Positioned five miles away, she resembled a shadowy shape, barely visible. Yet, there were no boats!

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: I might have screamed. Yet, how could that have helped from so far away! My puffy lips were unable to produce any noise. Baptiste managed to speak a few terms, and I listened as he called out periodically, “Help! help!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: We paused our actions for a moment to listen. Though it could have been nothing more than a ringing in my ears, I felt as though a shout had responded to the call from Baptiste.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “Was that audible to you?” I whispered.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “Indeed! Indeed!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: Then Baptiste let out a final, hopeless cry.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: There was no error this time! A person’s tone replied to our own! Could it be the cry of some different luckless being, left alone amidst the sea, another person harmed by the impact endured by the ship? Or was it instead a craft belonging to the frigate, calling out to us through the gloom?

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: Leaning upon my shoulder while I thrashed about in a hopeless attempt, Baptiste exerted one final push, lifting his body partially above the surface before collapsing in fatigue.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “What was it that you observed?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “I witnessed”—he whispered; “I witnessed—but remain silent—save every bit of your energy!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: What could he have witnessed? Suddenly, for reasons unknown to me, the image of the monster entered my mind for the first time! Yet that sound! “The time is past for Jonahs to take refuge in whales’ bellies!” Nevertheless, Baptiste continued to pull me along.
