Occasionally, he lifted his head, peered ahead, and let out a shout of acknowledgment, which was answered by a voice drawing closer and closer. I barely perceived it. My energy was spent; my digits grew rigid; my grip provided no more assistance; my jaws, opening in a spasm, took in brine. A chill spread through me. I lifted my face one final time, and then I went under.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: Just then, a solid form collided with me. I gripped it tightly, and soon I sensed myself being pulled upward, reaching the water’s top, and feeling my lungs fail:—I lost consciousness.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: I surely regained consciousness before long, owing to the energetic friction applied to my body. My eyelids lifted slightly.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “Baptiste!” I whispered.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “Is the master summoning me?” inquired Baptiste.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: At that precise moment, illuminated by the fading glow of the moon as it descended toward the skyline, I spotted a countenance that did not belong to Baptiste and which I identified at once.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “Tom!” I shouted.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “The very one, sir, who is in pursuit of his reward!” the Canadian answered.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “Did the impact on the frigate toss you into the ocean?” asked I.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “Indeed, Professor; however, I possessed better luck than you, as I managed to secure a foothold nearly immediately on a drifting isle,” I said.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “A landmass?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “Or, to put it more accurately, upon our massive narwhal.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “Tom, provide an explanation!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “It was not long before I discovered the reason my harpoon failed to pierce its hide and became dull,” I said.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “Why, Tom, why?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “For the reason that, Professor, that creature is constructed from iron plating.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: The final remarks from the Canadian sparked an abrupt shift in my thoughts. I squirmed rapidly toward the summit of the creature, or thing, protruding partially from the sea, which acted as our sanctuary. I struck it with my foot. Clearly, it was a rigid, unyielding mass rather than the yielding material composing the frames of massive sea mammals. Yet, this firm exterior could be a skeletal shell, similar to those of prehistoric beasts; and I would be at liberty to categorize this creature as an amphibious reptile, akin to alligators or tortoises.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “Well, no!” the dark-colored surface beneath me felt sleek and burnished, lacking any scales. The impact created a ringing, metallic noise; and despite how unbelievable it sounds, I could almost claim it appeared to be constructed from bolted metal sheets.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: There was no question regarding it! This beast, this occurrence in nature that had baffled the scholarly community and had both defeated and deceived the minds of mariners across the two hemispheres, had to be acknowledged as an even more surprising event, given that it was merely a creation of man.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: There was no moment to be wasted, though. We rested atop the hull of a submarine vessel, which seemed to my eyes to resemble an enormous metallic fish. Tom Harlan had reached a firm conclusion regarding this. Baptiste and I had no choice but to concur with him.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: At that precise moment, a churning started toward the rear of this odd object (which was clearly driven by a propeller), and it commenced its motion. We barely managed to grasp the top section, which stood roughly seven feet above the surface, and fortunately its velocity remained low.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “Provided it moves on a level plane,” Tom Harlan mumbled, “I am content; however, should it decide to submerge, I would not value my existence at even a pair of straws.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: The Canadian could have spoken even more briefly. It grew truly vital to establish contact with the creatures, of whatever nature, confined within the vessel. I scoured the exterior for any opening, hatch, or man-hole—to employ a technical term—yet the rows of iron rivets, firmly hammered into the seams of the metal plating, remained distinct and consistent. Furthermore, the moon vanished at that moment, plunging us into complete obscurity.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: Finally, the lengthy night concluded. Because my memory is hazy, I am unable to detail every impression left upon me. I remember but a single detail. In the moments when the wind and ocean quieted, I imagined hearing faint noises repeatedly—a kind of fleeting melody created by orders being shouted. What, then, was the secret behind this underwater vessel, for which the entire globe unsuccessfully hunted an answer? What sort of creatures lived inside this peculiar ship? What sort of machine was responsible for its incredible velocity?

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: Dawn arrived. Although the morning fog enveloped us, it dissipated quickly. I prepared to inspect the hull, which created a sort of flat stage upon the deck, just as I sensed it slowly submerging.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: “Blast it all!” shouted Tom Harlan, while he struck the echoing metal. “Release, you unwelcoming scoundrels!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: The downward motion fortunately halted. All at once, a sound resembling metal machinery being forcefully shoved away echoed from inside the vessel. A single steel panel shifted, a male figure emerged, let out a strange shout, and vanished at once.

chapter_title: CHAPTER VII AN UNKNOWN SPECIES OF WHALE
text: A short while later, eight robust individuals, their features concealed by masks, emerged without a sound and pulled us into their imposing apparatus.

With the speed of a lightning bolt, this violent kidnapping was executed in a brutal fashion. My entire body trembled. Who were our captors? Surely a unique breed of pirates, traversing the ocean by their own methods.

The slender shutter had barely latched behind me before I was swallowed by the gloom. Because my vision had been blinded by the brightness outside, I could perceive nothing. I sensed my bare soles gripping the metal steps of a ladder. Tom Harlan and Baptiste, held fast, came down behind me. Once we reached the base of the ladder, a portal swung wide, then slammed closed behind us instantly.

There was no one else with us. I could not name the location, nor could I scarcely conceive of it. Everything was dark, and the blackness was so thick that, even following several minutes, my vision remained unable to detect the slightest hint of light.
In the interim, Tom Harlan, enraged by these occurrences, expressed his resentment without restraint.

“Confound it!” he exclaimed, “these are individuals who approach the Scotch expecting hospitality. They are barely not cannibals. I would not be astonished by such a thing, yet I maintain that they will not consume me without my objection.”
“Settle down, friend Tom, settle down,” Baptiste answered, in a low voice. “Refrain from shouting until you have been injured. Our situation is not entirely hopeless.”

“Hardly,” the Canadian answered pointedly, “though certainly close, in any case. The situation appears grim. Fortunately, I retain my bowie knife, and my vision remains sufficient to employ it. The initial pirate among these scoundrels who touches me——”

“Try to remain calm, Tom,” I told the harpooner, “and avoid jeopardizing our position with unnecessary aggression. Is it not possible that they might hear us out? It would be better if we attempted to determine our location.”

I felt my way forward. After five paces, I reached a wall of iron, constructed from riveted plates. Upon reversing my direction, I collided with a table made of wood, situated beside a collection of stools. A dense phormium mat covered the floorboards of this cell, muffling the sound of footsteps. No aperture for a window or door was visible on the plain walls. Baptiste, having circled in the opposite direction, encountered me, and we returned to the center of the cabin, which was roughly twenty feet by ten in size. Regarding the vertical clearance, Tom Harlan, notwithstanding his own significant stature, was unable to determine it.

Thirty minutes had elapsed with no improvement to our circumstances, at which point the heavy blackness was abruptly replaced by an intense brilliance. Our confinement was instantly illuminated—meaning it grew saturated with a radiant substance, so powerful that initially I was unable to endure it. Within its stark whiteness and potency, I identified that same electric glow which had circled the submarine boat as a spectacular display of phosphorescence. Having reflexively closed my eyes, I reopened them to discover that this source of light originated from a matte hemispherical fixture set into the ceiling of the room.
“Finally, visibility is restored,” shouted Tom Harlan, while he held a blade and braced himself for an attack.
“Indeed,” I replied; “yet our own identities remain a mystery to us.”
“The master should exercise patience,” remarked the composed Baptiste.

The cabin’s abrupt illumination permitted me to inspect the space in detail. It held nothing but five stools and a table. The hidden door appeared to be airtight. There was no sound. Everything within this vessel felt lifeless. Was it in motion, was it drifting upon the sea’s surface, or had it plunged into the abyss? I had no way of knowing.
The sound of bolts echoed, the entrance swung wide, and a pair of men emerged.

He possessed a short, heavily muscled frame with wide shoulders, sturdy limbs, a powerful head, a thick mane of black hair, and a dense moustache, accompanied by a sharp, piercing gaze and the lively spirit typical of those from Southern France.

A more thorough account of the second stranger is warranted. Any follower of Gratiolet or Engel could have interpreted his features as easily as a printed text. I immediately discerned his dominant traits: self-assurance, indicated by the way his head sat firmly upon his shoulders and the icy certainty in his dark gaze; composure, suggested by his somewhat pallid complexion, which betrayed a steady temperament; vigor, displayed through the swift twitching of his high forehead; and bravery, as his heavy respiration signaled significant pulmonary strength.

I could not determine if this individual was fifty or thirty-five years old. He possessed a tall stature, a broad brow, a direct nose, a sharply defined mouth, and lovely teeth, alongside slender, tapering hands that suggested a deeply sensitive nature. Without question, this gentleman was the most impressive example of a human being I had encountered. A distinct characteristic was his eyes, positioned quite a distance apart, which allowed him to observe almost a fourth of the landscape simultaneously.

This ability—(which I confirmed subsequently)—provided him with a visual scope significantly better than that of Tom Harlan. Whenever this unknown man focused on a target, his brows drew together, his expansive lids narrowed to focus his sight, and he appeared to be enlarging items diminished by remoteness, as if he were penetrating those expanses of water that seemed so impenetrable to us, and as if he were discerning the absolute bottom of the oceans.

Wearing caps fashioned from sea otter fur and footwear crafted from seal skin, the pair of strangers wore garments of a distinct weave that permitted their limbs to move without restriction. The loftier individual, clearly the leader of the vessel, scrutinized us intently while remaining silent; he then pivoted toward his associate and conversed in a language I did not recognize. It was a resonant, melodic, and supple tongue, in which the vowels appeared capable of a wide range of emphasis.
My companion responded with a slight movement of his head, followed by a few entirely unintelligible syllables. He then appeared to be asking me something with his gaze.
My response was delivered in fluent French, stating that I lacked knowledge of his tongue; yet he appeared unable to grasp my meaning, and my predicament grew increasingly awkward.
“Should master relate our tale,” Baptiste remarked, “it is possible these gentlemen might grasp a few terms.”

I started recounting the story of our exploits, enunciating every sound with precision and leaving out not a solitary particular. I declared our identities and positions, presenting individually Professor Delorme, his attendant Baptiste, and the harpooner master Tom Harlan.

With intense focus, the individual possessing gentle, tranquil eyes heard me out in silence, indeed with courtesy; yet his expression betrayed no sign that he had grasped my account. Upon my conclusion, he uttered nothing. A single option persisted: to converse in English. It was possible they were familiar with this nearly global tongue. I possessed knowledge of it, similar to my grasp of German—sufficient to peruse it with ease, though inadequate for speaking it with precision. Regardless, we had to ensure our meaning was conveyed.
“Proceed when it is your opportunity,” I remarked to the harpooner; “utilize your finest Anglo-Saxon, and attempt to perform with more skill than I.”
Tom declined to excuse himself and took up our tale once more.

Much to his annoyance, the harpooner appeared to have been no more successful at being understood than I was. The visitors remained motionless. Clearly, they grasped neither the tongue of Arago nor that of Faraday.
Feeling deeply mortified, and having already depleted all our conversational options to no avail, I remained uncertain of how to proceed, at which point Baptiste said—
“Should master allow it, I shall tell the story in German,” I said.

Yet, notwithstanding the refined vocabulary and polished pronunciation of the speaker, the German tongue failed to achieve its purpose. Finally, feeling bewildered, I attempted to recall my earliest studies and recount our experiences using Latin, though this met with equal futility. Once this final endeavor proved fruitless, the pair of foreigners traded a few remarks in their mysterious dialect and withdrew.
The entrance closed.

“It is an infamous shame,” cried Tom Harlan, who erupted for the twentieth occasion. “We address those scoundrels in French, English, German, and Latin, yet not a single one possesses the courtesy to reply!”
“Settle down,” I told the hasty Tom, “getting angry won’t help.”
“However, do you perceive, Professor,” our irritable associate answered, “that we are certainly going to perish from starvation inside this metal prison?”
“Bah!” Baptiste remarked with philosophical detachment; “there is still time for us to endure.”
“I told my companions, “do not lose heart. We have faced more dire circumstances previously. Please grant me the courtesy of delaying your judgment regarding the captain and sailors of this vessel.”
“I have reached a conclusion,” Tom Harlan answered, with a sharp tone. “Those men are scoundrels.”
“Excellent! and which nation are you from?”
“Out of the territory of scoundrels!”

“My brave Tom, that land is not explicitly marked on the global map; yet I concede that the origin of the two foreigners is difficult to ascertain. They are definitely not English, French, or German. Still, I suspect the captain and his associate originated from southern regions. They possess southern blood. Nevertheless, I am unable to determine from their looks if they are Spaniards, Turks, Arabians, or Indians. Regarding their speech, it is entirely unintelligible.”
“The drawback of lacking knowledge of every tongue exists,” said Baptiste, “or the drawback of lacking a single common language.”

The door swung wide as he uttered those remarks. A steward walked in. He carried garments for us, consisting of coats and trousers fashioned from an unfamiliar material. I hurried to put mine on, and my associates did the same. Throughout that interval, the steward—who appeared to be mute, and possibly unable to hear—set the table and placed three plates upon it.
“Something like this,” remarked Baptiste.
“Pah!” remarked the bitter harpooner, “what do you imagine is served for meals in this place? Liver of tortoise, sliced shark, and steaks of beef from sea-dogs.”
“It remains to be determined,” said Baptiste.

Bell metal plates were set upon the table, and we sat down. We were clearly dealing with a civilized group, and if not for the electric illumination bathing us, I might have imagined myself in the dining hall of the Adelphi Hotel in Liverpool or the Grand Hotel in Paris. I have to note, though, that there was no wine or bread. The water was crisp and pure, yet it remained water, which did not please Tom Harlan. Of the platters served to us, I identified various fish prepared with care; yet regarding others, despite their quality, I could offer no judgment, nor could I identify their origin, be it vegetable or animal. The dining set was refined and displayed impeccable style. Every implement—fork, spoon, knife, and dish—bore an engraved letter accompanied by a motto above it, of which this is an exact facsimile:—
ALWAYS IN MOTION N.
Without a doubt, the letter N served as the starting character for the moniker of that mysterious individual who held authority deep beneath the ocean.

Baptiste and Tom gave little thought to the matter. They consumed their meal, and I followed suit. Furthermore, I felt confident regarding our future; it appeared clear that those who hosted us would not permit us to perish from starvation.
Yet, all things conclude, and everything fades, including the cravings of individuals who have gone fifteen hours without food. Once our hunger was sated, a heavy drowsiness descended upon us.
“I shall rest soundly, by my faith!” said Baptiste.
“I will do the same,” answered Tom Harlan.

Both my associates lay out upon the rug of the cabin, falling into slumber quickly. As for me, an excess of ideas swarmed my mind, a surplus of unanswerable inquiries weighed on me, and a multitude of notions held my eyelids partially lifted. Where had we arrived? What odd force propelled us forward? I sensed—or perhaps imagined I sensed—the vessel descending toward the deepest ocean floors. Terrifying visions plagued me; within those enigmatic retreats, I beheld a realm of unfamiliar creatures, and this underwater craft appeared to be one of their number, breathing, shifting, and just as menacing. Eventually, my intellect quieted, my thoughts drifted into indistinct oblivion, and I promptly dropped into a heavy sleep.

I have no idea how much time passed while we slumbered; however, the duration had to be significant, as we felt entirely recovered from our exhaustion. I was the initial one to stir. The others remained motionless, still lying extended in their nook.

Barely awakened from my rather firm bed, I sensed my intellect liberated and my thoughts lucid. I proceeded to conduct a careful inspection of our chamber. Within, nothing had altered. The confinement remained a confinement, and the captives, captives. Nevertheless, while we slumbered, the steward had removed the items from the table. I struggled to inhale. The dense atmosphere appeared to weigh upon my chest. Even though the room was spacious, we had clearly used up a significant portion of the oxygen held within it. In fact, every individual utilizes, over the course of one hour, the oxygen found in upwards of 176 pints of air, and this air, filled (as it was then) with an almost identical volume of carbonic acid, turns impossible to breathe.

The atmosphere inside our confinement, and indeed throughout the entire submarine boat, required replenishment. This situation prompted a query within me. In what manner would the captain of this aquatic residence go about it? Might he procure oxygen through chemical reactions, utilizing heat to extract it from chlorate of potash while neutralizing carbonic acid with caustic potash? Or, perhaps he would opt for the more practical, cost-effective, and therefore likely method of surfacing to inhale, much like a cetacean, thereby refreshing the air supply for another day?

Actually, I had already been forced to quicken my breathing to extract the meager oxygen present in this chamber, at which point a flow of clean air, scented with salty vapors, unexpectedly revived me. It was a bracing ocean wind, heavy with iodine. I parted my lips broadly, and my lungs filled with the crisp elements.

Simultaneously, I sensed the vessel swaying. Clearly, the iron-plated monster had merely ascended to the sea’s top to inhale, in the manner of whales. Through this, I discovered the method of aerating the boat.

Once I had breathed in this atmosphere without restraint, I looked for the duct that brought the welcome breeze to us, and it did not take me long to locate it. A ventilator was positioned over the entrance, and through it, currents of clean air replenished the depleted oxygen within the chamber.
As I conducted my examinations, Tom and Baptiste stirred simultaneously, roused by the restorative breeze. They wiped their eyelids, extended their limbs, and stood up immediately.
“Was the master’s sleep restful?” inquired Baptiste, maintaining his customary courtesy.
“All right, my courageous lad. And what about you, Mr. Land?”
“Deeply, Professor. However, I am uncertain of my accuracy; it feels as though a maritime wind is blowing!”
There was no possibility of misidentifying a sailor, so I recounted every event that had occurred while the Canadian was slumbering.
“Excellent!” he remarked; “that explains the bellowing sounds we detected, back when the alleged narwhal spotted the Evangeline.”
“Indeed, Master Harlan; it paused to inhale.”
“Except, M. Delorme, I am uncertain of the hour, provided it is not time for dinner.”
“Is it dinner-time, my dear friend? You ought to call it breakfast-time instead, as we have undoubtedly entered a new day,” I said.
“Thus,” remarked Baptiste, “have we been asleep for twenty-four hours?”
“That is how I see it.”
“I shall not argue with your point,” Tom Harlan answered. “Whether it is breakfast or dinner, the steward will be greeted gladly, no matter what he serves.”
“I suppose our hunger has arrived before the time for dinner, Master Harlan, and we are required to follow the regulations of the ship.”

“That is precisely your way, friend Baptiste,” Tom remarked, with impatience. “You remain perpetually serene, never losing your composure; you would offer gratitude prior to a meal, and expire from starvation before uttering a single grievance!”

The hour grew late, and our hunger had become intense; yet, the steward failed to show himself. It seemed an excessive amount of time to abandon us, provided their motives were truly sincere. Driven by the pangs of starvation, Tom Harlan grew increasingly furious; and, despite his vow, I feared a violent outburst the moment he encountered a member of the crew.

Tom Harlan’s irritability grew for an additional two hours; he wept and bellowed, yet to no avail. The partitions remained unresponsive. Within the vessel, not a single noise could be detected: everything was as quiet as the grave. It stayed motionless, as I would have perceived the vibrating stir of the frame caused by the propeller. Submerged deep beneath the waves, it pertained to the world above no more:—this stillness was terrifying.
Terror gripped me, Baptiste remained composed, and Tom Harlan bellowed.
At that moment, a sound emerged from the exterior. Footfalls echoed against the metallic floor plates. The latches rotated, the entrance swung wide, and the steward arrived.
The Canadian had already cast him to the ground and seized him by the neck before I was able to spring ahead to intervene. Beneath the pressure of his mighty hand, the steward gasped for air.

Baptiste had begun attempting to detach the harpooner’s grip from the person he was nearly strangling, and I prepared to rush to their aid, but I was abruptly frozen in place upon catching these words in French—
“Hush, Master Harlan; and you, Professor, would you kindly attend to me?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: The person in charge of the ship uttered those words.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: Tom Harlan stood up abruptly upon hearing these remarks. Following a signal from his superior, the steward stumbled away, appearing almost choked; yet the captain’s authority aboard the vessel was so absolute that not a single movement revealed the anger this individual surely harbored for the Canadian. Baptiste, drawn in against his own will, and I, stunned, remained quiet while anticipating how this encounter would conclude.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: Propped up by the table’s edge, the commander kept his arms crossed while observing us with intense scrutiny. Was he pausing before he continued? Was he feeling remorse for the French phrases he had recently uttered? It seemed quite possible.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: Following a brief period of quiet, during which none of us dared to speak, “Gentlemen,” he remarked, his tone steady and sharp, “I have an equal command of French, English, German, and Latin. Consequently, I might have replied to you when we initially met, yet I preferred to observe you and deliberate. The accounts provided by every one of you, which matched in all essential details, persuaded me of who you are. I am now aware that fate has placed before me M. Étienne Delorme, Professor of Natural History at the Museum of Paris, who is on a scientific mission in foreign lands, Baptiste, his attendant, and Tom Harlan, a native of Canada, who serves as a harpooner on the United States of America navy frigate Evangeline.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: I nodded in agreement. The commander had not asked me a question, so I offered no reply. He spoke with total comfort and lacked any trace of an accent. His phrasing was polished, his vocabulary precise, and his command of language was extraordinary. Even so, I did not identify him as a compatriot.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: In this manner, he persisted with the discussion:

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “You have surely assumed, sir, that I have waited a great while to return for this second call. The explanation is that, once your identity was established, I desired to consider carefully how I should behave regarding you. I have been very uncertain. Highly vexing events have placed you before a person who has severed every human connection. You have arrived to disturb my life.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “By accident!” I remarked.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “Unintentionally?” the stranger answered, his tone growing slightly louder; “was it by accident that the Evangeline chased me across every ocean? Was it by accident that you boarded this frigate? Was it by accident that your cannonballs bounced away from my ship’s armor? Was it by accident that Mr. Tom Harlan hit me with his harpoon?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: I perceived a suppressed annoyance within those remarks. Yet, I possessed a perfectly logical response to such accusations, and I delivered it.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “Sir,” I remarked, “surely you are unaware of the debates that have occurred regarding you throughout America and Europe. You remain uninformed that various mishaps, resulting from impacts with your submersible craft, have stirred intense public sentiment across both continents. I shall pass over the countless theories through which people attempted to account for the baffling occurrence that you alone hold the key to. Nevertheless, you must realize that, by tracking you across the vast Pacific, the Evangeline operated under the conviction that it was hunting a formidable sea-beast, which had to be cleared from the waters at all costs.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: The commander’s mouth twisted into a faint smirk: subsequently, with a more composed voice—

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “M. Delorme,” he answered, “do you have the courage to claim that your frigate would not have been just as likely to chase and fire upon a submarine vessel as it would a monster?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: I felt mortified by this inquiry, since Captain Hallett surely would not have paused. He might have considered it an obligation to annihilate such a device, just as he would a massive narwhal.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “Do you grasp, then, sir,” the stranger went on, “that I possess the authority to regard you as foes?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: I intentionally remained silent. What purpose would there be in debating this suggestion, given that violence could easily dismantle the most sound logic?

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “For a while, I wavered,” the commander went on; “I was under no compulsion to offer you shelter. Were I to decide to part ways with you, I would gain nothing by encountering you once more; I might set you on the deck of this craft that has acted as your sanctuary, submerge it, and erase any memory of your presence. Would that not be my prerogative?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “That could be the prerogative of a barbarian,” I replied, “yet it is not the privilege of a cultured individual.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “Professor,” the commander answered with haste, “I am not what you would term a civilised man! I have severed all ties with society, for motives that I alone possess the right to judge. Consequently, I do not follow its regulations, and I request that you never mention them in my presence again!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: The statement was made clearly. An ignited spark of scorn and fury appeared within the eyes of the Unknown, and I caught a fleeting view of a horrific history in this individual’s existence. He had not merely placed himself outside the boundaries of societal statutes, but he had rendered himself autonomous from them, liberated in the most absolute sense of the term, entirely outside their grasp! Who, therefore, might venture to chase him deep beneath the ocean, when, upon its crest, he challenged every effort directed toward him? What ship might endure the impact of his submarine monitor? What armor, regardless of its density, might survive the strikes of his ram? No person could require him to justify his deeds; the Almighty, provided he held faith in one—his own moral sense, provided he possessed one—remained the only arbiters to whom he was accountable.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: While the unknown individual remained quiet, preoccupied, and seemingly lost within his own thoughts, these musings darted through my brain. I observed him with a blend of trepidation and fascination, much like the way Œdipus surely looked upon the Sphinx.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: Following a fairly extended period of quiet, the commander picked up the discussion again.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “I have wavered,” he stated, “yet I have considered that my own concerns could perhaps align with the compassion that all people deserve. You are to stay upon my vessel, as destiny has placed you here. You shall be at liberty; and, in return for this freedom, I will require but one solitary stipulation. Your pledge of honour to abide by it is enough.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “Talk, sir,” I replied. “I assume this term is something a gentleman of integrity can agree to?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “Indeed, sir; it is the following. It may be that some occurrences, which cannot be anticipated, will force me to confine you to your quarters for a period of hours or perhaps days. Since I wish to avoid force at all costs, I look for a submissive compliance from you, above all others. By proceeding in this manner, I assume full accountability: I release you of all blame, as I render it impossible for you to witness that which should remain unseen. Do you agree to these terms?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: Afterwards, occurrences transpired aboard the vessel that were, to put it mildly, peculiar, and which should remain hidden from those not situated outside the boundaries of conventional societal regulations. Of the various shocks the days ahead held in store for me, this one might well prove to be among the most significant.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “We agree,” I replied; “however, I request your consent, sir, to pose a single inquiry to you—just one.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “Talk, mister.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “You claimed that we ought to possess liberty while on the vessel.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “Totally.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “What, I inquire of you, is your definition of this liberty?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “Only the freedom to depart, to arrive, to witness, and to watch everything that occurs here—except in infrequent situations—the freedom, in essence, that my associates and I possess ourselves.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: It was clear that our mutual comprehension was lacking.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “Excuse me, sir,” I continued, “but this freedom is merely the same allowance every captive possesses to walk within his cell. It is not enough for us.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “It will have to be enough for you, though.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “How! are we to give up all hope of ever beholding our homeland, our companions, our kin once more?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “Indeed, sir. However, casting off that intolerable earthly burden that people mistake for freedom is possibly less agonizing than you imagine.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “Well,” Tom Harlan cried out, “I shall never pledge my word of honour that I will not attempt to flee.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “I never requested your promise of integrity, Master Harlan,” the commander replied, with coldness.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “Sir,” I answered, my temper rising against my will, “you are misusing your position regarding us; it is an act of cruelty.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “No, sir, it is mercy. You are my captives of war. I am holding you, even though I could, with a single command, cast you into the abyss of the sea. You assaulted me. You arrived to uncover a mystery that no human being on earth is permitted to fathom—the mystery of my entire life. And you imagine that I intend to return you to that realm which must never again hear of me? Never! By keeping you here, it is not you that I am watching—it is myself,” I said.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: Such language signaled a decision reached by the commander, one that no reasoning could alter.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “Therefore, sir,” I replied, “are you offering us nothing but the alternative of living or dying?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “Simply.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “To a query posed in such a manner, I have no response,” I stated. “However, we are under no obligation of integrity to the captain of this ship.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “There are zero, sir,” the Unknown replied.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: Next, using a softer voice, he went on—

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “Allow me to conclude my remarks to you. I am acquainted with you, M. Delorme. It is possible that you and your associates shall not find yourselves aggrieved by the fortune that has linked your destinies to mine. Within the collection of volumes that I study most frequently, you will discover the treatise you authored regarding ‘the depths of the sea.’ I have perused it many times. You pursued your research as extensively as earthly knowledge allowed. Yet you remain ignorant of the whole—you have not witnessed everything. Therefore, Professor, I assure you that you will not lament the duration spent aboard my vessel. You are about to explore a realm of wonders.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: The commander’s statement impacted me deeply. I must admit it. My vulnerability had been struck; momentarily, I lost sight of the fact that pondering such magnificent topics did not justify sacrificing my freedom. Furthermore, I relied on the time to come to settle this serious matter. Therefore, I simply replied—

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “How should I refer to you?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “I am merely Captain Sorel to you,” the commander answered, “and you and your fellow travelers are simply the passengers of the Meridian to me.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: Captain Sorel summoned someone. A steward arrived. The captain issued his instructions to him in that odd tongue that I was unable to comprehend. Afterward, pivoting to face the Canadian and Baptiste—

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “There is a meal prepared for you in your quarters,” he stated. “Kindly accompany this individual.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “Our morning meal is prepared, M. Delorme. Allow me to guide you.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “Captain, I am at your service.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: I trailed behind Captain Sorel, and upon crossing the threshold, I discovered a corridor illuminated by electric bulbs, much like the midsection of a vessel. Once we had walked twelve yards, another door swung open in my path.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: Afterward, I walked into a dining-hall, appointed and adorned with austere elegance. At both ends of the chamber were tall oak sideboards featuring ebony inlays, and their ledges held a shimmering display of priceless china, porcelain, and glassware. The tableware gleamed under the glow cast by the radiant ceiling, and the illumination was diffused and mellowed by fine works of art.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: A table, lavishly prepared, stood in the middle of the chamber. Captain Sorel pointed to the seat I was meant to take.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: A specific quantity of plates made up the morning meal, all of which contained items provided solely by the ocean; I remained unaware of what several of these were or how they had been cooked. I admitted their quality, though they possessed a strange taste that I quickly grew used to. It seemed to me that these various foods contained a high concentration of phosphorus, leading me to conclude that they surely came from the sea.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: Captain Sorel gazed in my direction. Although I posed no inquiries, he discerned what I was thinking and voluntarily provided the responses to the queries I was eager to put to him.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “Most of these meals are unfamiliar to you,” he remarked to me. “Nevertheless, you can eat them safely. They are nutritious and healthy. I have long since given up terrestrial food, and I am currently never sick. My crew, who are in good health, consume these same provisions.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “Thus,” I remarked, “every one of these food items originates from the ocean?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “Indeed, Professor, the ocean provides for every one of my needs. At times, I trail my nets behind me, pulling them back in on the verge of snapping. Occasionally, I pursue prey within this realm, which seems beyond human reach, and I stalk the creatures living in my underwater woods. My herds, much like the livestock of Neptune’s ancient keepers, feed without alarm across the vast meadows of the sea. I possess an expansive estate there, which I tend to personally, and which is perpetually seeded by the palm of the Maker of all existence,” I said.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “I am able to grasp quite clearly, sir, that your nets provide superior fish for your meals; I am also able to grasp that you pursue sea creatures within your underwater woods; however, I am unable to grasp in any way how a morsel of flesh, regardless of its size, could appear on your menu,” said I.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “This, which you consider to be meat, Professor, is actually nothing but turtle fillet. You will also find some dolphin livers here, which you mistake for pork ragout. My cook is a skillful man, who is excellent at preparing these diverse marine offerings. Try each of these plates. Here is a holothuria preserve, which a Malay would claim is unmatched globally; here is a cream, for which the milk was provided by cetacea, and the sugar by the large fucus of the North Sea; and finally, allow me to present you with some anemone preserve, which rivals the most exquisite fruits,” said I.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: Driven by inquisitiveness rather than expertise, I sampled the fare, all the while being captivated by the remarkable tales shared by Captain Sorel.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “Do you find the ocean agreeable, Captain?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “Indeed; I adore it! The ocean is all things. It blankets seven-tenths of the earth’s surface. Its exhalation is clean and invigorating. It is a vast wasteland, yet one is never solitary there, for one senses existence pulsing everywhere. The sea is merely the manifestation of a miraculous and otherworldly being. It is composed entirely of affection and passion; it is the ‘Living Infinite,’ as one of your poets remarked. Truly, Professor, Nature reveals herself within it through her three realms: mineral, vegetable, and animal. The ocean serves as the great storehouse of Nature. The world commenced with the sea, so to speak; and who can say if it might not conclude with it? Within it lies ultimate peace. The ocean is not property of tyrants. On its crest, humans may persist in enforcing unfair statutes, warring, slaughtering each other, and being consumed by earthly atrocities. Yet at a depth of thirty feet, their dominion terminates, their sway is extinguished, and their authority vanishes. Oh! sir, reside—reside within the heart of the waves! Only there is liberty! There I acknowledge no superiors! There I am liberated!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: Captain Sorel abruptly fell quiet during this display of fervor, which had previously swept him off his feet. He walked back and forth for several instants, visibly troubled. After that, he grew composed, recovered his usual icy demeanor, and pivoted in my direction—

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “At this moment, Professor,” he remarked, “should you desire to cross the Meridian, my services are available to you.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: Captain Sorel stood up. I went after him. A set of two doors, fashioned into the rear of the dining-room, swung wide, and I stepped into a chamber matching the size of the one I had recently left.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: The room was a library. Tall cabinets, crafted from black violet ebony and decorated with brass inlays, held a vast quantity of matching volumes upon their expansive shelves. These units mirrored the contour of the space, ending near the floor in massive, curved divans upholstered in brown leather, designed for maximum ease. Lightweight, adjustable desks that could be slid back and forth as needed provided a place to support a book during study. Positioned in the middle was a colossal table strewn with pamphlets and a selection of newspapers that were already dated. Electric illumination bathed the entire area, emanating from four matte globes partially embedded within the ceiling’s ornamental scrolls. I gazed upon this cleverly arranged chamber with genuine wonder, finding it difficult to trust my own sight.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “Captain Sorel,” I remarked to my host, as he collapsed onto one of the sofas, “this collection of books would be a credit to many a palace on the continent, and I am truly amazed to think that it accompanies you to the ocean floor.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “In what location might a person discover more profound isolation or stillness, Professor?” answered Captain Sorel. “Was your research at the Museum able to provide you with such absolute tranquility?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “No, sir; and I have to admit that it is quite a meager collection compared to your own. You surely possess six or seven thousand books in this place.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “Twelve thousand, M. Delorme. These represent the sole connections tethering me to the globe. However, I finished with society the moment my Meridian submerged for the initial occasion under the waves. On that date, I acquired my final books, my final brochures, my final journals, and since then I prefer to believe that humanity has ceased to contemplate or compose. These volumes, Professor, are available for your needs as well, and you are welcome to utilize them without restriction.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: I expressed my gratitude to Captain Sorel before ascending to the library’s bookcases. Volumes concerning literature, morals, and science were plentiful in all tongues; yet, I failed to spot a solitary text regarding political economy; that particular topic seemed to be entirely forbidden. Oddly, these books were placed in a disorganized fashion, regardless of the language of their composition; this chaotic collection suggested that the Captain of the Meridian had perused, without preference, whichever books he happened to select.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “I am grateful to you for granting me access to this library,” I remarked to the Captain. “It holds scientific riches, and I intend to make good use of them.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “This chamber serves as more than just a library,” Captain Sorel said, “it functions as a smoking-room as well.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “A smoking-room!” I exclaimed. “So it is permitted to smoke aboard?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “Of course.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “In that case, sir, I must conclude that you have maintained contact with Havannah.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “None at all,” the Captain replied. “Take this cigar, M. Delorme; even if it did not originate in Havannah, you shall find it agreeable, provided you are a judge of such things.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: Accepting the cigar that was presented to me, I noted that while its form brought to mind those from London, it appeared to be crafted from golden leaves. I ignited it using a small brazier held up by a graceful bronze stalk, inhaling the initial puffs with the pleasure of a tobacco enthusiast who had been deprived for forty-eight hours.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “It is superb, yet it is not tobacco.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “No!” replied the Captain, “this tobacco originates neither from the East nor from Havannah. It is a variety of nicotine-rich sea-weed that the ocean supplies me with, though rather infrequently.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: Just then, Captain Sorel unlatched a portal positioned across from the one I had utilized to gain access to the library, and I stepped inside a vast parlor illuminated with brilliance.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: The chamber was an expansive quadrilateral, measuring thirty feet in length, eighteen in breadth, and fifteen in height. A glowing overhead surface, adorned with delicate arabesques, cast a gentle, bright illumination across every wonder amassed within this gallery. Indeed, it functioned as a museum, where a brilliant and lavish touch had assembled the full bounty of nature and craftsmanship, arranged with the creative disarray characteristic of an artist’s workspace.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: Along the walls, which were draped in austere tapestry, hung thirty high-quality paintings, each in a matching frame and divided by vivid curtains. I observed numerous priceless pieces, most of which I had previously appreciated within European private galleries and art displays. The various traditions of the classical painters were showcased through a Raphael Madonna, a Leonardo da Vinci Virgin, a Corregio nymph, a Titan woman, a Veronese Adoration, a Murillo Assumption, a Holbein portrait, a Velasquez monk, a Ribera martyr, a Rubens fair, a pair of Teniers Flemish landscapes, a trio of small “genre” works by Gerard Dow, Metsu, and Paul Potter, two examples by Géricault and Prudhon, and several maritime scenes by Backhuysen and Vernet. Included among the contemporary artists’ creations were canvases signed by Delacroix, Ingres, Decamps, Troyon, Meissonier, Daubigny, and others; furthermore, exquisite marble and bronze sculptures, modeled after the most excellent ancient works, were positioned on stands in the room’s corners. Wonder, just as the Captain of the Meridian had foretold, was starting to overcome me.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “Professor,” this peculiar individual remarked, “you really ought to pardon the informal manner of my greeting, as well as the disarray of this chamber.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “I perceive you are an artist,” I replied, “though I do not ask your identity, sir.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “A mere novice, nothing beyond that, sir. In the past, I took pleasure in gathering these exquisite pieces fashioned by human hands. I pursued them with hunger and hunted them down tirelessly, and I managed to amass a collection of significant worth. These represent the final mementos I possess from a realm that has ceased to exist for me. To my perspective, your contemporary creators are already ancient; they possess a history spanning two or three millennia; I merge them all together in my thoughts. True masters are ageless.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “What about these composers?” I inquired, gesturing toward several compositions by Weber, Rossini, Mozart, Beethoven, Haydn, Meyerbeer, Hérold, Wagner, Auber, Gounod, and various others, which were strewn across a substantial mechanical piano that took up one of the parlor’s wall sections.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “These musicians,” answered Captain Sorel, “are Orpheus’s peers; because within the recollections of the departed, every distinction of time is erased; and I am deceased, Professor; just as deceased as those among your companions currently resting six feet beneath the soil!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: Captain Sorel remained quiet, appearing absorbed in a deep daydream. I studied him with intense curiosity, quietly examining the peculiar look upon his face. Resting his elbow on the corner of an expensive mosaic table, he did not perceive me anymore—my existence had slipped from his mind.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: I refrained from interrupting this daydream, and persisted in examining the oddities that adorned this parlor.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: The most valuable marine specimens ever displayed to a scientist were organized and tagged beneath refined glass enclosures, secured by copper fasteners. The joy I felt as a professor can be imagined.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: The section housing the zoophytes displayed the most intriguing examples from the two categories of polypi and echinodermes. Within the initial category, the tubipores, were fan-shaped gorgones, Syrian soft sponges, Moluccan ises, pennatules, a magnificent virgularia from the seas of Norway, multicolored unbellulairæ, alcyonariæ, and an entire array of madrepores—which Milne Edwards, my master, has categorized with such skill—amongst which I took note of some exquisite flabellinæ oculinæ from the Island of Bourbon, the “Neptune’s car” of the Antilles, and magnificent coral varieties; in summary, every type of those fascinating polypi that construct entire islands, which shall eventually grow into continents. Regarding the echinodermes, noted for their spiny coverings, the asteri, sea-stars, pantacrinæ, comatules, astérophons, echini, holothuri, and others, each served as a comprehensive specimen for this group.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: Any conchyliologist feeling even slightly anxious would surely have collapsed in the presence of other, more crowded displays containing the mollusc specimens. This collection held priceless worth, and I lack the time to provide a detailed account. From these, I shall list from recollection only the graceful royal hammer-fish from the Indian Ocean, featuring vivid white markings against a base of red and brown; an imperial spondyle, vibrant in hue and covered in sharp points, which is seldom seen in European museums—(I valued this piece at a minimum of £1000); a standard hammer-fish from the waters of New Holland, which is notoriously hard to obtain; exotic buccardia originating in Senegal; delicate white bivalves so thin that a mere puff of air could break them like soap-bubbles; various types of the aspergillum from Java, a sort of lime-based tube bordered by foliage-like ridges, which is often a subject of argument among collectors; an entire range of trochi, including some yellowish-green ones from American waters, others of a reddish-brown tint hailing from Australia, and still others from the Gulf of Mexico, noted for their overlapping shells; stellari gathered in the Southern Seas; and finally, the most uncommon of all, the superb spur of New Zealand; along with every sort of refined and brittle shell that has been properly classified by scientific study.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: Distributed across individual sections lay strings of pearls of immense splendor, casting back the glow of the electric lamps in tiny glimmers of flame; rose-hued pearls, harvested from the pinna-marina in the Red Sea; emerald pearls from the haliotyde iris; gold, azure, and ebony pearls, those strange creations of various molluscs from all the seas, along with specific mussels found in northern streams; and finally, a few pieces of priceless worth collected from the most uncommon pintadines. A number of these pearls exceeded the size of a pigeon’s egg, matching or exceeding the value of the gem Tavernier the voyager traded to the Shah of Persia for three millions, and they outshone the pearl owned by the Imaum of Muscat, which I had previously considered to be without equal globally.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: Consequently, calculating the worth of this assortment was entirely out of the question. Captain Sorel surely spent millions to obtain these diverse items, and I was pondering the origin of the funds he utilized to indulge his passion for gathering them, when these words broke my train of thought—

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “Are you inspecting my collection of shells, Professor? They are undoubtedly fascinating to a scientist; yet they possess a much deeper allure for me, as I gathered every single one personally, and there is no ocean across the entire world that I have not explored.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “I am able to grasp, Captain, the joy found in roaming among these bounties. You belong to the group of individuals who have gathered their own valuables. No gallery in Europe holds an assortment of marine yields like this one. Yet, if I spend all my wonder on these items, I will have nothing remaining for the ship that holds them. I have no desire to investigate your private matters; however, I must admit that this Meridian, along with the energy source held within, the mechanisms that allow its operation, and the potent force driving it, all stir my interest to an extreme degree. I notice hanging upon the partitions of this chamber devices for which I do not know the purpose.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “In my personal quarters, Professor, you shall discover these identical devices, and I will be delighted to demonstrate how they function. However, please accompany me now to view the stateroom designated for you. It is necessary that you observe the manner in which you will be lodged aboard the Meridian,” I said.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: I trailed behind Captain Sorel, as he returned to the waist through one of the doorways leading off each section of the drawing-room. He led me in the direction of the bow, where I discovered an upscale chamber rather than a cabin, furnished with a bed, a vanity, and various additional items.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: My only option was to express my gratitude to my host.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “Your quarters are adjacent to my own,” he stated, while unlatching a door, “and my chamber leads directly into the parlor we have recently departed.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: I stepped into the Captain’s quarters, which possessed a stark, near-ascetic quality. A modest metal cot, a desk, and a few grooming implements occupied the space, all illuminated from above by a skylight. There were no luxuries, merely the most essential items.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: A chair was indicated by Captain Sorel.

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: “Kindly take a seat,” he remarked. I occupied a chair, and he commenced in this manner:

chapter_title: CHAPTER X THE MAN OF THE SEAS
text: The state-room of Captain Sorel

“Sir,” Captain Sorel remarked, gesturing toward the apparatuses suspended upon his cabin walls, “these are the devices essential for navigating the Meridian. Just as in the drawing-room, I keep them constantly in view, and they reveal my precise location and heading while in the heart of the sea. You are familiar with some, like the thermometer, which measures the Meridian’s internal heat; the barometer, which registers atmospheric pressure and predicts weather shifts; the hygrometer, which records the air’s humidity; the storm-glass, which signals coming gales through the decomposition of its contents; the compass, which directs my path; the sextant, which determines latitude via the sun’s height; chronometers, which allow me to figure the longitude; and day and night glasses, which I employ to survey the horizon whenever the Meridian ascends to the surface of the waves.”

“These are the standard maritime tools,” I answered, “and I am familiar with their operation. Yet these additional items surely fulfill the specific needs of the Meridian. This gauge featuring an adjustable pointer is a manometer, correct?”
“In truth, it is a manometer. Yet, by connecting to the water, which exerts the pressure it measures, it simultaneously reveals our depth.”
“And these remaining devices, whose purpose I am unable to surmise?”
“I should provide you with some clarifications, Professor. Would you be so good as to hear me out?” said I.
After a brief period of quiet, he remarked—

“A potent, submissive, swift, and simple force exists, which adapts to all requirements and holds absolute sway throughout my ship. It accomplishes every task. It provides illumination, generates heat, and serves as the essence of my mechanical equipment. This force is electricity,” I said.
“Electricity?” I exclaimed, astonished.
“Affirmative, sir.”

“All the same, Captain, your speed of travel is exceptionally high, a fact that contradicts the known capabilities of electricity. Up to this point, its kinetic energy has been kept in check, managing to generate only a limited degree of force,” I said.

“Professor,” Captain Sorel remarked, “the electricity I utilize is unique. You are aware of the composition of sea-water. Within every thousand grammes, there is 96½ per cent water, along with roughly 2-2/3 per cent chloride of sodium; additionally, there are lesser amounts of magnesium chloride, potassium chloride, magnesium bromide, magnesia sulphate, and lime sulphate and carbonate. It is evident, therefore, that chloride of sodium constitutes a significant portion. Consequently, I derive this sodium from the ocean to create my components. I am indebted to the sea entirely; it generates electricity, and that electricity provides the Meridian with heat, illumination, propulsion, and, essentially, existence.”
“However, not the atmosphere you inhale?”

“Oh! I am capable of producing the oxygen required for my own respiration, yet there is no need, as I ascend to the ocean’s surface whenever I desire. Nevertheless, while electricity does not supply the air I inhale, it powers the high-capacity pumps kept in large tanks, allowing me to extend my time beneath the waves for as long as I choose. It provides a steady, constant illumination, unlike the sun. Observe this timepiece; it functions via electricity and operates with a precision that surpasses the finest chronometers. I have partitioned it into twenty-four hours, similar to Italian clocks, since I experience neither day nor night, sun nor moon, but only the artificial radiance I carry into the deep. See! at this moment, it is ten o’clock in the morning.”
“Precisely.”

“One more use for electricity. This gauge suspended before us shows the velocity of the Meridian. A wire of electricity connects it to the propeller, and the pointer displays the actual pace. Observe! we are currently traveling at a steady rate of fifteen miles an hour,” I said.
“It is marvelous! And I see, Captain, you were right to make use of this agent that takes the place of wind, water, and steam.”
“Our business is incomplete, M. Delorme,” Captain Sorel stated, standing up. “Please accompany me, and we shall inspect the Meridian’s stern.”

In truth, I was previously acquainted with the forward section of this submersible vessel, which is organized in this precise manner, beginning at the prow:—the dining saloon, measuring five yards in length, partitioned from the library by a bulkhead impervious to water; the library, five yards in length; the expansive lounge, ten yards in length, divided from the Captain’s quarters by another water-tight bulkhead; the aforementioned cabin, five yards long; my own, two and a half yards; and, finally, an air reservoir, seven and a half yards, reaching to the bow. The entire length is thirty-five yards, or one hundred and five feet. These bulkheads featured doors sealed hermetically through the use of india-rubber devices, providing security for the Meridian should a breach occur.

Trailing behind Captain Sorel across the waist, I reached the middle of the vessel. A type of shaft gaped between a pair of bulkheads. A metal ladder, secured to the partition by a metal hook, ascended to the top. I inquired of the Captain regarding the purpose of that ladder.
“This goes to the little craft,” he said.
“Do you possess a boat?” I cried out, astonished.
“Certainly; a superb craft, buoyant and unsinkable, which functions as both a vessel for angling and for recreation.”
“Yet, at the moment you desire to depart, are you compelled to ascend to the water’s surface?”

“Certainly not. This craft is fastened to the Meridian’s upper hull section, sitting inside a hollow space designed for it. It features a deck, is entirely sealed against water, and is secured with sturdy bolts. This staircase connects to an access hatch in the Meridian’s hull, which aligns with a matching aperture on the boat’s side. Through these two entryways, I enter the compact vessel. They seal the hatch on the Meridian; I secure the other using screw-tightened pressure. I release the bolts, and the small boat ascends to the ocean’s surface with immense speed. I then unlock the bridge’s panel, which had been kept tightly closed; I raise the mast, set my sail, grab my oars, and depart.”
“However are you able to return onto the vessel?”
“I am not returning, M. Delorme; the Meridian is arriving to fetch me.”
“Under your command?”
“Under my command. A wire of electricity links us. I send a signal to it, and that suffices,” said I.
“In truth,” I remarked, amazed by these wonders, “nothing could be simpler.”

I walked past the stairwell cage toward the platform and observed a six-foot cabin where Baptiste and Tom Harlan, delighted by their meal, were eating greedily. A door then swung into a nine-foot kitchen positioned between the spacious storerooms. Inside, electricity performed all culinary tasks, proving superior to gas. Currents beneath the ovens provided a steady, well-distributed heat to the platinum sponges. These same currents warmed a distilling device that produced high-quality potable water through evaporation. Adjacent to this kitchen stood a well-appointed bathroom equipped with faucets for hot and cold water.

The vessel’s berthroom, measuring sixteen feet in length, was situated adjacent to the galley. Because the entrance remained closed, I was unable to observe its arrangement, a sight that could have provided me with an estimate regarding the quantity of crew members working upon the Meridian.

A fourth partition sat at the base, acting as a buffer between this workspace and the engine-room. Upon the opening of a door, I entered the space where Captain Sorel—an engineer of exceptional caliber, to be sure—had installed his locomotive apparatus. This brightly illuminated engine-room spanned no fewer than sixty-five feet. It was split into two sections: the initial one held the components required for electricity generation, while the latter housed the mechanisms linking that power to the screw. I inspected it with profound curiosity, seeking to grasp the inner workings of the Meridian.

“Observe,” the Captain remarked, “that I employ Bunsen’s devices rather than those of Ruhmkorff. The latter lacked sufficient power. Bunsen’s units are limited in quantity, yet they are substantial and robust, a configuration that practice has shown to be superior. The generated current travels ahead to operate massive electro-magnets, which actuate a mechanism of cogs and levers to convey motion to the screw’s axle. This component, measuring nineteen feet across with a thread length of twenty-three feet, executes approximately one hundred and twenty rotations every second.”
“And do you obtain it then?”
“Fifty miles per hour is the velocity.”

“I have witnessed the Meridian manœuvre prior to the Evangeline, and I possess personal theories regarding its velocity. However, this is insufficient. It is necessary that we observe our destination. We require the ability to steer it rightward, leftward, upward, and downward. By what means do you reach the immense depths, where you encounter a mounting resistance, measured by hundreds of atmospheres? In what manner do you ascend back to the ocean’s surface? And how do you sustain your position within the necessary medium? Am I requesting an excessive amount?”

“By no means, Professor,” the Captain answered, pausing slightly; “for you might never depart from this submarine boat. Enter the saloon, which serves as our regular study, and there you shall discover everything you desire regarding the Meridian.”

Shortly after we had taken our seats upon a divan in the saloon to smoke, the Captain presented me with a drawing illustrating the layout, cross-section, and profile of the Meridian. He then commenced his explanation by saying:—

“Here, M. Delorme, are the various measurements of the vessel you occupy. It consists of an extended cylinder featuring tapered extremities. Its form closely resembles a cigar, a design previously utilized in London for multiple builds of an identical nature. Measuring from bow to aft, this cylinder is exactly 232 feet long, while its greatest width reaches twenty-six feet. Although its construction differs from that of your long-distance steamers, the lines are adequately elongated and the curves sufficiently drawn out so that water glides away smoothly, presenting no resistance to its movement. Through a basic calculation, these two dimensions allow you to determine the surface area and cubic volume of the Meridian. Its area totals 6032 feet, and its capacity is roughly 1500 cubic yards—meaning that when fully submerged, it displaces 50,000 feet of water, or has a weight of 1500 tons.”

“At the time I drafted the designs for this submarine vessel, my intention was for nine-tenths to remain underwater: as a result, it should only displace nine-tenths of its volume—which is to say, it should only weigh that specific number of tons. I should not, in that case, have surpassed that weight while building it to those stated proportions.”

“The Meridian consists of a pair of hulls, an inner and an outer, connected by T-shaped iron pieces, providing it with great durability. In fact, because of this cellular design, it withstands pressure like a solid mass, as though it were a single piece. Its flanks are incapable of giving way; it holds together naturally rather than through the tightness of its rivets; and the uniformity of its build, resulting from the flawless joining of its components, allows it to withstand the most violent waves.”

“The density of the steel plates forming these two hulls ranges between .7 and .8 of water’s density. Measuring at least two and a half inches in thickness, the primary hull weighs 394 tons. The secondary casing, known as the keel, stands twenty inches tall with a thickness of ten inches, and its weight is sixty-two tons by itself. My engine, ballast, various accessories, auxiliary apparatus, partitions, and bulkheads total 961.62 tons. Are you keeping up with all of this?” said I.
“I agree.”

“Once the Meridian is buoyant in this state, one-tenth of it remains above the surface. If I construct tanks matching that tenth, or with a capacity of 150 tons, and I admit water into them, the craft, reaching a weight of 1507 tons, will be entirely submerged. That is what would occur, Professor. These tanks are located in the Meridian’s base. I open the valves to let them fill, and the ship, which was previously flush with the waterline, descends.”

“So, Captain, we have arrived at the actual problem. I comprehend your ability to ascend to the top; however, when submerging, does your underwater vessel not meet a force, and therefore experience a vertical lift of one atmosphere for every thirty feet of depth, which is roughly fifteen pounds for each square inch?” said I.
“Exactly, sir.”
“In that case, provided you do not entirely occupy the Meridian, I fail to understand how it is possible for you to pull it into those profound reaches,” I said.

“Professor, you must not confuse dynamics with statics, or else you shall encounter serious mistakes. Very little effort is needed to reach the depths of the sea, as all objects naturally gravitate downward. To determine how much additional weight was needed to submerge the Meridian, I merely had to compute how much the volume of seawater decreases at specific depths,” I said.
“It is clear.”

“Assuming water is not entirely incompressible, it possesses at least a minimal capacity for compression. In fact, current mathematical estimates suggest this decrease is merely .000436 of an atmosphere for every thirty feet of submersion. Should we intend to descend 3000 feet, I must factor in the volume reduction resulting from pressure equivalent to a thousand-foot water column. This computation is simple to confirm. Furthermore, I possess auxiliary tanks with a capacity of one hundred tons. Consequently, I am able to submerge to a significant depth. Whenever I desire to ascend to the ocean surface, I simply discharge the water, emptying every reservoir if I require the Meridian to surface by one-tenth of her overall volume.”
There was no part of these arguments that I could dispute.
“I acknowledge your figures, Captain,” I answered; “it would be a mistake for me to contest them, given that everyday practice validates them; however, I anticipate a genuine obstacle ahead.”
“In what way, sir?”

“At a depth of approximately 1000 feet, the Meridian’s hull sustains a pressure of 100 atmospheres. If you were to discharge the auxiliary tanks at this moment to reduce the ship’s weight and ascend, the pumps would be required to surmount that 100-atmosphere pressure, equivalent to 1500 pounds for every square inch. From that, a force——” said I.

“Electricity provides that by itself,” the Captain remarked, with haste. “I reiterate, sir, that my engines possess nearly limitless dynamic force. You surely noticed the immense capacity of the Meridian pumps when their water streams erupted like a deluge against the Evangeline. Furthermore, I employ auxiliary tanks merely to reach an average profundity of 750 to 1000 fathoms, which assists in the operation of my apparatus. Additionally, whenever I desire to explore the oceanic abyss five or six miles beneath the waves, I utilize methods that are more gradual yet equally certain.”
“What are those, Captain?”
“It requires that I explain the operation of the Meridian to you.”
“My eagerness to acquire knowledge is great.”

“For steering this vessel to the left or right, for turning—in short, moving along a horizontal plane, I employ a standard rudder attached to the rear of the stern-post, utilizing a wheel and various ropes for guidance. However, I am also capable of causing the Meridian to ascend and descend, or descend and ascend, through vertical motion using a pair of slanted planes secured to its flanks, positioned against the center of buoyancy, which shift in any direction and are operated by strong interior levers. When these planes remain level with the boat, it travels horizontally. When tilted, the Meridian, depending on the angle and the force of the screw, either dives diagonally or climbs diagonally as I desire. Furthermore, should I need to reach the surface with greater speed, I disengage the screw, and the water’s force makes the Meridian shoot upward vertically just like a hydrogen-filled balloon,” said I.
“Well done, Captain! Yet in what manner might the helmsman track the course amidst the sea?”
“The pilot is situated within a glass enclosure, which is elevated above the Meridian’s frame and equipped with optical lenses,” I said.
“Can these lenses withstand this amount of pressure?”

“Entirely. Although glass shatters upon impact, it can still provide significant durability. Throughout various 1864 trials involving electric light fishing within the Northern Seas, we observed panes under one-third of an inch in depth withstand sixteen atmospheres of pressure. Currently, the glass I employ is at minimum thirty times that thickness.”
“Accepted. Still, ultimately, for vision to occur, illumination needs to surpass shadow, and surrounded by the gloom within the sea, in what way is it possible for you to perceive?”
A potent electric reflector is situated aft of the steersman’s cage, casting beams that illuminate the ocean for a distance of half a mile ahead.

“Bravo, bravo, Captain! I am finally able to explain the phosphorescence of this supposed narwhal that left us so perplexed. I must now inquire whether the boarding of the Meridian and of the Caledon, which caused such an uproar, was merely the outcome of a chance rencontre?” said I.
“Entirely by chance, sir. My vessel was navigating merely a single fathom beneath the waves at the moment of the impact. No negative consequences followed.”
“Nothing to report, sir. However, what of your encounter involving the Evangeline?”

“Professor, I regret the damage to one of the finest ships in the American navy; nevertheless, they assaulted me, and I had to protect my own vessel. I chose only to disable the frigate; she will easily find the means to be mended at the nearest harbor,” said I.
“Oh, Commander! your Meridian is truly a wonderful vessel.”

“Indeed, Professor; and I cherish it like a limb of my own body. Should peril confront one of your ships at sea, the initial sensation is the dread of a chasm both overhead and beneath. Within the Meridian, the courage of men remains unshaken. There are no flaws to dread, as the dual hull possesses the solidity of iron; no masts or ropes to manage; no canvas for the gale to destroy; no steam engines to explode; no conflagration to dread, since the craft is constructed of iron rather than timber; no fuel to exhaust, as electricity serves as the sole motive power; no impact to dread, for it navigates the depths alone; no storm to endure, for by submerging, it attains total serenity. There, sir! that represents the ideal ship! And if it holds that the designer possesses greater faith in the craft than the constructor, and the constructor more than the master himself, you can grasp the reliance I place in my Meridian; for I serve simultaneously as master, constructor, and designer.”
“However, by what means were you able to build this marvelous Meridian in private?”

“Every individual segment, M. Delorme, arrived from various corners of the world. The keel was cast at Creusot, the screw shaft at Penn & Co.’s in London, the hull’s iron plating at Laird’s of Liverpool, and the screw itself at Scott’s in Glasgow. Cail & Co. in Paris manufactured the reservoirs, Krupp in Prussia built the engine, Motala’s workshop in Sweden fashioned the beak, and Hart Brothers of New York produced the mathematical instruments; furthermore, I provided instructions to every one of these suppliers using a variety of aliases.”
“However, were these components required to be assembled and organized?”
