“Professor, I established my laboratories on an isolated isle in the sea. It was there that my laborers—the courageous individuals I trained and taught—and I assembled our Meridian. Once the construction was complete, flames obliterated every sign of our activities on that landmass, which I could have leaped across had I chosen to.”
“So the price of this ship is high?”

“M. Delorme, the price for an iron ship is £45 for every ton. Since the Meridian had a weight of 1500, the total reached £67,500, plus an additional £80,000 for its outfitting, and roughly £200,000 including the artistic pieces and the various collections housed within.”
“A final inquiry, Captain Sorel.”
“Pose the question, Professor.”
“Are you wealthy?”
“Extremely wealthy, sir; and I possess the means to settle the French national debt without feeling the loss.”
I gazed at the solitary individual who uttered those words. Could he be testing my gullibility? Time would eventually reveal the answer.

It is calculated that more than eighty million acres of the Earth’s surface are submerged beneath water. This liquid volume consists of two billion two hundred and fifty million cubic miles, creating a sphere with a diameter of sixty leagues that would weigh three quintillion tons. To grasp the significance of these statistics, one must note that a quintillion relates to a billion just as a billion relates to one; stated differently, a quintillion contains as many billions as a billion contains units. This total fluid quantity is roughly equivalent to the amount of water that would be released by every river on the planet over a span of forty thousand years.

Following the aqueous era, the igneous age arrived throughout the geological epochs. At first, the sea covered the entire globe. Gradually, during the Silurian period, mountain peaks started to surface, islands rose, vanished under localized floods, surfaced once more, stabilized, and developed into continents, until finally the world attained the geographical layout visible today. The land had claimed thirty-seven million six hundred and fifty-seven square miles from the water, which is equivalent to twelve billion nine hundred and sixty millions of acres.

The configuration of the landmasses permits the categorization of the seas into five vast segments: the Arctic or Frozen Ocean, the Antarctic or Frozen Ocean, the Indian, the Atlantic, and the Pacific Oceans.

Stretching from the northern to the southern polar circles, the Pacific Ocean spans from Asia to America across 145 degrees of longitude. This body of water is the most tranquil; it features wide, sluggish currents, moderate tides, and heavy precipitation. This was the sea that I was fated to traverse initially under these peculiar circumstances.
“Sir,” Captain Sorel stated, “if it is agreeable to you, we shall determine our position and establish the origin of this journey. It is currently 11:45; I intend to return to the surface.”

The Captain pushed an electric timepiece on three occasions. Water started being forced out of the reservoirs by the pumps; the manometer’s needle indicated the Meridian’s rise through a varying pressure, before it ceased movement.
“Our arrival is complete,” the Captain stated.
Making my way to the main stairway that led out onto the deck, I climbed the metal rungs and arrived at the top level of the Meridian.

Rising a mere three feet above the surface, the platform sat low. Because the bow and stern of the Meridian were tapered into a spindle-like form, it was frequently and accurately likened to a cigar. I observed that the iron plating, with its subtle overlapping, mirrored the scales covering the hide of our massive land-dwelling reptiles. This clarified for me why, notwithstanding the use of any lenses, this vessel was so easily mistaken for a creature of the sea.

Near the center of the deck, the long-boat, partially embedded within the ship’s frame, created a minor protrusion. At the bow and stern stood two moderately tall enclosures with slanted walls, each partially sealed by heavy, lens-shaped glass; one was reserved for the pilot steering the Meridian, while the other held a luminous lamp to illuminate the path ahead.

The ocean appeared lovely, the heavens clear. The elongated craft barely perceived the expansive swells of the sea. A gentle wind blowing from the east stirred the water’s face. Because the horizon lacked mist, viewing was simple. There was nothing to be seen. No shifting sands, no isle. An immense wilderness.

Using his sextant, Captain Sorel measured the sun’s altitude, a calculation intended to reveal the latitude. He paused briefly until the solar disc made contact with the horizon. Throughout the observation, he remained perfectly still; the device appeared as steady as if held by a hand carved from marble.
The Sun’s altitude was measured by Captain Sorel.
“It is noon, sir,” he stated. “Whenever you are ready——”
Glancing one final time at the ocean, tinted a faint shade of yellow near the Japanese coast, I made my way down to the saloon.

“Now, sir, I shall leave you to your research,” the Captain continued; “we are steering E.N.E. at a depth of twenty-six fathoms. I have provided large-scale charts so that you might track our progress. You have full access to the saloon, and if you will excuse me, I am going to withdraw.” Captain Sorel inclined his head, and I stayed behind by myself, absorbed in reflections centered entirely upon the leader of the Meridian.

I remained absorbed in these thoughts for sixty minutes, attempting to uncover the secret that held such fascination for me. My gaze then landed on the expansive map laid out across the desk, and I set my fingertip precisely where the specified coordinates of latitude and longitude intersected.

Like the continents, the ocean possesses vast rivers. These are unique streams identifiable by their specific hues and thermal properties. The Gulf Stream is the most noteworthy among them. Researchers have mapped the paths of five major currents across the planet: one located in the North Atlantic, another in the South, a third within the North Pacific, a fourth in the South, and a fifth found in the Southern Indian Ocean. It is also likely that a sixth current was present at some point in the Northern Indian Ocean, back when the Aral and Caspian Seas were joined as a single, expansive body of water.

On the planisphere, the spot marked showed one of these streams in motion, the Kuro-Scivo of the Japanese, or Black River. Originating in the Gulf of Bengal, where the vertical beams of a tropical sun heat its waters, it traverses the Straits of Malacca by the Asian coastline, veers into the North Pacific toward the Aleutian Islands, transports native goods and camphor-tree logs, and borders the oceanic swells with the deep indigo of its heated flow. The Meridian was destined to track this very current. I traced its path visually, watched it vanish into the immense Pacific, and sensed myself being pulled along with it, just as Tom Harlan and Baptiste arrived at the saloon entrance.
The pair of courageous associates I was with stood frozen, gazing at the marvels displayed in their view.
“Are we where, are we where?” the Canadian cried out. “At the museum in Quebec?”
“My friends,” I replied, gesturing for them to come inside, “you are not in Canada, but rather aboard the Meridian, fifty yards beneath the surface of the ocean.”
“However, M. Delorme,” Tom Harlan remarked, “are you able to inform me of the total number of individuals aboard? Is it ten, twenty, fifty, or perhaps a hundred?”

“I am unable to reply to you, Mr. Land; it is preferable to temporarily relinquish any notion of capturing the Meridian or fleeing from it. This vessel represents a pinnacle of contemporary engineering, and I would regret missing the chance to observe it. Numerous individuals would embrace the circumstances imposed on us, if merely to walk among such marvels. Therefore, remain silent and permit us to attempt to observe what occurs in our vicinity,” said I.
“Look!” the harpooner cried, “yet we perceive naught within this metallic cell! We are pacing—we are navigating—without sight.”

Hardly had Tom Harlan finished uttering those remarks before the area was plunged into total blackness. The glowing overhead panel had vanished, and the speed of the transition caused a sharp ache in my vision.

We stayed silent, motionless, and uncertain of the surprise in store for us, be it pleasant or unpleasant. A scraping sound emerged: it was as if panels were shifting along the flanks of the Meridian.
“This is the conclusion of the conclusion!” said Tom Harlan.

Abruptly, illumination pierced both flanks of the saloon by way of a pair of rectangular apertures. The aqueous volume looked brightly illuminated by the electrical radiance. A couple of glass panes divided us from the ocean. Initially, I shook with the notion that this delicate barrier could shatter, yet sturdy copper hoops secured them, bestowing a nearly boundless capacity for endurance.

For a mile in every direction, the ocean could be clearly seen around the Meridian. How magnificent a sight! What writing instrument might capture it? Who possesses the ability to illustrate how the light plays through those clear layers of liquid, or the gentleness of the fading shades as they transition from the depths to the upper levels of the sea?

It is understood that the sea possesses a transparency that exceeds that of water found in rocks. The suspension of organic and mineral matter within it serves to increase this clarity. In specific regions of the ocean near the Antilles, a sandy floor is visible with remarkable distinctness at a depth of seventy-five fathoms. The ability of sunlight to penetrate does not appear to end at a depth of one hundred and fifty fathoms. However, within this central fluid traversed by the Meridian, electric radiance was generated deep inside the waves. This was not merely glowing water, but light in liquid form.

To either side, a window gave way to this unmapped chasm. Because the saloon was so dim, the radiance beyond appeared all the more striking, and we gazed out as though this clear crystal were the pane of a vast aquarium.
“You wanted a look, friend Tom; indeed, you are looking now.”

“Strange! strange!” the Canadian whispered, his previous irritation abandoned as he appeared to yield to an undeniable pull; “and a person would travel even further than this to behold a spectacle like this!”
“Oh!” I mused internally, “I grasp the existence of this individual; he has fashioned a separate universe for his own, where he guards all his most magnificent marvels.”

An aquatic host accompanied the Meridian for a duration of two full hours. Throughout their leaps and play, while they competed in speed, radiance, and grace, I identified the green labre; the banded mullet, distinguished by two black stripes; the round-tailed goby, white in hue with violet markings upon its back; the Japanese scombrus, a stunning mackerel native to those waters, possessing a silver head and blue torso; the radiant azurors, whose very title eludes definition; various banded spares, featuring multicolored fins of yellow and blue; the woodcocks of the seas, certain examples of which reach a length of one yard; Japanese salamanders, spider lampreys, serpents measuring six feet in length, equipped with lively, tiny eyes and massive maws lined with teeth; along with numerous additional species.

Our excitement remained intense, with remarks exchanged in rapid succession. Tom identified the fish, while Baptiste categorized them. I felt sheer delight at the liveliness of their motions and the elegance of their shapes. It had never before been my privilege to observe these creatures, living and unrestrained, within their own habitat. I shall omit listing every species that drifted past my overwhelmed vision, or the entire assortment from the seas of China and Japan. These fish, outnumbering the birds in the sky, arrived, drawn, surely, by the intense glow of the electric light.

Light unexpectedly filled the saloon, the metal shutters slid shut once more, and the captivating sight vanished. Yet I remained lost in thought for a considerable period until my gaze landed upon the gauges mounted on the bulkhead. The needle of the compass continued to point N.N.E., the manometer registered a pressure of five atmospheres—matching a depth of twenty-five fathoms—and the electric log recorded a velocity of fifteen miles an hour. I anticipated the arrival of Captain Sorel, though he failed to show. The time displayed on the clock was five.

Baptiste and Tom Harlan went back to their quarters, while I withdrew to my own room. My evening meal awaited me. It consisted of a turtle soup crafted from the finest hawksbills, a surmullet accompanied by puff pastry (the liver, cooked separately, was exquisite), and emperor-holocanthus fillets, which tasted better to me than salmon.

My evening was spent in study, composition, and reflection. Eventually, slumber claimed me, and I lay down upon my bed of zostera, falling into a deep rest, as the Meridian moved swiftly along the flow of the Black River.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: It was the 9th of November when the following day arrived. Following a twelve-hour slumber, I stirred. As was his habit, Baptiste appeared to inquire “how I had passed the night,” and to provide his assistance. He had departed, leaving the Canadian, his friend, resting as soundly as someone who had spent his entire existence doing nothing but that. I permitted the kind man to talk away to his heart’s content, feeling no urge to reply. My thoughts were consumed by the Captain’s failure to attend our meeting the previous day, and I held onto the expectation of encountering him this day.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: Upon finishing my dressing, I proceeded to the saloon. The space stood empty.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: I immersed myself in examining the collections of shells concealed behind the glass panes. I took delight as well in massive botanical volumes packed with the most uncommon sea flora, which, despite being desiccated, kept their beautiful hues. Within these valuable hydrophytes, I noted various vorticellæ, pavonariæ, fine-textured ceramies displaying crimson shades, certain agari shaped like fans, and some natabuli resembling level mushrooms, all of which were formerly categorized as zoophytes; in summary, an impeccable array of algæ.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: Not once during the entire day was I graced with a call from Captain Sorel. The saloon’s wall sections remained shut. It is possible they preferred that we not grow weary of such lovely objects.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: The Meridian held an E.N.E. heading, traveling at a rate of twelve knots, with the water beneath her measuring from twenty-five to thirty fathoms deep.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: On the 10th of November, the following day, the identical abandonment and loneliness persisted. Not a single member of the ship’s crew appeared before me; Tom and Baptiste remained by my side for most of the day. They expressed amazement regarding the mysterious disappearance of the Captain. “Was this peculiar individual unwell?—had he changed his plans concerning us?” they asked.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: In the end, as Baptiste remarked, we possessed absolute freedom, and we were provided with refined and plentiful meals. Our provider honored the conditions of the agreement. We found no cause for grievance, and, in truth, the uniqueness of our destiny had set aside such extraordinary rewards for us that we possessed no justification to blame it at this stage.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: On that date, I began the record of these experiences, which has allowed me to recount them with greater precise accuracy and granular particularity. My writing was done upon sheets fashioned from zostera marina.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: Early on the morning of 11th November, the crisp breeze circulating throughout the Meridian indicated that we had ascended to the sea's surface to replenish our oxygen reserves. I made my way toward the middle stairway and climbed onto the platform.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: At six o’clock, the sky was overcast, and the ocean appeared grey yet tranquil. There was hardly a swell. Would Captain Sorel, the man I expected to encounter, be present? I observed nobody except the helmsman confined within his glass enclosure. Resting on the ledge created by the pinnace’s hull, I breathed in the briny air with pleasure.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: Gradually, the mist vanished as the sun’s beams took effect, and the glowing sphere ascended past the horizon in the east. The ocean ignited beneath its gaze, resembling a line of ignited powder. High above, the dispersed clouds were painted in vivid, lovely hues, along with many “mare’s tails,” signaling that wind was coming that day. Yet, what did wind matter to this Meridian, which no storm could intimidate!

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: I stood observing the cheerful, life-sustaining ascent of the sun, when the sound of footsteps neared the platform. Expecting to greet Captain Sorel, I was met instead by his second—a man I had encountered during the Captain’s initial visit. He walked onto the platform, apparently unaware of my presence. He held a powerful glass to his eye, surveying the entire horizon with intense focus. Once he finished this inspection, he walked to the panel and spoke a specific phrase. I committed it to memory, as it was uttered under identical circumstances each morning. It was phrased as follows—

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “Nautron respoc lorni virch.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: I could not state what it signified.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: Once these terms were uttered, the second individual went below. It seemed to me that the Meridian prepared to resume its underwater journey. I made my way back to the board and retreated to my quarters.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: For five days, our circumstances remained entirely unaltered. Each dawn, I ascended the platform. That identical expression was uttered by that very person. Yet, Captain Sorel failed to show himself.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: My decision had been reached that I would not encounter him once more, until, on the 16th November, while arriving back at my quarters accompanied by Tom and Baptiste, I discovered a letter directed to me sitting on my desk. I tore it open with eagerness. Its script was firm and distinct, with somewhat sharp letters that brought to mind German typography. The message was phrased in this manner—

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: November 16th, 1867.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: FOR PROFESSOR DELORME, Aboard the Meridian.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: Captain Sorel asks Professor Delorme to attend a hunting-party scheduled for to-morrow morning within the woods of the island of Carrizo. He trusts that no obstacles will keep the Professor from attending, and he would be delighted to see his companions accompany him.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: CAPTAIN SOREL, who serves as Commander of the Meridian.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “A hunt!” cried Tom.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “Plus the woods located on Carrizo island!” Baptiste supplemented.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “Oh! so the man is traveling on dry land?” responded Tom Harlan.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “It appears to be plainly suggested,” I remarked, as I perused the missive again.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “We have no choice but to agree,” the Canadian stated. “However, when we are back on solid earth, we will figure out our next move. Truly, I will be glad to have some fresh venison to consume.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: I chose not to attempt a resolution of the conflict between Captain Sorel’s clear dislike of landmasses and his request that I join him for a forest hunt, and instead I simply answered—

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “We should begin by locating the island of Carrizo.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: Upon checking the planisphere, I located a tiny island at 32° 40′ north lat. and 157° 50′ west long., which Captain Carrizo had identified in 1801 and which appeared on old Spanish charts as Rocca de la Plata, translated as “The Silver Rock.” At that moment, we had traveled roughly eighteen hundred miles from our point of departure, and the Meridian’s path, having shifted slightly, was steering it once more in a south-easterly direction.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: To my companions, I presented this tiny stone adrift in the center of the North Pacific.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “In the event that Captain Sorel occasionally sets foot on land,” I remarked, “he invariably selects deserted islands.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: Without uttering a word, Tom Harlan gave a shrug, after which he and Baptiste departed, leaving me behind.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: Following the evening meal, brought to me by the silent and expressionless steward, I retired to my quarters, feeling a certain degree of apprehension.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: On the morning of the 17th of November, upon waking, I perceived that the Meridian had come to a complete halt. I donned my clothes with haste and stepped into the saloon.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: Captain Sorel stood there, expecting my arrival. Standing up and offering a bow, he inquired whether I was prepared to go with him. Because he did not refer to the fact that he had been gone for the previous eight days, I chose not to bring it up, replying only that my associates and I were prepared to go where he led.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: The dining-room was where we arrived, and there the morning meal was laid out.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “M. Delorme,” the Captain said, “please, join me for breakfast informally; we shall converse while we dine. Because while I did pledge a forest stroll to you, I did not guarantee finding any inns along the way. Therefore, eat like someone who will probably wait until quite late for his evening meal.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: I paid tribute to the meal. It featured various species of fish, portions of holothuridæ (superb zoophytes), and diverse varieties of marine vegetation. We drank clear water, into which Captain Sorel poured a few droplets of an alcoholic beverage, distilled via the Kamschatcha technique from a type of sea-weed called Rhodomenia palmata. Captain Sorel consumed his food in silence initially. Then he commenced—

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “When I suggested that you hunt within my submarine forest of Carrizo, you clearly believed I had lost my mind, Sir. You ought to refrain from judging any man so flippantly, Sir.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “However, Captain, trust me——”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “Please pay attention, and you shall discover if there is any reason for you to charge me with foolishness and inconsistency.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “I am listening.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “Professor, you are as aware as I am that human beings are capable of existing beneath the waves, so long as they are equipped with an adequate reserve of oxygen. When performing tasks underwater, a laborer, outfitted in a watertight suit and a metallic headpiece, is supplied with air from the surface through the use of pressure pumps and control valves,” I said.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “That’s a piece of underwater equipment,” I remarked.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “Precisely, although in these circumstances the individual lacks freedom; he remains connected to the pump that delivers air to him via an india-rubber hose, and were we compelled to be tethered to the Meridian in such a fashion, our range would be limited.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “And how shall we secure our liberation?” I inquired.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “The Rouquayrol apparatus, a device created by a pair of your fellow citizens, is what I have refined for personal application, and it shall enable you to expose yourself to these novel physiological states without any bodily harm. It is comprised of a heavy iron tank where I hold air compressed to fifty atmospheres. This container is secured to the back with straps, much like a military pack. Its top section is a chamber where air is retained by a bellows, ensuring it only releases at standard pressure. In the version of the Rouquayrol apparatus we employ, a pair of rubber hoses extend from this box to a mask covering the mouth and nose; one hose supplies oxygen, the other discharges waste, while the tongue regulates the flow based on the breather’s needs. However, to withstand the intense pressures of the ocean floor, I had to enclose my head within a copper sphere, and it is into this copper globe that the two tubes, for inhalation and exhalation, connect,” said I.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “Everything is fine, Captain Sorel; however, the atmosphere you are transporting will be exhausted before long; once the oxygen level drops to fifteen per cent, it will be impossible to inhale.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “Indeed! However, M. Delorme, I informed you that the Meridian’s pumps permit me to compress the air significantly, and with these provisions, the device’s reservoir is capable of supplying respirable air for a duration of nine or ten hours,” I said.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “I possess no more protests to offer,” I replied; “I shall merely inquire of you one detail, Captain—in what manner do you illuminate your path upon the ocean floor?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “Using the Ruhmkorff apparatus, M. Delorme; one unit is worn upon the back, while the second is secured to the waist. It consists of a Bunsen pile, though I utilize sodium rather than bichromate of potash. A wire is inserted to gather the generated electricity and channel it into a specially crafted lantern. Inside this lantern sits a glass spiral holding a small amount of carbonic gas. Once the device is activated, this gas turns luminous, emitting a steady, white light. Equipped in this manner, I am able to breathe and I am able to see.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “Captain Sorel, your replies to every one of my protests are so overwhelming that I can no longer harbor any skepticism. Although I am compelled to accept the Rouquayrol and Ruhmkorff apparatus, I must be permitted to maintain certain doubts concerning the firearm I am expected to bear,” said I.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “However, that weapon does not utilize gunpowder,” the Captain replied.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “In that case, it is an air-gun.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “Undoubtedly! In what way do you expect me to produce gunpowder while on this vessel, lacking saltpetre, sulphur, or charcoal?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “Furthermore,” I continued, “in order to discharge a weapon submerged in a medium that possesses eight hundred and fifty-five times the density of air, we are required to overcome quite significant resistance.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “That would present no problem. As Fulton states, there are guns developed in England by Philip Coles and Burley, in France by Furcy, and in Italy by Landi, equipped with a unique locking mechanism that allows them to discharge in such circumstances. However, I reiterate, since I lack gunpowder, I employ highly compressed air, which the Meridian pumps provide in great supply,” said I.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “However, is this atmosphere required to be consumed quickly?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “Is it not the case that I possess my Rouquayrol reservoir, capable of supplying it whenever necessary? Merely turning a tap is sufficient. Furthermore, M. Delorme, you surely recognize that throughout our underwater pursuit, our consumption of both air and ammunition must remain minimal,” said I.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “However, it appears to me that within this dusk, and surrounded by this liquid, which possesses high density relative to the air, projectiles would be unable to travel a great distance, nor would they readily result in death,” I remarked.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “On the contrary, sir, this weapon ensures that each strike proves fatal; and no matter how slight the contact with the creature, it drops as though hit by a lightning bolt,” I said.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “Why?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “For the projectiles fired by this weapon are not standard bullets, but small glass containers (the creation of an Austrian chemist named Leniebroek), a significant quantity of which I possess. Each glass vessel is encased in steel and balanced by a lead weight; they function as genuine Leyden bottles, containing electricity compressed to an extreme degree of tension. Upon the most minor impact, they release their energy, causing any creature, regardless of its power, to drop lifeless. I should inform you that these containers are of the fourth size, whereas a standard firearm would require a charge of ten.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: “I shall cease this debate,” I answered, standing up from the furniture; “I possess no alternative but to retrieve my firearm. In any case, I will accompany you wherever you travel.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XIV A NOTE OF INVITATION
text: Captain Sorel guided me toward the stern; as we went by the quarters belonging to Tom and Baptiste, I summoned my pair of associates, and they joined us at once. We arrived at a small chamber adjacent to the engine-room, where we were required to don our suits for walking.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XV A WALK ON THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA
text: To be precise, this chamber served as the Meridian’s storage area for gear and clothing. Suspended from the wall were twelve sets of underwater equipment, held in readiness for us.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XV A WALK ON THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA
text: Upon observing them, Tom Harlan displayed clear aversion to donning one.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XV A WALK ON THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA
text: “However, my esteemed Tom, the woods on the Island of Carrizo consist entirely of underwater forests,” I said.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XV A WALK ON THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA
text: “Excellent!” remarked the frustrated harpooner, watching his visions of a meal of fresh meat vanish. “And what about you, M. Delorme, do you intend to put on those garments?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XV A WALK ON THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA
text: “There is no other choice, Master Tom.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XV A WALK ON THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA
text: “Whatever you wish, sir,” the harpooner answered, giving his shoulders a shrug; “but personally, I shall avoid entering one unless I have no other choice.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XV A WALK ON THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA
text: “You are under no compulsion, Master Tom,” stated Captain Sorel.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XV A WALK ON THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA
text: “Will Baptiste take the chance?” inquired Tom.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XV A WALK ON THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA
text: “Wherever my master travels, I accompany him,” answered Baptiste.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XV A WALK ON THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA
text: Following the Captain’s summons, a pair of the vessel’s sailors arrived to assist us in donning these cumbersome, watertight garments, fashioned from seamless india-rubber and built specifically to withstand immense force. It resembled a suit of plate armour, simultaneously flexible and durable. This attire consisted of a waistcoat and trousers. The trousers terminated in thick footwear, anchored by substantial lead soles. Copper bands secured the fabric of the waistcoat, traversing the chest to shield it against the intense aquatic pressure while permitting the lungs to function; the sleeves concluded in gloves that did not impede hand mobility. A significant contrast was apparent between these sophisticated devices and the cork breastplates, jackets, and various other inventions popular throughout the eighteenth century.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XV A WALK ON THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA
text: Captain Sorel, along with Baptiste—a man resembling Hercules who surely held immense power—and I, quickly donned the suits. All that was left was to secure our heads inside the metallic casing. Prior to beginning that task, I requested that the Captain allow me to inspect the firearms we would be taking with us.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XV A WALK ON THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA
text: A member of the Meridian crew handed me a basic firearm, featuring a somewhat oversized steel stock that was hollowed out. This section functioned as a chamber for pressurized air, released into a metallic pipe by a spring-loaded valve. Housed within a slot in the thick stock, a container held roughly twenty electric spheres, which were pushed into the weapon’s bore by a spring mechanism. Each time a discharge occurred, a fresh round was immediately positioned.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XV A WALK ON THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA
text: “Captain Sorel,” I remarked, “this weapon is flawless and simple to operate: I merely request permission to test it. Yet, by what means will we reach the ocean floor?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XV A WALK ON THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA
text: “Right now, Professor, the Meridian sits stuck in five fathoms, and our only option is to depart.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XV A WALK ON THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA
text: “Yet in what manner are we to depart?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XV A WALK ON THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA
text: “You will observe.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XV A WALK ON THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA
text: Captain Sorel pushed his head inside the helmet, and Baptiste and I followed suit, though not before the Canadian offered an ironical “Good sport!” The top section of our suits ended in a copper collar where the metal helmet was fastened. Three openings, shielded by heavy glass, permitted us to view our surroundings in every direction by merely rotating our heads within the headgear. Once it was secured, the Rouquayrol apparatus situated on our backs commenced functioning; and, as for me, I found I could inhale without difficulty.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XV A WALK ON THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA
text: Equipped with the Ruhmkorff lamp suspended at my waist and my firearm gripped firmly, I prepared to depart. Yet, in all honesty, confined within this cumbersome attire and anchored to the floorboards by my weighted footwear, moving even a single pace was beyond my ability.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XV A WALK ON THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA
text: I prepared myself to depart.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XV A WALK ON THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA
text: However, this situation had been anticipated. I sensed myself shoved toward a small chamber adjacent to the wardrobe-room. My associates trailed behind, pulled along in an identical fashion. I listened as a water-tight door, equipped with stopper-plates, shut behind us, and we were enveloped in absolute blackness.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XV A WALK ON THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA
text: A few minutes later, a sharp whistling noise echoed. The chill climbed from my ankles up to my torso. Clearly, someone had opened a valve somewhere on the ship, allowing the ocean to pour in and rapidly submerge the chamber. Next, an additional hatch carved into the hull of the Meridian swung wide. A dim glow appeared. A moment later, we stepped onto the ocean floor.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XV A WALK ON THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA
text: How might I describe the sensation that stroll beneath the waves imprinted upon me? Language fails to convey such marvels! Captain Sorel led the way, with his associate trailing a few paces back. Baptiste and I kept close, acting as though communication were feasible despite our metal suits. The burden of my attire, my footwear, my oxygen tank, and my heavy helmet—inside which my skull shook like a nut in its husk—had vanished from my awareness.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XV A WALK ON THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA
text: I was amazed by the intensity of the illumination that brightened the ground thirty feet under the sea's surface. The sun's beams penetrated the liquid volume without difficulty, neutralizing every hue, and I could plainly make out items one hundred and fifty yards away. Past that point, the shades deepened into subtle transitions of ultramarine before dissolving into indistinct shadows. In reality, the liquid encircling me was merely a different type of air, thicker than the atmosphere of the earth, yet nearly as clear. The tranquil face of the ocean rested overhead.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XV A WALK ON THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA
text: Our path lay across smooth, uniform sand, devoid of the ripples found on a level beach that typically hold the marks of the waves. This brilliant surface acted as a mirror, casting back the sun’s beams with remarkable force, a phenomenon that explained the shimmering movement permeating every particle of the water. Will anyone credit my claim that, thirty feet down, I possessed the same clarity of vision as if I stood in the full light of day?

chapter_title: CHAPTER XV A WALK ON THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA
text: I walked across this ground covered in fine, powdery shell fragments for fifteen minutes. Gradually, the body of the Meridian vanished, looking much like a stretched-out sandbank; however, once night fell upon the sea, its light would shine clearly to lead us back to the vessel.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XV A WALK ON THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA
text: Shapes of items appearing far off were eventually visible. I identified grand stones, draped in a covering of zoophytes of the loveliest variety, and initially, I felt amazed by the strange influence of this environment.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XV A WALK ON THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA
text: The hour was ten o’clock; sunlight hit the water’s crest at a slanted trajectory, and as its beams met the surface, split by refraction like light through a prism, the borders of shells, polyps, plants, rocks, and flowers were tinted with the seven hues of the sun. This intricate display of shades was a wonder, a banquet for the vision, a complete kaleidoscope of indigo, blue, violet, orange, yellow, and green; in short, the entire collection of an ardent painter! How I wished I could share the vivid feelings rising in my mind with Baptiste, or match his exclamations of wonder? It was possible that Captain Sorel and his associate possessed the ability to trade ideas using prearranged signals. Thus, lacking a better outlet, I spoke to my own self; I recited aloud inside the copper helmet encasing my skull, wasting more oxygen on useless speech than was likely wise.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XV A WALK ON THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA
text: An assortment of isis, groups of unadulterated tuft-coral, spiny fungi, and anemones created a radiant floral garden, adorned with porphitæ, embellished by their blue-tentacled collars, sea-stars dotting the floor of sand, along with asterophytons resembling delicate lace stitched by the fingers of naïads, their garlands swaying in the soft ripples generated by our movement. I felt genuine sorrow at treading upon the vivid mollusc examples that littered the earth in their thousands, consisting of hammer-heads, donaciae (authentic leaping shells), staircases, and red helmet-shells, angel-wings, and numerous additional varieties generated by this boundless sea. Nevertheless, we were obligated to proceed, so we continued, while schools of physalides drifted overhead, trailing their tentacles behind them, and medusæ, their opal or rose-pink umbrellas scalloped with a blue border, provided us shade from the sun’s beams and fiery pelagiæ, which, during the night, would have scattered our way with glowing phosphorescence.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XV A WALK ON THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA
text: I witnessed all these marvels within a distance of a quarter of a mile, barely pausing as I trailed Captain Sorel, who signaled for me to continue. Before long, the composition of the ground altered; the sandy expanse gave way to a stretch of viscous mire, termed “ooze” by the Americans, which consisted of balanced proportions of silicious and calcareous shells. We proceeded across a field of seaweed characterized by untamed and abundant growth. This turf possessed a dense weave, felt gentle beneath our steps, and competed with the finest rugs produced by human craftsmanship. Yet, while greenery carpeted the ground below, it also remained above us. A delicate lattice of aquatic flora, belonging to that boundless lineage of seaweeds comprising over two thousand identified species, flourished upon the water’s surface. I observed lengthy strands of fucus drifting by, some spherical and others bulbous; there were laurenciæ and cladostephi featuring highly intricate leaves, alongside rhodomeniæ palmatæ that mimicked the shape of a cactus fan. I remarked that the green vegetation remained closer to the ocean’s surface, whereas the red varieties occupied deeper zones, entrusting the black or brown hydrophytes with the task of cultivating gardens and flowerbeds in the distant depths of the sea.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XV A WALK ON THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA
text: An hour and a half had passed since we left the Meridian. It was approaching midday; I was certain of this because the sun’s beams were vertical and had ceased to refract. Gradually, the enchanting hues faded, and the emerald and sapphire tones were wiped away. Our steady pace echoed against the floor with surprising force; even the faintest sound traveled with a speed unfamiliar to those on the surface, as water transmits acoustics four times more effectively than air. At that point, the ground began to incline, and the illumination became consistent. We had reached a depth of one hundred and five yards and twenty inches, where we endured a pressure of six atmospheres.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XV A WALK ON THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA
text: Even at this level, the sun’s beams remained visible, albeit weakly; the vivid brightness had been replaced by a crimson dusk, that dim transition period separating light from dark. Nevertheless, our vision remained clear; there was no call to utilize the Ruhmkorff apparatus quite yet. Just then, Captain Sorel halted; he lingered until I caught up to him, at which point he gestured toward a vague shape emerging from the gloom a little ways off.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XV A WALK ON THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA
text: “This is the woods of the Island of Carrizo,” I reflected;—and my assumption was correct.

Finally, we reached the edge of this woodland, surely among the most magnificent of the vast territories belonging to Captain Sorel. He viewed the area as his personal holding, believing his authority there matched that of the earliest humans during the dawn of time. Truly, who might have challenged his ownership of this underwater estate? What alternative, more courageous settler would arrive, axe in grip, to fell the shadowy thickets?

The woods consisted of massive tree-like vegetation; and as soon as we entered beneath those expansive arches, the unique arrangement of their limbs caught my attention—an arrangement I had not previously witnessed.

Neither the vegetation covering the earth nor the limbs dressing the woods showed signs of snapping or curving, and none grew out to the side; every one reached toward the sea’s top. No thread or strip, no matter how slender, failed to remain as rigid as a steel bar. Because of the thickness of the medium that fostered them, the fuci and llianas developed in stiff vertical rows. They stayed still, though if pushed aside by a hand, they immediately returned to their original stance. It was indeed the domain of perpendicularity!

I quickly grew used to this strange situation, along with the relative gloom that enveloped us. The ground of the woodland appeared strewn with jagged stones, which were hard to dodge. The underwater vegetation impressed me as being quite flawless, and more abundant than it might have been in the arctic or tropical regions, where such growths are less common. Yet for a few moments I unintentionally confused the species, mistaking zoophytes for hydrophytes, animals for plants; and who could have avoided such an error? In this undersea realm, the animal and plant life are linked too intimately.

These vegetations propagate themselves, their fundamental mode of being rooted in the water, which sustains and feeds them. Most of them sprouted blades of whimsical forms rather than leaves, displayed across a spectrum of hues—pink, carmine, green, olive, fawn, and brown. I observed there—not desiccated like our Meridian samples—pavonari fanned out as though to trap the wind; scarlet ceramies, with laminaries stretching out their consumable, fern-like nereocysti shoots that reach fifteen feet tall; groups of acetabuli, featuring stems that widen toward the top; and a multitude of additional sea plants, every one lacking blossoms!
“Strange irregularity, marvelous feature!” remarked a clever scientist, “where the fauna flourishes, and the flora does not!”

Beneath those many shrubs—comparable in scale to temperate-zone trees—and within their humid shade, gathered authentic thickets of vibrant blooms, hedges of zoophytes, where zebrameandrines with winding furrows and yellow caryophylliæ flowered; and, to finish the impression, fish-flies darted between branches resembling a cluster of humming-birds, while yellow lepisacomthi possessing spiny jaws, dactylopteri, and monocentrides ascended from our feet in a manner similar to a flock of snipes.

Roughly sixty minutes later, Captain Sorel signaled for us to stop. I certainly did not mind, and we laid ourselves out beneath a canopy of alariæ, whose slender, elongated leaves pointed upward resembling arrows.

To me, this brief respite felt exquisite; the only thing missing was the pleasure of talk. Since speaking or responding was out of the question, I simply pressed my massive copper helmet against that of Baptiste. I observed the honest man’s eyes shining with joy, and to demonstrate his contentment, he vibrated within his air-filled cuirass in the most amusing manner imaginable.

Following four hours of trekking, I was astonished that I did not feel ravenous. I remained unable to explain this condition of my belly. Conversely, I was overcome by an irresistible urge to doze, a sensation common to every diver. My eyelids shut quickly beneath the heavy lenses, and I drifted into a deep sleep, which the constant motion had previously hindered. Captain Sorel and his sturdy associate, lying within the transparent crystal, provided us with the model.

I am unable to determine the duration of my slumber; however, upon my awakening, the sun appeared to be descending near the skyline. Captain Sorel had stood up already, and as I commenced extending my arms and legs, a sudden vision caused me to spring up rapidly.

A short distance away, a gargantuan sea-spider, standing roughly thirty-eight inches tall, observed me with narrow eyes, prepared to leap. Even though my diving-suit possessed sufficient thickness to shield me from the creature’s jaws, I felt a shudder of revulsion. At that instant, Baptiste and the seaman from the Meridian stirred. Captain Sorel indicated the grotesque crustacean, which was toppled by a strike from the stock of a rifle, and I watched the beast’s ghastly pincers twist in violent spasms. This incident served as a reminder that more dangerous creatures might inhabit these murky waters, against which my suit would offer no defense. I had not previously considered this, yet I now determined to remain vigilant. I truly believed this pause signaled the end of our trek; however, I was wrong, as Captain Sorel pressed on with his daring journey rather than heading back to the Meridian. The terrain continued to slope, its gradient appearing to steepen as it guided us toward profounder depths. It was approximately three o’clock when we arrived at a constricted gorge, flanked by towering vertical cliffs, located at a depth of seventy-five fathoms. Owing to the excellence of our equipment, we had descended forty-five fathoms past the boundary that nature appears to have set for human underwater exploration.

I estimate the depth at seventy-five fathoms, despite lacking any device to measure the span. Yet I was certain that sunlight could not reach beyond that point, even in the most transparent seas. Consequently, the gloom grew more intense. Nothing could be discerned at a distance of ten paces. I was feeling my way forward when a vivid white glow appeared. Captain Sorel had activated his electric gear; his associate did likewise, and Baptiste and I mimicked them. By rotating a screw, I connected the wire to the spiral glass, and the ocean, brightened by our quartet of lanterns, became visible within a radius of thirty-six yards.

Captain Sorel continued to push forward into the gloom of the woods, where the timber grew thinner with each stride. I observed that the flora vanished more rapidly than the fauna. The medusæ had departed the parched earth, yet a vast array of creatures, including zoophytes, articulata, molluscs, and fishes, continued to find nourishment there.

While we moved, it occurred to me that the glow from our Ruhmkorff apparatus would surely entice some dweller out of its shadowy resting place. Yet, should they draw near, they maintained a cautious gap between themselves and the hunters. On multiple occasions, I observed Captain Sorel pause, raise his firearm to his shoulder, only to lower it after a brief interval and continue forward. Finally, following a duration of roughly four hours, this extraordinary journey concluded. A barrier of magnificent stones, standing in a grand formation, towered ahead of us—a pile of massive boulders, a towering, precipitous granite coastline, creating gloomy caverns, yet offering no climbable incline; it served as the foundation for the Island of Carrizo. It was land! Captain Sorel halted abruptly. A motion from him forced us all to cease our movement, and, despite my eagerness to climb the cliff, I was compelled to remain still. At this point, the territories of Captain Sorel reached their limit. He refused to venture past them. Beyond lay a segment of the world he was forbidden to tread upon.

The journey back commenced. Captain Sorel had resumed his position at the front of our small group, guiding our path with absolute certainty. It seemed to me that we were not retracing the route we had taken to reach the Meridian. This alternative path was quite precipitous, and as a result, extremely arduous. We drew near to the sea’s surface with speed. Yet, this ascent to the higher layers was not so abrupt as to alleviate the pressure too quickly, which could have triggered grave physiological disturbances and caused internal injuries, so perilous for divers. Before long, light returned and intensified, and with the sun hanging low in the sky, refraction gave the various items a spectral halo. At a depth of ten and a half yards, we moved through a school of small fish of every variety, more plentiful than the birds in the sky, and equally swift; however, no sea life worth hunting had yet appeared, when suddenly I watched the Captain swiftly raise his rifle and track a shifting target into the brush. He discharged his weapon;—I caught the sound of a faint whistle, and a beast dropped, dazed, a short way from us. It was a superb sea-otter, an enhydrus, the sole mammal that lives entirely in the ocean. This otter measured five feet in length and was surely of great worth. Its pelt, brown as a chestnut on the back and silver on the belly, would have produced one of those exquisite furs highly prized in the markets of Russia and China; the quality and sheen of its hair would surely command £80. I gazed at this strange creature, noting its curved head decorated with small ears, its circular eyes, and white whiskers reminiscent of a cat’s, along with its clawed, webbed feet and bushy tail. This valuable animal, pursued and stalked by hunters, is now quite scarce, having retreated mostly to the northern regions of the Pacific, or else its species would likely vanish before long.

The associate of Captain Sorel hoisted the creature onto his back, and we resumed our trek. A sandy expanse extended ahead of us for sixty minutes. Occasionally, it ascended to a distance of two yards and a few inches from the water’s top. At that point, I observed our reflection distinctly, rendered upside down, while overhead a matching assembly mirrored our gestures and deeds; in short, they were our exact doubles, save for the fact that they strode with their craniums pointed toward the ground and their soles facing the sky.

A further phenomenon I observed was the emergence and swift disappearance of dense clouds; yet, upon further consideration, I realized these apparent clouds resulted from the fluctuating density of the reeds submerged below, and I was able to perceive the frothy foam that their fractured tips increased upon the water, as well as the silhouettes of immense birds flying overhead, whose swift transit I could make out upon the ocean's surface.

At that time, I observed one of the most magnificent shots that has ever stirred a sportsman’s pulse. A massive avian with an expansive wingspan, easily seen, drew near, drifting above our heads. The associate of Captain Sorel lifted his firearm and discharged it while the target was merely a short distance over the swells. The animal dropped, dazed, and the momentum of its descent placed it inside the range of the skilled marksman’s reach. It was an albatross of the superior variety.

This event did not halt our trek. We traversed these stretches of sand for two hours, followed by patches of algæ that proved quite unpleasant to navigate. Honestly, I had reached my limit when a faint glow appeared, piercing the gloom of the sea for a distance of half a mile. It was the light from the Meridian. In less than twenty minutes, we would reach the vessel, and I would finally draw a comfortable breath, as the air provided by my tank felt severely lacking in oxygen. However, I failed to anticipate an unforeseen encounter, which postponed our return for a while.

I stayed a few paces back, until I noticed Captain Sorel rushing in my direction. Using his powerful grip, he forced me down to the earth, while his associate performed the identical action to Baptiste. Initially, I was confused by this abrupt assault, but my mind was quickly put at ease when I watched the Captain stretch out next to me and stay perfectly still.
Lying flat upon the earth beneath the cover of an algæ shrub, I lifted my head and observed a colossal shape, emitting glowing light, move noisily past.

A chill ran through my body when I identified a pair of dangerous sharks that posed a danger to us. They were two tintoreas, horrific beasts, possessing vast tails and vacant, vitreous gazes, with glowing substances emitted from apertures bored near their snouts. “Monstrous brutes!” which possessed the power to pulverize an entire human within their metallic maws. I was unsure if Baptiste paused to categorize them; personally, I observed their metallic-colored underbellies and their massive, tooth-filled gullets, from a perspective far from academic, and more as a potential prey item than a scholar of nature.

Fortunately, those ravenous beasts possess poor eyesight. They glided past us unnoticed, their tan fins grazing our bodies, and we survived a peril surely more severe than encountering a tiger head-on in the woods by a stroke of luck. Thirty minutes later, following the glow of the electric lamp, we arrived at the Meridian. Because the exterior hatch remained unlatched, Captain Sorel secured it immediately upon our entry into the initial chamber. Next, he pushed a button. I listened to the machinery of the pumps operating deep within the craft, sensed the liquid receding from my surroundings, and shortly thereafter, the compartment stood completely drained. The interior portal swung wide, and we stepped into the vestry.

After some difficulty, our diving-dress was removed; and, completely exhausted from a lack of nourishment and rest, I went back to my quarters, filled with amazement regarding this extraordinary trip to the ocean floor.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FOUR THOUSAND LEAGUES UNDER THE PACIFIC
text: On the morning of the 18th of November, having fully shaken off the exhaustion of the previous day, I climbed onto the platform at the precise moment the second lieutenant was speaking his customary sentence.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FOUR THOUSAND LEAGUES UNDER THE PACIFIC
text: While I was observing the impressive view of the sea, Captain Sorel arrived. Apparently oblivious to me, he commenced a sequence of celestial measurements. Once he concluded, he moved to rest against the watch-light enclosure, staring vacantly at the water. During this time, several crew members of the Meridian, each robust and fit, ascended to the deck. Their task was to retrieve the nets left out throughout the night. It was clear these seamen hailed from various countries, yet they all possessed European features. I identified several distinct Irishmen, Frenchmen, a few Sclaves, and one Greek or Candiote. They behaved politely, speaking only in that strange tongue I could neither identify nor ask them about.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FOUR THOUSAND LEAGUES UNDER THE PACIFIC
text: We pulled the nets aboard. They consisted of a substantial variety of “chaluts,” similar to the ones found along the Normandy coasts, which were vast pouches held agape by the currents and a chain secured within the finer webbing. These pouches, pulled by metal rods, moved across the depths and collected all items in their path. On that occasion, they retrieved strange examples from those fertile shores.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FOUR THOUSAND LEAGUES UNDER THE PACIFIC
text: I estimated that the catch amounted to over nine hundredweight of fish. It was an impressive haul, though hardly surprising. In truth, because the nets remain submerged for many hours, they capture a vast assortment of life. We suffered no shortage of superior sustenance, as the speed of the Meridian combined with the lure of the electric light ensured our stores were constantly replenished. These various marine yields were promptly sent down via the panel to the steward’s room, where some were prepared for immediate consumption and others were preserved.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FOUR THOUSAND LEAGUES UNDER THE PACIFIC
text: Once the angling concluded and the oxygen supply was replenished, I assumed the Meridian was set to resume its underwater voyage, so I began making my way back to my cabin, but the Captain pivoted toward me and stated, without any introductory remarks:

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FOUR THOUSAND LEAGUES UNDER THE PACIFIC
text: “Professor, does this sea not possess genuine vitality? It experiences both irritable and mild dispositions. While it slumbered alongside us yesterday, it has stirred following a peaceful night. Observe!” he added, “it rouses beneath the sun’s touch. It is preparing to begin its daily life once more. Observing the mechanics of its structure is a fascinating pursuit. It features a heartbeat, vessels, and contractions; and I concur with the esteemed Maury, who identified within it a flow as authentic as the movement of blood through living creatures.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FOUR THOUSAND LEAGUES UNDER THE PACIFIC
text: “Indeed, the sea possesses circulation, and to encourage this, the Creator has brought about the multiplication of elements within it—caloric, salt, and animalculae,” I said.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FOUR THOUSAND LEAGUES UNDER THE PACIFIC
text: The manner in which Captain Sorel delivered those words made him appear entirely transformed, and he stirred a profound agitation within me.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FOUR THOUSAND LEAGUES UNDER THE PACIFIC
text: “Furthermore,” he continued, “authentic life resides there; and I am able to envision the bases of seafaring settlements, groups of underwater dwellings, that, similar to the Meridian, would rise each dawn to inhale at the water’s level, liberated towns, autonomous cities. Still, who can say if some tyrant——”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FOUR THOUSAND LEAGUES UNDER THE PACIFIC
text: Captain Sorel concluded his statement using a sharp motion. Next, speaking to me as though to banish a melancholy idea:

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FOUR THOUSAND LEAGUES UNDER THE PACIFIC
text: “Do you know the depth of the ocean, M. Delorme?” he inquired.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FOUR THOUSAND LEAGUES UNDER THE PACIFIC
text: “What the main depth measurements have revealed to us is all I am aware of, Captain.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FOUR THOUSAND LEAGUES UNDER THE PACIFIC
text: “Would you be able to relate them to me, in order that I might adapt them to my own ends?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FOUR THOUSAND LEAGUES UNDER THE PACIFIC
text: “These are a few,” I answered, “that stay in my memory. Provided I am correct, a measurement of 8,000 yards in depth has been reached within the North Atlantic, while 2,500 yards has been recorded in the Mediterranean. The most noteworthy depth readings occurred in the South Atlantic, close to the thirty-fifth parallel, where results of 12,000 yards, 14,000 yards, and 15,000 yards were obtained. In conclusion, it is estimated that should the ocean floor be made flat, the average depth would reach approximately one and three-quarter leagues.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FOUR THOUSAND LEAGUES UNDER THE PACIFIC
text: “Well, Professor,” the Captain answered, “I trust we will demonstrate something superior to that. Regarding the average profundity of this segment of the Pacific, I inform you that it is merely 4,000 yards.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FOUR THOUSAND LEAGUES UNDER THE PACIFIC
text: After stating this, Captain Sorel walked to the panel and vanished down the ladder. I trailed behind him, entering the spacious drawing-room. The screw began to turn at once, and the log recorded a speed of twenty miles an hour.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FOUR THOUSAND LEAGUES UNDER THE PACIFIC
text: As the days and weeks went by, Captain Sorel visited quite infrequently. I rarely caught sight of him. Because the lieutenant consistently marked the path of the vessel upon the map, I remained capable of identifying the precise trajectory of the Meridian at all times.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FOUR THOUSAND LEAGUES UNDER THE PACIFIC
text: For a period, the drawing-room panels were slid back almost daily, and we remained perpetually fascinated by the secrets of the underwater realm.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FOUR THOUSAND LEAGUES UNDER THE PACIFIC
text: The Meridian maintained a south-easterly course, holding a depth ranging from 100 to 150 yards. On one occasion, though, for reasons unknown to me, the vessel was pulled along an angle by its inclined planes and made contact with the ocean floor. A reading of 4.25 (cent.) was shown on the thermometer: a degree of heat that appeared uniform across every latitude at that particular level.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FOUR THOUSAND LEAGUES UNDER THE PACIFIC
text: On the 26th of November at three in the morning, the Meridian passed the tropic of Cancer at 172° longitude. The 27th of the same month marked the sighting of the Sandwich Islands, the location of Cook’s death on February 14, 1779. By that time, we had traveled 4,860 leagues from our point of departure. Upon stepping onto the platform in the morning, I observed Hawaii, the biggest of the seven islands comprising the archipelago, situated two miles to windward. I had a clear view of the farmed hills, the various mountain ranges extending parallel to the coast, and the volcanoes towering above Mouna-Rea, which reach an elevation of 5,000 yards over the sea surface. Among the items retrieved by the nets were various flabellariae and elegant polypi, which are unique to that oceanic region. The Meridian continued its path toward the south-east. It passed the equator on December 1 at 142° longitude; then, on the 4th of that month, having traveled quickly and without notable incident, we spotted the Marquesas islands. Three miles away, I observed Martin’s peak on Nouka-Hiva, the primary island of the group under French control. I viewed only the forested mountains silhouetted against the skyline, as Captain Sorel chose not to bring the ship to the wind. The nets collected lovely fish there: some possessing azure fins and golden tails, with flesh that is unmatched; others lacking many scales but offering superb taste; and still others with bony jaws and gills tinged with yellow, comparable to bonitos; all of which were fish that would prove useful to us. Following our departure from these delightful islands under the French flag, the Meridian covered roughly 2,000 miles between the 4th and 11th of December.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FOUR THOUSAND LEAGUES UNDER THE PACIFIC
text: On the 11th of December, throughout the daylight hours, I occupied myself with a book inside the spacious drawing-room. Baptiste and Tom Harlan observed the glowing sea by way of the partially opened panels. The Meridian remained stationary. As its tanks underwent filling, the vessel maintained a position 1,000 yards below the surface, a zone infrequently explored by the sea and where substantial fish were rarely encountered.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FOUR THOUSAND LEAGUES UNDER THE PACIFIC
text: At that time, I was perusing a delightful volume authored by Jean Mace, titled The Slaves of the Stomach, and gaining useful insights from its pages, until Baptiste broke my concentration.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FOUR THOUSAND LEAGUES UNDER THE PACIFIC
text: “Could master step over here for a second?” he remarked, using an odd tone.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FOUR THOUSAND LEAGUES UNDER THE PACIFIC
text: “Baptiste, what is wrong?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FOUR THOUSAND LEAGUES UNDER THE PACIFIC
text: “I desire for master to observe.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FOUR THOUSAND LEAGUES UNDER THE PACIFIC
text: Standing up, I walked over and rested my weight on my forearms against the glass, gazing out.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FOUR THOUSAND LEAGUES UNDER THE PACIFIC
text: Bathed in brilliant electric illumination, a massive, stationary dark object hung suspended within the sea. I observed it with focus, attempting to discern the identity of this colossal whale-like creature. Then, an abrupt idea occurred to me. “A vessel!” I said, half aloud.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FOUR THOUSAND LEAGUES UNDER THE PACIFIC
text: “Indeed,” the Canadian answered, “a crippled vessel that has foundered vertically.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FOUR THOUSAND LEAGUES UNDER THE PACIFIC
text: Tom Harlan’s assessment was accurate; we neared a ship with frayed rigging dangling from its chains. The hull appeared intact, and the wreck had occurred no more than a few hours prior. Three mast remnants, snapped roughly two feet over the bridge, indicated the craft had been forced to jettison its masts. Having capsized, the vessel had taken on water and was listing to port. This remains of a former ship was a melancholy view as it rested submerged, yet the bridge offered a more tragic sight, where several bodies, secured by lines, remained. I tallied five—four males, one positioned at the wheel, and a female near the poop, cradling a baby. She appeared quite youthful. I could make out her face, untouched by decay thanks to the vivid illumination from the Meridian. In a final, hopeless act, she had lifted her child high—the unfortunate infant!—whose limbs were wrapped around its mother’s throat. The posture of the four mariners was ghastly, twisted by the spasmodic motions they had made in a final attempt to break the ropes tying them to the ship. Only the helmsman, serene, with a solemn, distinct expression, his silver hair plastered to his brow, and his fingers gripping the steering wheel, appeared even then to be navigating the three fractured masts across the deep sea.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FOUR THOUSAND LEAGUES UNDER THE PACIFIC
text: Such a spectacle! We stood speechless; our pulses raced at the sight of this wreck, appearing as if it had been snatched from reality and captured in its final instant. And I observed, approaching it with ravenous gazes, massive sharks, drawn by the scent of human meat.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XVII FOUR THOUSAND LEAGUES UNDER THE PACIFIC
text: Nevertheless, the Meridian veered, circling the sunken craft, and in a single moment I saw the words “The Florida, Sunderland” upon the stern.

That ghastly sight served as a precursor to the succession of nautical disasters the Meridian was fated to encounter on its journey. While we traversed more heavily traveled seas, we frequently observed the carcasses of sunken ships decaying in the abyss, and further below, artillery, projectiles, cables, iron links, and countless other metallic objects consumed by oxidation. Nevertheless, on the 11th of December, we spotted the Pomotou Islands, the former “dangerous group” of Bougainville, which span a distance of 500 leagues from E.S.E. to W.N.W., stretching from Ducie Island to that of Lazareff. This archipelago encompasses 370 square leagues and consists of sixty island clusters, notably the Gambier group, which is under French authority. These are coral formations, gradually elevated yet unbroken, fashioned by the constant labor of polyps. Eventually, this nascent landmass will merge with adjacent clusters, and a fifth continent will extend from New Zealand and New Caledonia, reaching as far as the Marquesas.
On an occasion while I was proposing this hypothesis to Captain Sorel, he answered in a frigid manner:
“New men are what the earth requires, not new continents.”

The Meridian had been steered by chance to the Island of Clermont-Tonnere, which is among the most intriguing of the cluster, having been found in 1822 by Captain Bell of the Minerva. I was at last able to examine the madreporic structure, responsible for the formation of the islands throughout this sea.

Madrepores, which should not be confused with corals, possess tissue covered by a limestone shell, and the variations in this composition led M. Milne Edwards, my esteemed mentor, to divide them into five categories. The tiny creatures produced by the marine polypus dwell in the millions within the base of their cavities. These lime-based secretions transform into stones, shoals, and islands of varying sizes. In some locations, they construct a circular shape enclosing a small interior lagoon that connects to the ocean through openings. Elsewhere, they build reef barriers similar to the ones found along the shores of New Caledonia and the different Pomoton islands. In other areas, such as those near Reunion and Maurice, they construct fringed reefs, which are tall, vertical embankments situated where the sea is quite deep.

A few cable-lengths from the coast of the Island of Clermont, I gazed in wonder at the immense structures built by these tiny laborers. These barriers are primarily the product of madrepores identified as milleporas, porites, madrepores, and astraeas. Such polyps inhabit the turbulent ocean floors, specifically close to the surface; therefore, they commence their building from the top down, gradually entombing themselves within the remnants of the secretions that sustain them. This is, at any rate, the hypothesis of Darwin, who describes the development of atolls in this manner—a concept I find more convincing than the alternative explanation that madreporic formations originate as the peaks of mountains or volcanoes that have sunk a few feet beneath the ocean’s surface.

I was able to examine these strange walls with care, as they descended more than 300 yards vertically, and our electric sheets illuminated this limestone substance with great brightness. In response to an inquiry from Baptiste regarding the duration required for these massive barriers to form, I greatly surprised him by stating that scholars estimated the rate at roughly an eighth of an inch every century.

As dusk approached, Clermont-Tonnerre vanished from view, and the Meridian adjusted its course noticeably. Having passed the tropic of Capricorn at 135° longitude, the vessel steered W.N.W., heading back toward the tropical region. Despite the intensity of the summer sun, we remained comfortable, as the water temperature at a depth of fifteen to twenty fathoms stayed between ten and twelve degrees.

On the 15th of December, we departed, leaving the enchanting Society Islands and the elegant Tahiti, monarch of the Pacific, to our east. During the morning, I observed the high peaks of the island positioned a few miles upwind. Our meals were supplied by these waters with superb fish, including bonitos, mackerel, and several types of sea-serpent.

The Meridian entered the center of the New Hebrides on December 25th, a location found by Quiros in 1606, investigated by Bougainville in 1768, and designated by its current title by Cook in 1773. This archipelago consists mainly of nine major islands, which create a strip 120 leagues long from N.N.S. to S.S.W., situated between 15° and 2° S. lat., and 164 deg. and 168° long. Our vessel traveled quite close to the Island of Aurou, which appeared at midday as a cluster of verdant forests topped by an extremely tall summit.

As it was Christmas Day, Tom Harlan appeared to deeply lament the lack of a “Christmas” observance, that domestic festival so cherished by Protestants. A full week had passed since my last encounter with Captain Sorel, until he entered the spacious drawing-room on the morning of the 27th, carrying himself with that habitual air of having seen you only moments ago. I was occupied with mapping the Meridian’s course upon the planisphere. Approaching me, the Captain touched a specific location on the chart and uttered this single word.
“Vanikoro.”
It felt enchanted! That was the title of the archipelago where La Perouse had vanished! I stood up abruptly.
“Has the Meridian transported us to Vanikoro?” I inquired.
“Indeed, Professor,” the Captain replied.
“And is it possible for me to see the famous isles upon which the Boussole and the Astrolabe ran aground?”
“Should you wish it, Professor.”
“At what time will we arrive?”
“We have arrived.”
With Captain Sorel trailing behind me, I ascended the platform and hungrily searched the skyline.

Two volcanic landmasses of differing scales rose to the N.E., encircled by a coral barrier spanning forty miles around. We had neared Vanikoro, specifically the portion Dumont d’Urville designated as Isle de la Recherche, and were positioned directly before the small port of Vanou, located at 16° 4′ S. lat. and 164° 32′ E. long. From the coast to the inland peaks, the ground appeared cloaked in greenery, topped by the 476-foot-tall Mount Kapogo. After navigating a slender passage through the exterior ring of stones, the Meridian entered waters filled with reefs where the depth ranged from thirty to forty fathoms. Beneath the leafy cover of several mangroves, I spotted a group of savages who seemed intensely astonished by our arrival. Within the elongated dark hull, gliding between the air and the waves, did they perhaps mistake us for a dangerous whale they viewed with distrust?
At that exact moment, Captain Sorel inquired as to my knowledge regarding the La Perouse shipwreck.
“Nothing beyond the common knowledge, Captain,” I answered.
“And would you mind informing me what is common knowledge regarding the matter?” he asked, with irony.
“With ease.”
I recounted to him everything revealed by the latest publications of Dumont d’Urville, of which the subsequent text provides a concise summary.

Louis XVI dispatched La Perouse, along with his second-in-command, Captain de Langle, on a global expedition in 1785. The pair set sail aboard the corvettes Boussole and the Astrolabe, vessels that were never reported from again. Concerned by the disappearance of these two sloops, the French Government outfitted the Recherche and the Esperance, a pair of substantial merchant ships, which departed from Brest on the 28th of September led by Bruni d’Entrecasteaux.

Sixty days later, word reached them via Bowen, who captained the Albemarle, that wreckage from sunken ships had surfaced along the shores of New Georgia. Nevertheless, D’Entrecasteaux disregarded this intelligence—which was, in any case, somewhat dubious—and steered instead for the Admiralty Islands, a location identified in a dispatch by Captain Hunter as the site of La Perouse’s disaster.

Their search proved fruitless. The Esperance and the Recherche sailed past Vanikoro and did not halt, and indeed, this expedition was highly calamitous, resulting in the deaths of D’Entrecasteaux, two of his lieutenants, and a number of his sailors.

The initial discovery of clear evidence regarding the shipwrecks was made by Captain Dillon, a clever veteran of Pacific voyages. On May 15, 1824, the St. Patrick, his ship, sailed near Tikopia, a location in the New Hebrides. A Lascar approached in a small boat and traded a silver sword handle featuring engraved markings on its grip. The Lascar claimed that half a dozen years prior, while visiting Vanikoro, he observed a pair of Europeans who were part of the crews from ships that had struck the coral reefs some time before.

Dillon surmised that he was referring to La Perouse, the man whose vanishing had disturbed the entire globe. He attempted to reach Vanikoro, a location where the Lascar claimed he would discover abundant remains of the shattered vessel, yet the currents and gales hindered his progress.

Dillon arrived back in Calcutta. Once there, he engaged the interest of the Indian Company and the Asiatic Society regarding his findings. A ship, christened the Recherche, was provided for his use, and he departed on the 23rd January, 1827, with a French agent in his company.
