Following visits to various Pacific locations, the Recherche dropped anchor off Vanikoro on 7th July, 1827, within the identical Vanou harbour occupied by the Meridian at that moment.

It gathered a variety of artifacts from the disaster site there—metal kitchenware, anchors, pulley-strops, swivel-guns, an 18 lb.-shot, pieces of scientific tools, a segment of crown work, and a bronze timepiece, marked with the engraving—“Bazin m’a fait,” the signature of the Brest arsenal foundry around 1785. The uncertainty had vanished.

After completing his investigations, Dillon remained at the ill-fated location until October. He subsequently departed Vanikoro and set a course for New Zealand; he arrived in Calcutta on 7th April, 1828, and traveled back to France, receiving a cordial reception from Charles X.

Simultaneously, unaware of the path taken by Dillon, Dumont d’Urville had commenced his own search for the site of the disaster. They had been informed by a whaling vessel that various medals along with a cross of St. Louis were discovered in the possession of indigenous people from Louisiade and New Caledonia. Dumont d’Urville, in command of the Astrolabe, had departed, arriving at Hobart Town two months after Dillon had exited Vanikoro. Upon reaching that location, he gathered the findings of Dillon’s investigation and discovered that James Hobbs, a second lieutenant serving on the Union of Calcutta, had observed iron bars and red fabrics utilized by the local inhabitants after coming ashore on an island at 8° 18′ S. lat. and 156° 30′ E. long. Uncertain and wary of trusting accounts from minor newspapers, Dumont d’Urville resolved to pursue the route of Dillon.

The Astrolabe arrived near Tikopia on February 10, 1828, where it recruited a runaway discovered on the island to serve as an interpreter and pilot; it then proceeded toward Vanikoro, coming into view of the location on the 12th of the month, remained positioned amidst the coral formations until the 14th, and only on the 20th did it drop anchor inside the reef at the port of Vanou.

On the 23rd, a number of officers circumnavigated the island, returning with a few insignificant items. By employing a strategy of evasion and denial, the locals declined to escort them to the ill-fated location. This equivocal behavior caused the officers to suspect that the inhabitants had mistreated the survivors; in fact, the natives appeared apprehensive that Dumont d’Urville had arrived to seek retribution for La Perouse and his doomed shipmates.
Nevertheless, on the 26th, having been calmed by a few gifts and realizing that there was no need to dread any retaliation, they guided M. Jacquireot to the location of the shipwreck.

Resting in water three to four fathoms deep, situated amidst the Pacou and Vanou reefs, were anchors, cannons, and ingots of lead and iron, all encased within calcareous deposits. The Astrolabe dispatched its large boat and whaler to that location, where the crews, encountering a degree of hardship, managed to hoist an anchor of 1,800 lbs., a cannon made of brass, several iron ingots, and a pair of copper swivel-guns.

Upon interrogating the local inhabitants, Dumont d’Urville discovered as well that La Perouse, having seen both of his ships destroyed against the reefs of this island, had built a tinier craft, which subsequently vanished once more. Nobody possessed knowledge of the location.

However, the French Government, anxious that Dumont d’Urville might be unaware of Dillon’s activities, dispatched the sloop Bayonnaise, under the leadership of Legoarant de Tromelin, to Vanikoro, having previously been positioned off the western shores of America. The Bayonnaise dropped anchor at Vanikoro a few months following the exit of the Astrolabe, yet discovered no fresh records; nevertheless, it reported that the local inhabitants had left the memorial to La Perouse undisturbed. This is the essence of the information I relayed to Captain Sorel.
“Therefore,” he remarked, “is there currently no knowledge regarding the location where the third ship was lost that the survivors built on the island of Vanikoro?”
“Nobody has any idea.”
Captain Sorel remained silent, yet gestured for me to accompany him inside the spacious saloon. The Meridian descended a few yards beneath the surface of the water, and the shutters were slid back.

I hurried toward the opening, and beneath the coral crusts, veiled by fungi, syphonules, alcyons, and madrepores, amidst countless delightful fish—girelles, glyphisidri, pompherides, diacopes, and holocentres—I identified various remnants that the dredges had failed to dislodge—iron stirrups, anchors, cannons, projectiles, capstan parts, and a ship’s prow, every item plainly confirming the destruction of a craft, currently draped in living blossoms. As I observed this grim spectacle, Captain Sorel remarked, in a mournful tone:

“Commander La Perouse departed on 7th December, 1785, aboard the ships La Boussole and the Astrolabe. His initial anchorage was at Botany Bay, followed by stops at the Friendly Isles and New Caledonia, before he steered toward Santa Cruz and entered Namouka, a member of the Hapai group. Subsequently, the vessels collided with the uncharted reefs of Vanikoro. The Boussole, leading the way, grounded upon the southern shore. The Astrolabe attempted a rescue, only to ground as well. The former ship suffered near-instant destruction. The latter, lodged leeward, endured for several days. The local inhabitants greeted the survivors hospitably. The men settled on the island and built a modest craft from the wreckage of the two primary ships. Certain crew members chose to remain at Vanikoro; the rest, suffering from illness and fatigue, embarked with La Perouse. They sailed in the direction of the Solomon Islands, where they met their end, along with all their belongings, on the western coast of the archipelago’s main island, situated between Capes Deception and Satisfaction.”
“In what way are you aware of that?”
“Through this, which I discovered at the location of the final shipwreck.”

A tin-plate box, marked with the French arms and eaten away by seawater, was presented to me by Captain Sorel. Upon his opening of the container, I observed a stack of documents that were yellowed yet remained legible.
These were the directives from the minister of the navy addressed to Commander La Perouse, with notes scribbled in the border by the hand of Louis XVI.
“Oh! a sailor’s death is a noble one!” Captain Sorel finally remarked. “A resting place of coral provides a peaceful burial; and it is my hope that my shipmates and I encounter nothing else.”

Between the night of December 27th and the 28th, the Meridian departed the coast of Vanikoro at high velocity. Steering a south-westerly path, the vessel traversed the 750 leagues between the location of La Perouse’s group and the south-east extremity of Papua within three days.
On the morning of January 1st, 1863, Baptiste met me at the platform.
“Will you allow me to offer you my best wishes for a happy New Year, Master?”

“What! Baptiste; precisely like I was in my office at the Jardin des Plantes in Paris? I appreciate your kind thoughts, and I offer my thanks. However, I must inquire as to your definition of a ‘Happy New Year’ given our current situation? Are you referring to the year that concludes our confinement, or the year that witnesses us persisting in this peculiar journey?” said I.

“Truly, I am uncertain how to respond, master. We will certainly witness strange sights, and for the past two months, boredom has had no place here. The most recent wonder is perpetually the most surprising; and, should this trend persist, I cannot say where it might conclude. It is my belief that we will never again behold such things. I conclude, therefore, with no disrespect to master, that a fortunate year would be one during which we might observe it all.”

By the 2nd of January, we had traveled 11,340 miles, equivalent to 5,250 French leagues, from the place where we began in the Japan Seas. The perilous coastlines of the coral sea, situated off the north-eastern edge of Australia, lay ahead of the ship’s bow. We were positioned a few miles from the formidable reef where the vessel belonging to Cook foundered on the 10th of June, 1770. The boat commanded by Cook impacted a rock, and the only reason it avoided sinking was that a fragment of coral snapped off during the collision and wedged firmly into the fractured keel.

My desire had been to see the reef, measuring 360 leagues in length, where the restless ocean crashed with immense force, producing a sound akin to thunder. However, the Meridian was pulled to a significant depth by the inclined planes at that moment, preventing me from viewing the towering coral barriers. I was forced to settle for observing the various fish samples retrieved by the nets. I took note, in particular, of some germons, a type of mackerel comparable in size to a tunny, featuring blue-tinted flanks marked by crosswise stripes that fade once the creature dies.

Schools of these fish trailed our vessel, providing us with a meal of great refinement. We additionally caught many gilt-heads measuring roughly one and a half inches in length, which possessed a flavor similar to dorys; furthermore, we captured flying pyrapeds resembling underwater swallows, creatures that illuminate the sea and sky in turns with their bioluminescence during pitch-black nights. Within the collection of zoophytes and molluscs, I discovered various types of alcyonarians, echini, hammers, spurs, dials, cerites, and hyalleae tangled in the net’s weave. The plant life consisted of exquisite drifting seaweeds, macrocystes, and laminariae, all saturated with the mucilage exuded from their pores; from this vegetation, I collected a magnificent Nemastoma Geliniarois, which was subsequently categorized as one of the museum’s natural wonders.

On 4th January, forty-eight hours following our transit of the Coral Sea, the shores of Papua appeared before us. At that time, Captain Sorel told me of his plan to reach the Indian Ocean via the Strait of Torres. He said nothing further.

Spanning nearly thirty-four leagues, the Torres Straits are hindered by a countless multitude of rocks, breakers, islets, and islands, rendering passage through them nearly impossible; consequently, Captain Sorel employed every necessary measure to traverse the area. Moving at a measured speed, the Meridian drifted between the wind and the water. The vessel’s screw struck the swells with a slow rhythm, resembling the tail of a whale.

Taking advantage of this, my two associates and I climbed onto the abandoned deck. The steersman’s cage stood ahead, and I anticipated finding Captain Sorel inside, guiding the Meridian. I held the superior maps of the Straits of Torres, which I studied with care. Violent waves crashed all around the Meridian. Moving from the south-east toward the north-west at a speed of two and a half miles, the swells shattered against the coral visible in scattered spots.
“The ocean is treacherous!” observed Tom Harlan.
“Truly loathsome, and a choice that fails to befit a vessel such as the Meridian.”
“I observe fragments of coral that could serve as a keel should the vessel merely graze them, so the Captain surely possesses great certainty regarding his course,” I said.

The circumstances were certainly perilous, yet the Meridian appeared to glide past those stones as if by enchantment. It did not replicate the paths taken by the Astrolabe and the Zelee, as those had resulted in tragedy for Dumont d’Urville. Instead, it inclined further north, skirted the Islands of Murray, and returned south-west in the direction of Cumberland Passage. I believed it intended to bypass the opening, but it turned north-west once more, navigating through a vast collection of obscure islands and islets, heading for the Island Sound and Canal Mauvais.

I questioned whether Captain Sorel, in his reckless lack of caution, might guide his ship toward the channel where the two corvettes of Dumont d’Urville had struck; then, veering once more and carving a direct path westward, he directed his course toward the Island of Gilboa.

At three o’clock in the afternoon, the tide, which had been at its peak, started to ebb. The Meridian drew near the island, which remained in my view, characterized by its distinct fringe of screw-pines. He maintained a distance of roughly two miles from it. All at once, I was knocked over by a jolt. The Meridian had grazed a stone and remained stuck, tilting slightly to the port side.
Upon rising, I noticed Captain Sorel and his lieutenant standing on the deck. They were observing the ship’s condition while speaking to one another in their unintelligible tongue.

Her position was as follows: Gilboa lay two miles off the starboard bow, extending from north to west in the shape of a giant limb. In the direction of the south and east, the receding tide had exposed patches of coral. We had struck bottom, and in a sea where the tides are only moderate—a dismal circumstance for the Meridian to get afloat. Nevertheless, the ship remained undamaged, as her keel was firmly connected. Yet, since she could neither slide away nor shift, she faced the danger of being permanently anchored to those stones, which would mean the end of Captain Sorel’s submarine vessel.
My thoughts were occupied in this manner, at which point the Captain, composed and collected, ever in command of his own temperament, drew near to me.
“A mishap?” I inquired.
“Not a; a happening.”
“However, a circumstance that might force you to reside in this country you are escaping?”
With a look of curiosity, Captain Sorel signaled his refusal, conveying that no power could compel him to step onto dry land once more. He then stated:

“Furthermore, M. Delorme, the Meridian has not been destroyed; it shall transport you still toward the heart of the oceanic wonders. Our expedition has merely commenced, and I have no desire to be robbed so quickly of the privilege of your presence,” said I.

“Nevertheless, Captain Sorel,” I answered, oblivious to the sarcasm in his remark, “the Meridian struck bottom in the middle of the ocean. Since the currents in the Pacific are weak, I fail to understand how the Meridian will be refloated if you are unable to reduce its weight.”

“The currents lack power throughout the Pacific: your assessment is correct, Professor; however, within Torres Straits, a variation of a yard and a half persists between the heights of the ebb and flow. This date is 4th January, and the moon reaches its fullness in five days. At this time, I would be greatly surprised if that celestial body fails to elevate these volumes of water enough to provide me with a favor for which I would owe her my gratitude.”

After stating this, Captain Sorel, with his lieutenant trailing behind him, went back down into the Meridian. The ship itself remained stationary, fixed in place as though the coralline polypi had encased it within their permanent mortar.
“Well, sir?” asked Tom Harlan, approaching me once the Captain had left.
“We shall bide our time for the tide on the 9th instant, friend Tom; it seems the moon is kind enough to delay it once more,” I said.
“Truly?”
“Indeed.”
“And this Captain is not going to cast anchor at all since the tide will suffice?” asked Baptiste, plainly.
The Canadian gazed toward Baptiste, before he gave a shrug of his shoulders.

“You can trust my word, sir, that this iron object is incapable of traveling upon or beneath the ocean ever again; its only value lies in being traded for its mass. Consequently, I feel the moment has arrived to sever my ties with Captain Sorel.”

“Friend Tom, I have not lost hope for this sturdy Meridian, unlike you; and within four days we will understand our situation regarding the Pacific tides. Furthermore, escaping might be an option were we visible to the English or Provencal coast; however, upon the Papuan shores, the circumstances differ; and we shall have sufficient time to reach that final measure should the Meridian fail to right itself, an occurrence I consider to be quite serious.”

“However, are they aware of how to behave with discretion? There exists an island; upon that island, trees grow; beneath those trees, land-dwelling creatures reside, providers of steaks and roasted beef, which I would gladly sample.”

“Friend Tom is correct in this,” Baptiste remarked, “and I am of the same opinion. Might the master not secure authorization from his acquaintance Captain Sorel to set us ashore, if merely to avoid forgetting how to walk upon the firm sections of our world?”
“I am able to inquire of him, yet he shall decline.”
“Is the master going to take the chance?” inquired Baptiste, “and we will discover how much we can count on the Captain’s good nature.”

Captain Sorel granted the request I made, much to my astonishment, and he did so quite pleasantly, not even requiring that I pledge to come back to the ship; however, traversing New Guinea could prove extremely dangerous, and I would not have advised Tom Harlan to try it. It is preferable to remain a captive upon the Meridian than to be captured by the locals.

Equipped with hatchets and firearms, we disembarked from the Meridian at eight o’clock. The ocean remained quite still, while a light wind drifted toward the shore. As Baptiste and I pulled the oars, we traveled with speed, and Tom guided us through the direct channel created by the surrounding surf. The vessel was managed skillfully and surged forward at a fast pace.
Tom Harlan found it impossible to contain his delight. He resembled a captive who had broken free from confinement, unaware that a return to it was inevitable.
“Meat! We shall consume some meat; and what meat!” he answered. “Genuine game! no, bread, in fact.”

“It is not my claim that fish lacks quality; we ought not to overindulge in it; however, a portion of venison, prepared over glowing embers, would provide a pleasant change to our standard fare,” said I.
“Greedy!” remarked Baptiste, “he causes my mouth to water.”
“Whether these woods contain prey, and whether that prey might turn the tables to stalk the stalker, is yet to be determined,” I said.

“You spoke truly, M. Delorme,” the Canadian answered, his teeth appearing as keen as a hatchet blade; “yet I shall consume tiger—tiger sirloin—provided there exists no alternative four-legged beast upon this island.”
“Baptiste noted, “Friend Tom is uneasy about it.”
“No matter what it is,” Tom Harlan went on, “any creature possessing four featherless paws, or two featherless paws, shall be greeted by my initial round.”
“All right! The foolish actions of Master Harlan are commencing.”
“Have no anxiety, M. Delorme,” the Canadian answered; “it will not take me twenty-five minutes to provide a meal, of my own style.”
The Meridian boat drifted gently onto a dense sandbank at eight-thirty, having successfully navigated the coral reef encircling the Island of Gilboa.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: The moment I stepped onto the shore, I felt a deep sense of awe. Tom Harlan tested the ground beneath his boots, appearing to claim it as his own. Yet, it had been a mere two months since we were, in the words of Captain Sorel, “passengers on board the Meridian,” though we were truly captives of its captain.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: Before long, we had approached the shoreline to within the range of a musket. A magnificent screen of woodland obscured the entire horizon. Massive trees, possessing trunks that reached 200 feet tall, were connected by festoons of bindweed, forming genuine natural hammocks that swayed in a gentle wind. These were a dense mixture of palm trees, hibisci, figs, and mimosas; beneath the protection of their leafy canopy flourished ferns, leguminous plants, and orchids.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: Yet, ignoring every one of those lovely examples of Papuan vegetation, the Canadian traded the pleasant for the practical. He located a coco-tree, knocked loose several of the fruits, cracked them open, and we consumed the milk and the meat with a contentment that served as a rebuke to the standard fare aboard the Meridian.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “Splendid!” remarked Tom Harlan.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “Magnificent!” answered Baptiste.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “And I do not believe,” the Canadian remarked, “that he would mind us bringing a shipment of coco-nuts aboard.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “I don’t believe he’d do it, yet he wouldn’t sample them,” I said.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “It is all the more unfortunate for him,” stated Baptiste.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “It is all the more advantageous for our side,” Tom Harlan answered. “A greater portion shall remain for us.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “Just a single word, Master Harlan,” I remarked to the harpooner, as he started to strip another coco-nut tree. “Coco-nuts are fine, but prior to loading the canoe with them, it would be prudent to scout the area to determine if the island offers any other equally beneficial items. The Meridian would certainly appreciate some fresh vegetables.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “The master is correct,” Baptiste answered; “and I suggest setting aside three spots aboard our craft, one for produce, another for greens, and the final one for the game, of which I have not witnessed even the tiniest example.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “We must not lose hope, Baptiste,” the Canadian stated.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “We should proceed,” I replied, “and stay hidden. Even if this island appears deserted, there could be inhabitants who are less demanding than we are regarding the treatment of prey.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “Ho! ho!” Tom Harlan remarked, shifting his jaw in a meaningful way.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “Tom, well!” said Baptiste.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “I am amazed!” the Canadian replied, “I am starting to grasp the appeal of cannibalism.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “Tom! Tom! what is it you are telling me? You, a cannibal? I would not consider myself secure in your company, particularly since we occupy the same cabin. It is possible I could awaken one morning to discover I had been partially consumed,” said I.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “I am quite fond of you, friend Baptiste, though not to the extent that I would consume you without cause.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “I wouldn't place any faith in you,” Baptiste answered. “However, that is enough. It is vital that we manage to kill some prey to appease this cannibal, otherwise, one of these pleasant mornings, master will discover nothing but fragments of his servant to provide for his meal.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: As we conversed in this manner, we made our way into the dark, vaulted passages of the woods, and for a duration of two hours, we examined the area throughout every quarter.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: Fortune favored our hunt for edible greens, and a highly beneficial tropical plant provided us with the valuable nourishment we lacked while aboard. I refer to the bread-fruit tree, which grows in great numbers on the island of Gilboa; I took particular note of the seedless type, known throughout Malaya as “rima.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: These fruits were familiar to Tom Harlan. Having consumed many throughout his frequent travels, he understood the method for readying the edible portion. Furthermore, the appearance of them stirred his enthusiasm, and he was unable to restrain himself any longer.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “I will perish,” he remarked, “unless I consume some of this bread-fruit pie.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “Sample it, companion Tom—sample it however you desire. We have arrived to conduct trials—conduct them.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “It will not be a lengthy process,” stated the Canadian.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: With a lens in hand, he ignited a blaze of dry timber that popped with delight. Meanwhile, Baptiste and I selected the finest bread-fruit specimens. A few had not yet reached a proper state of ripeness, their heavy rinds concealing a pulp that was pale yet somewhat stringy. The rest, mostly yellow and jelly-like, were ready for harvesting.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: No pits were contained within these fruits. A dozen were delivered by Baptiste to Tom Harlan, who sliced them into chunky pieces and set them upon a coal fire, all the while reciting:

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “You shall observe, master, the quality of this bread. Especially after one has gone without it for such an extended period. It is not truly bread,” he continued, “but rather a fine pastry. Have you not consumed any, master?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “Tom, no.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “All right, get ready for something succulent. Should you fail to return for another helping, then I have lost my title as the king of harpooners,” said I.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: Once a few minutes had passed, the section of the fruits facing the flames had been entirely cooked. Inside, it resembled a white paste, similar to a tender crumb, possessing a taste comparable to an artichoke.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: I must admit that this loaf was superb, and I consumed it with immense enjoyment.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “Is it currently what hour?” the Canadian inquired.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “It is two o’clock at the very least,” answered Baptiste.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “The speed at which hours pass when one is on solid earth!” Tom Harlan lamented.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “We should depart,” answered Baptiste.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: Back through the woods we made our way, finishing our gathering with an assault on the cabbage-palms, which we harvested from the tree crowns, along with small beans I identified as the “abrou” of the Malays, and yams of an excellent grade.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: Upon arriving at the boat, our cargo was already stowed. Tom Harlan, nevertheless, felt his supplies were inadequate. Luck, though, was on our side. At the exact moment we began to shove away, he noticed a group of palm-trees, standing between twenty-five and thirty feet tall.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: Finally, when the clock struck five in the afternoon, we departed the coast burdened by our treasures, and thirty minutes later we signaled the Meridian. Upon our return, nobody showed themselves. That vast cylinder of iron plating looked abandoned. Once the supplies were brought aboard, I went down to my cabin, ate my evening meal, and fell into a deep slumber.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: On 6th January, the following day, the ship remained unchanged. Within, there was neither noise nor any indication of existence. Our vessel lay moored at the margin, occupying the identical spot where we had abandoned it. We determined to head back to the island. Tom Harlan expressed a desire to explore a different section of the woods, hoping his luck in the hunt would improve compared to the previous day.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: We departed at daybreak. Propelled toward the coast by the surging tide, the boat arrived at the island within minutes.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: Upon landing, I decided it was wiser to yield to the Canadian, so we trailed after Tom Harlan, whose lengthy legs risked leaving us behind. He navigated the shoreline in a westerly direction, subsequently crossing several rushing streams to reach a plateau fringed by magnificent woods. A few kingfishers fluttered near the brooks, yet they refused to be drawn near. Their wariness convinced me that these creatures understood what to anticipate from humans like us, leading me to deduce that while the island might lack permanent residents, it was nonetheless visited by people from time to time.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: Following our traversal of an expansive grassland, we reached the edge of a small forest, which was animated by the soaring and vocalizations of numerous birds.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “Only birds exist here,” said Baptiste.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “However, they can be consumed,” the harpooner answered.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “I disagree with your assessment, friend Tom, as my eyes perceive nothing but parrots in that location.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “Friend Baptiste,” Tom remarked with gravity, “the parrot tastes like pheasant to individuals possessing no other food.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “Furthermore,” I continued, “this fowl, when properly cooked, deserves to be eaten with a knife and fork.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: Truly, beneath the dense canopy of these woods, a multitude of parrots darted between limbs, requiring merely diligent training to articulate human speech. Presently, they conversed with parrots of every hue and solemn cockatoos that appeared to be contemplating some intellectual riddle, as vibrant red lories flitted by like streamers caught in a gust, alongside papuans displaying the most exquisite shades of azure, and altogether a diversity of avian creatures most delightful to observe, though rarely suitable for consumption.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: Nevertheless, a creature of the avian variety unique to this region, which has never ventured beyond the boundaries of the Arrow and Papuan islands, was missing from this assortment. Yet, luck held it in store for me shortly thereafter.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: Having traversed a somewhat dense thicket, we came upon a field hindered by shrubs. It was then that I beheld those splendid birds, whose lengthy plumage necessitates that they travel into the breeze. Their rhythmic soaring, elegant arcs through the sky, and the tinting of their hues, drew and captivated my gaze. I experienced no difficulty in identifying them.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “Birds of paradise!” I cried out.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: The Malays, who conduct extensive commerce in these avian creatures with the Chinese, possess various methods for capturing them that we were unable to utilize. Occasionally, they set traps atop the towering trees that the birds of paradise favor. At other times, they ensnare them using a sticky birdlime that renders them immobile. They even resort to poisoning the springs where the birds typically quench their thirst. Conversely, we were forced to shoot at them while they were airborne, which provided us with minimal opportunity to secure them; consequently, we squandered half of our supply of ammunition to no avail.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: Around eleven in the forenoon, we crossed the initial chain of peaks constituting the island’s heart, having bagged no game. We were pushed forward by starvation. The hunters had counted on the fruits of the hunt, but their expectations were misplaced. Fortunately, Baptiste, much to his own astonishment, fired twice and obtained our morning meal. He downed a white pigeon and a wood-pigeon, which, after being skillfully cleaned and hung on a spit, were grilled over a glowing fire of dry timber. As these intriguing fowl roasted, Tom readied the bread-tree fruit. Subsequently, the wood-pigeons were consumed down to the skeleton and pronounced superb. The nutmeg, which they customarily consume to fill their gullets, seasons their meat and makes it a delectable dish.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “Tell me, Tom, what are you longing for at this moment?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “A four-legged creature, M. Delorme. These pigeons are merely appetizers and trivialities; and I will not be satisfied until I have shot a beast with cutlets,” I said.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “If I fail to capture a bird of paradise, neither shall I, Tom.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “We should keep on searching,” answered Baptiste. “Let us head in the direction of the ocean. Since we have reached the initial slopes of the mountains, I believe it would be best for us to return to the forested area.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: That counsel was logical, and we acted upon it. Following sixty minutes of travel, we reached a woodland filled with sago-trees. A few harmless snakes slithered out of our path. The birds of paradise took flight as we drew near, and I genuinely lost hope of ever reaching one until Baptiste, leading the way, dropped low, let out a shout of victory, and returned to me carrying a splendid example.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “Bravo, Baptiste, ah!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “The Master is truly excellent.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
