chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “Should master inspect this, he shall observe that I have earned no significant praise,” I said.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “For what reason, Baptiste?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “Since this avian creature is intoxicated to the degree of a quail.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “Intoxicated!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “Indeed, sir; intoxicated by the nutmegs it consumed beneath the nutmeg-tree, where I discovered it. Observe, companion Tom, witness the hideous consequences of excess!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “Good heavens!” the Canadian cried, “just because I have consumed gin for two months, you feel compelled to rebuke me!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: Nevertheless, I inspected the strange creature. Baptiste had spoken the truth. Intoxicated by the nectar, the bird was entirely helpless. It was unable to take flight; it could barely move on foot.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: Of the eight varieties located throughout Papua and the adjacent islands, this creature was a member of the most exquisite. It was the “large emerald bird, the most rare kind.” The specimen reached a length of three feet. Its head was relatively diminutive, featuring small eyes situated close to the base of the beak. The coloration was stunning, consisting of a yellow beak, brown claws and feet, wings the color of nuts with purple extremities, a head and neck of pale yellow, a throat of emerald hue, and a breast and belly of chestnut. Extending from beneath the tail were two downy, horned nets that lengthened the delicate, light feathers, finishing the appearance of this extraordinary animal, which the local inhabitants have lyrically titled the “bird of the sun.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: Although the bird of paradise fulfilled my desires, the Canadian remained unsatisfied. Fortunately, near two o’clock, Tom Harlan successfully hunted a superb hog; it belonged to the group the local people name “bari-outang.” This creature arrived just as we were able to obtain genuine four-legged meat, and it was welcomed. Tom Harlan took great pride in his marksmanship. Struck by the electric projectile, the hog dropped instantly dead. After removing six cutlets intended to provide us with a roasted meal that night, the Canadian properly skinned and dressed the carcass. The expedition then continued, becoming even more defined by the achievements of Tom and Baptiste.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: Truly, the pair of companions, thrashing through the undergrowth, startled a group of kangaroos which escaped and leapt away upon their springy feet. Yet, these creatures did not retreat with such haste that the electric capsule was unable to halt their path.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “Ah, Professor!” shouted Tom Harlan, swept up in the thrill of the hunt, “what magnificent prey, and already braised! Such a bounty for the Meridian! Two! three! five secured! And to imagine that we will feast on this meat, while the fools aboard will not receive a morsel!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: I suspect that, had the Canadian not been so talkative in his overwhelming delight, he might have slaughtered the entire group. Instead, he settled for capturing twelve of these fascinating marsupials. These creatures were diminutive. They belonged to a variety of those “kangaroo rabbitss” that typically dwell within tree cavities and possess remarkable swiftness; nevertheless, they are reasonably plump and provide, at the very least, respectable sustenance. We felt quite pleased with our hunting success. Happy Tom suggested coming back to this delightful island the following day, as he intended to clear it of every edible four-legged animal. However, he had failed to account for the circumstances.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: By six in the evening, we had returned to the coast, securing our vessel at the customary spot. Positioned two miles off the sands, the Meridian rose above the surf, resembling an elongated stone. Immediately, Tom Harlan set to work on the vital task of preparing our meal. He possessed a true talent for culinary arts. Before long, the aroma of the “bari-outang” roasting over the embers drifted through the atmosphere, smelling exquisite.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: The meal was, in truth, superb. This remarkable bill of fare was rounded out by a pair of wood-pigeons. We were delighted by the sago pasty, the artocarpus bread, a selection of mangoes, six pineapples, and the drink made from fermented coco-nuts. I suspect that the thoughts of my esteemed associates lacked a certain necessary simplicity.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “What if we fail to make it back to the Meridian tonight?” asked Baptiste.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: “What if we don’t make it back?” Tom Harlan inquired.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XX A FEW DAYS ON LAND
text: At that exact moment, a rock landed right by our feet, abruptly ending the harpooner’s suggestion.
Remaining seated, we gazed toward the woods’ boundary, my own hand arrested mid-motion as I reached for my lips, while Tom Harlan’s finished its task.
“Rocks do not descend from the heavens,” Baptiste noted, “otherwise they would be called aerolites.”

A further rock, thrown with precision, which caused a tasty pigeon leg to drop from the grasp of Baptiste, lent additional gravity to his remark. The three of us stood up, hoisted our firearms, and prepared ourselves to answer a potential assault.
“Do those creatures happen to be apes?” shouted Tom Harlan.
“Almost—they are barbarians.”
“To the boat!” I exclaimed, rushing toward the ocean.

A withdrawal was certainly required, as approximately twenty indigenous people carrying slings and bows emerged at the edge of a small wood obscuring the skyline to our right, barely one hundred paces away.
Approximately sixty feet away, our vessel lay anchored. The savages drew near, refraining from a sprint, yet displaying aggressive gestures. A dense shower of arrows and stones descended upon us.

Tom Harlan was reluctant to abandon his supplies, yet he moved at a reasonable pace, ignoring the threat posed by the pig nearby and the kangaroos flanking him. Within two minutes, we reached the coastline. It took only a moment to stow the weapons and food in the vessel, shove it into the water, and set the oars. We had traveled no more than two cable-lengths before a hundred natives, screaming and waving their arms, waded into the surf until the water reached their waists. I kept my eyes on the platform to see if their sudden arrival might draw anyone from the Meridian. However, there was nothing. The massive craft, anchored offshore, remained entirely empty.
We boarded twenty minutes afterward. The hatches stood ajar. Once we had secured the vessel, I stepped inside the Meridian.
I went down to the drawing-room, where the sound of chords reached me. Captain Sorel stood there, leaning across his organ, lost in a state of musical rapture.
“Captain!”
I was not heard by him.
“Captain!” I exclaimed, making contact with his hand.
He trembled, and, pivoting about, remarked, “Ah! it is you, Professor? Well, have you enjoyed a productive search, have you botanised with success?”
“Indeed, Captain; however, we have unhappily transported a group of bipeds, and their proximity disturbs me,” I said.
“What bipeds?”
“Barbarians.”

“Savages!” he repeated, with irony. “Are you surprised, Professor, to have stepped onto an unfamiliar territory and encountered savages? Savages! where do they not exist? Furthermore, are these individuals you label as savages any more depraved than the rest?”
“However, Captain——”
“What is the total you have tallied?”
“At minimum, a hundred.”

“M. Delorme,” Captain Sorel answered, resting his hands upon the organ keys, “once the entirety of the Papua population has gathered along this coast, the Meridian shall face no danger from their assaults.”

The Captain’s digits moved across the device’s keys, and I noted that he played merely the black ones, lending his tunes a distinctly Scotch quality. Before long, he was oblivious to my being there, having sunk into a daydream I chose not to interrupt. I ascended once more to the platform: darkness had descended; because, at this shallow latitude, the sun drops quickly and lacks any twilight. I could perceive the island only vaguely; yet the many flames, kindled upon the shore, indicated that the inhabitants had no intention of departing. I remained solitary for a few hours, at times pondering the inhabitants—though lacking any fear of them, as the Captain’s unshakable assurance proved infectious—at other times ignoring them to take in the magnificence of the tropical night. My thoughts drifted toward France, following those zodiacal stars destined to glow in a few hours. The moon gleamed surrounded by the constellations at the zenith.

The darkness passed by free of any mishap, as the islanders were surely intimidated by the appearance of a beast beached within the bay. Because the panels remained unfastened, they would have provided a simple entry point into the inside of the Meridian.

I climbed onto the platform at six o’clock on the morning of the 8th January. Daybreak was occurring. As the mists cleared, the island became visible, revealing the coastline initially, followed by the peaks.

The indigenous people were present, in greater numbers than the previous day—possibly five or six hundred—and a few, taking advantage of the receding tide, had stepped onto the coral, within two cable-lengths of the Meridian. I could see them clearly; they were genuine Papuans, possessing muscular builds, men of a fine lineage, with tall, prominent foreheads, and teeth that were large but neither wide nor flattened. Their frizzy hair, tinted with red, stood out against their glistening black skin, reminiscent of Nubians. Hanging from their pierced and stretched earlobes were strings of bones. The majority of these wild men wore no clothing. I noticed several women among them, wearing skirts of herbs reaching from their hips to their knees, supported by a belt made of vegetation. Certain leaders had decorated their throats with crescents and necklaces of red and white glass beads; nearly every one of them held bows, arrows, and shields, and slung over their backs were nets filled with the spherical stones they launched from their slings with impressive precision. One such chief, positioned quite close to the Meridian, studied it with focus. He was likely a “mado” of significant status, as he was wrapped in a banana-leaf mat, trimmed with notches along the borders and decorated in vibrant hues.

I might have readily struck this native down, as he stood only a short distance away; yet I decided it was preferable to hold off until actual aggressive actions occurred. When dealing with savages, it is right for Europeans to defend themselves decisively, rather than to strike first.

When the water level was down, the local people wandered in the vicinity of the Meridian, though they caused no bother; I often listened to them say the word “Assai,” and from their physical motions I gathered they were asking me to step ashore, a request I refused.
Consequently, the vessel failed to depart that afternoon, much to the annoyance of Master Harlan, as he remained unable to finish gathering his supplies.

That skillful Canadian spent his hours readying the food and flesh he had retrieved from the island. Regarding the savages, they went back to the coast near eleven in the morning, once the coral summits started to vanish beneath the swelling tide; yet I noticed their count had grown quite a bit on the beach. They likely arrived from nearby islands, or perhaps from Papua. Still, I had not spotted one native canoe. With no superior task at hand, I considered dredging those lovely clear waters, where I observed an abundance of shells, zoophytes, and sea vegetation. Furthermore, it was the final day the Meridian would spend in this vicinity, provided it drifted in the open ocean the following day, per the pledge of Captain Sorel.

I summoned Baptiste, and he handed me a small dredge, similar to the ones utilized in the oyster trade. Time to begin! We hauled in our catch continuously for two hours, though we discovered no curiosities. The net contained midas-ears, harps, melames, and especially the finest hammers I have witnessed. We also retrieved a few sea-slugs, pearl-oysters, and twelve small turtles, which were set aside for the ship’s kitchen.

Yet at the moment I anticipated it the least, my fingers brushed against a marvel, perhaps a biological anomaly, that is encountered quite seldom. Baptiste was in the middle of dragging, and his mesh arrived at the surface brimming with various common shells, when, suddenly, he observed me thrust my hand rapidly into the netting to retrieve a shell, and he listened to me let out a shout.
“Is something wrong, sir?” he inquired, looking astonished. “Has master received a bite?”
“Not at all, lad; though I would have gladly sacrificed a digit for the sake of my finding,” I said.
“Which finding?”
“This shell,” I remarked, as I raised the item representing my victory.
“It is merely a porphyry olive, of the olive genus, belonging to the order pectinibranchidæ, within the class of gasteropods, and the sub-class mollusca.”
“Indeed, Baptiste; however, rather than rotating from the right toward the left, this olive spins from the left toward the right,” I said.
“Could it be?”
“Indeed, lad; that is a shell from the left side.”
With few deviations, shells possess a right-handed orientation; should their coil happen to turn left, collectors are prepared to offer their equivalent in gold.

Baptiste and I were engrossed in examining our prize, and I was vowing to donate it to the museum, when a rock unluckily cast by a native hit and shattered the valuable item Baptiste held. I let out a wail of misery! Baptiste grabbed his rifle and took aim at a savage who was readying his sling ten yards away. I attempted to restrain him, but his shot landed and smashed the string of amulets wrapped around the savage’s arm.
Baptiste grabbed his firearm.
“Baptiste!” I shouted. “Baptiste!”
“Is it not apparent to you, sir, that the cannibal has initiated the assault?”
“The life of a man is worth more than a shell,” I remarked.
“Oh! that villain!” exclaimed Baptiste; “I prefer he had fractured my shoulder!”

Baptiste spoke sincerely, yet I disagreed with him. Nevertheless, circumstances had altered moments earlier, though we remained unaware. Twenty canoes encircled the Meridian. These vessels, hollowed from tree trunks, slender and elongated, designed for rapid travel, were steadied by a lengthy bamboo spar resting upon the surface. Expert, partially unclothed rowers operated them, and I observed their approach with a measure of anxiety. It was clear these Papuans possessed prior experience with Europeans and recognized their vessels. Yet, what might they surmise regarding this elongated iron tube moored within the inlet, lacking both stacks and sails? Nothing favorable, as they initially maintained a cautious interval. Still, observing its stillness, they gradually grew bold and attempted to grow accustomed to it. This intimacy was exactly what had to be prevented. Our weaponry, being silent, could only exert a limited influence upon these natives, who value little beyond clamorous objects. A lightning bolt devoid of the rumble of thunder would scarcely alarm a person, even if the peril resides in the flash rather than the sound.
The Meridian was reached by the canoes just then, and a rain of arrows landed upon her.
Descending to the saloon, I discovered it was deserted. I took the chance to rap upon the entrance leading to the Captain’s quarters. “Come in,” came the reply.
Upon entering, I discovered Captain Sorel immersed in the algebraical computation of x and various other values.
“My presence is an intrusion,” I remarked, out of politeness.
“That is correct, M. Delorme,” the Captain answered; “yet I suspect you possess grave motives for desiring an audience with me?”
“Extremely serious ones; the local people are encircling our vessel with their canoes, and before long we will undoubtedly be assaulted by several hundred savages,” I said.
“Ah!” Captain Sorel murmured, “have they arrived in their canoes?”
“Affirmative, sir.”
“We are required to secure the hatches, sir,” I said.
“Precisely, and my purpose in coming was to tell you——”
“It could not be any more straightforward,” Captain Sorel stated. Then, by pushing a button powered by electricity, he sent a command to the crew of the ship.

“Everything is finished, sir,” he stated, following a brief pause. “The pinnace stands prepared, and the hatches are secured. I assume you do not worry that these gentlemen might break through bulkheads that withstood the cannon fire of your frigate?”
“There is still a threat, Captain; no.”
“Sir, what is that?”

“It is the case that tomorrow, near this time, we are required to unseal the hatches to refresh the atmosphere of the Meridian. If the Papuans were to seize the platform at that instant, I fail to perceive how you might stop them from coming inside,” said I.
“In that case, sir, do you believe they intend to board us?”
“I am positive.”

“Indeed, sir, allow them to approach. I perceive no cause to obstruct them. Ultimately, these Papuans are miserable beings, and I am reluctant for my stay on the island to result in the death of even one of these unfortunates,” I said.

I prepared to depart, yet Captain Sorel held me back, requesting that I take a seat beside him. He inquired curiously regarding our trips onto land and our pursuit of game; he appeared unable to grasp the hunger for flesh that gripped the Canadian. The talk shifted to diverse topics, and while remaining no more forthcoming, Captain Sorel appeared friendlier.
We discussed, among various topics, the predicament of the Meridian, which had gone aground in the very location within this strait where Dumont d’Urville had almost met his end. Regarding this:

“D’Urville was among your finest mariners,” the Captain remarked to me, “a navigator of the highest intellect. He serves as the Captain Cook for you French people. A tragic scholar, who survived the South Pole’s ice, the reefs of Oceania, and the Pacific’s cannibals, only to meet a wretched end on a train! If that vigorous individual had the chance to ponder his final seconds, what do you imagine occupied his mind?”

As he spoke, Captain Sorel appeared touched, and this display of feeling improved my estimation of him. Next, holding the map, we went over the journeys of the French navigator, including his trips around the globe, his two-time confinement at the South Pole, which resulted in the finding of Adelaide and Louis Philippe, and the determination of the hydrographical coordinates for the main islands of Oceania.

“What your D’Urville accomplished upon the ocean’s surface,” Captain Sorel remarked, “that have I achieved beneath it, and with greater ease and more thoroughness than he. The Astrolabe and the Zelee, constantly buffeted by the gale, could never compare to the Meridian, a serene sanctuary of industry that she is, perfectly still amidst the waves.”
“To-morrow,” the Captain remarked, as he stood up, “at twenty minutes to three p.m., the Meridian will be afloat, and will depart the Strait of Torres without damage.”
After stating these words in a clipped manner, Captain Sorel gave a brief bow. I understood this as a signal to leave, so I returned to my quarters.
Upon arriving there, I encountered Baptiste, who was eager to learn how my meeting with the Captain had concluded.

“My lad,” I remarked, “at the moment I pretended to credit the notion that his Meridian was under threat from the Papua locals, the Captain retorted with great irony. I possess only a single statement for you: Trust in him, and rest easy.”
“Do you require no assistance from me, sir?”
“Negative, my companion. In what activity is Tom Harlan engaged?”
“Pardon me, sir,” replied Baptiste, “friend Tom is occupied preparing a kangaroo-pie that shall be a wonder.”

Left by myself, I retired to my quarters, though my rest was fitful. The clamor of the savages reached my ears as they pounded upon the deck, letting out shrieks that were ear-splitting. The hours of darkness went by in this fashion, failing to interrupt the usual slumber of the ship's company. They were as indifferent to the existence of these cannibals as the gunners of a hidden battery are to the insects creeping across their emplacement.

I got up at six o’clock. No hatches had been unsealed. Although the interior air remained stale, we turned to the reserves, which were prepared for such crises, and released a few cubic feet of oxygen into the depleted atmosphere of the Meridian.
Until midday, I remained occupied in my quarters, never once catching sight of Captain Sorel. There were no signs of any arrangements for leaving on the ship.

I remained motionless for a while, before entering the spacious saloon. The timepiece indicated two-thirty. High tide was due in ten minutes: and, provided Captain Sorel had not given a reckless pledge, the Meridian was to be released at once. Otherwise, a great many months would elapse before she might depart from her coral resting place.
Nevertheless, certain cautionary tremors started to manifest throughout the vessel. I perceived the keel scraping along the jagged lime-based floor of the coral reef.
Captain Sorel entered the saloon at twenty-five minutes before three.
“The commencement is at hand,” he stated.
“Oh!” I answered.
“The command to unseal the hatches has been issued by me.”
“What about the Papuans?”
“The Papuans?” Captain Sorel replied, giving his shoulders a slight shrug.
“Are they not going to enter the Meridian?”
“How?”
“You can only succeed by jumping across the hatches that you have unsealed.”
“M. Delorme,” Captain Sorel replied in a low voice, “they are not going to get through the Meridian hatches like that, regardless of whether they are left unsealed.”
My gaze rested upon the Captain.
“Are you failing to grasp this?” he asked.
“Scarcely.”
“You shall see if you come along.”

My path led me to the main stairs. There, Baptiste and Tom Harlan were covertly observing a few of the ship’s crew as they unsealed the hatches, amidst the echoing of furious shouts and terrified clamor from beyond.

Outside, the port lids had been lowered. Twenty ghastly visages emerged. Yet the initial native to set his hand upon the stair-rail was hit from the rear by a power unseen, I know not what, and he retreated, screaming terrifying shrieks and performing the most frantic contortions.
A group of ten associates trailed behind him. They encountered an identical outcome.
Baptiste felt ecstatic. Driven by his fierce impulses, Tom Harlan sprinted toward the stairs. Yet, the instant he gripped the banister with both hands, he was likewise knocked down.
“A lightning bolt has hit me,” he shouted, swearing.

Everything was now clear. It was not a rail, but rather a metal wire electrified by the deck and linked to the platform. Any person who made contact with it experienced a strong jolt—a jolt that would have proven fatal had Captain Sorel sent the entire intensity of the current into the conductor. One could accurately claim that he had placed a web of electricity between his attackers and his own person, which no one could cross without suffering the consequences.

In the interim, the frustrated Papuans had withdrawn, frozen by fear. We, for our part, were partially amused as we comforted and massaged the distressed Tom Harlan, who cursed with the intensity of a demon.

Just then, the Meridian, lifted by the final swells of the tide, departed from her coral resting place precisely at the fortieth minute designated by the Captain. Her propeller churned the sea with a slow and majestic motion. Gradually, her velocity rose, and as she navigated the ocean’s surface, she exited the perilous channels of the Straits of Torres without a scratch.

On the 10th of January, the day after, the Meridian maintained her path amidst two oceans, yet at a velocity so extraordinary that I judged it to be no fewer than thirty-five miles per hour. The propeller spun with such haste that I found it impossible to track or tally its rotations. As I considered how this wondrous electric power, having provided the Meridian with propulsion, warmth, and illumination, also shielded her from external assault, turning her into a sanctuary that no unhallowed touch could approach without meeting a lightning-bolt’s end, my awe knew no limits, moving from the vessel’s design to the creator who had brought it to life.

We steered a westerly path, and on January 11th we rounded Cape Wessel, located at 135° longitude and 10° north latitude, serving as the eastern boundary of the Gulf of Carpentaria. Although reefs remained plentiful, they were more uniform and mapped with great accuracy. The Meridian navigated past the Money breakers on the port side and the Victoria reefs to the starboard without difficulty, as they were situated at 130° longitude along the 10th parallel, which we adhered to precisely.
Captain Sorel reached the Sea of Timor on the 13th of January, where he identified the island bearing that same name at 122° longitude.

At this juncture, the Meridian began to veer in a south-westerly course. Her bow was pointed in the direction of the Indian Ocean. To what destination would the whims of Captain Sorel lead us? Might he steer back toward the Asian coastline, or would he once more draw near to the borders of Europe? Both were unlikely theories for an individual who escaped from populated landmasses. Would he then travel toward the south? Was it his intention to round the Cape of Good Hope, followed by Cape Horn, and ultimately reach the Antarctic pole? Would he eventually return to the Pacific, a place where his Meridian might navigate with liberty and autonomy? The future would reveal the answer.

Following our passage along the sands of Cartier, of Hibernia, Seringapatam, and Scott—those final remnants of solid ground resisting the liquid expanse—we ceased to see land on the 14th of January. The Meridian moved at a much slower pace, and as she traveled an uneven path, she would occasionally submerge within the depths or drift upon the top of the waves.

Throughout this phase of the journey, Captain Sorel conducted intriguing trials regarding the fluctuating heat of the ocean at various levels. Typically, such measurements are taken using intricate tools that frequently yield questionable data, such as thermometric sounding-leads—which often shatter from aquatic pressure—or devices based on how metal resistance shifts in response to electrical currents. Findings gathered in this manner were impossible to determine with precision. Conversely, Captain Sorel personally examined the temperatures within the deep ocean, and his thermometer, linked to the distinct layers of water, provided the necessary readings instantly and precisely.

In this manner, whether through the overfilling of her tanks or by way of an angled descent utilizing her slanted planes, the Meridian reached depths of three, four, five, seven, nine, and ten thousand yards in turn, and the conclusive finding of this trial was that the ocean maintained a mean heat of four and a half degrees at a distance of five thousand fathoms down across every latitude.

On January 16th, the Meridian appeared to be stalled just a few feet under the ocean swell. Its electrical systems were dormant, and because the propeller was not turning, the vessel drifted wherever the tides took it. I assumed the staff was busy with maintenance inside, which had become essential due to the intensity of the engine’s physical vibrations.

A strange sight then presented itself to me and my associates. Because the Meridian’s beacon was inactive, the saloon hatches stood open, leaving the surrounding depths in a state of murky darkness. As I examined the ocean in this gloom, even the biggest fish seemed like nothing more than vague silhouettes, until the Meridian was abruptly bathed in intense illumination. Initially, I assumed the beacon had been activated, projecting its electric glow through the water. I was wrong, and a quick glance revealed my misapprehension.

The Meridian drifted through a glowing expanse that grew remarkably radiant within the darkness. Countless tiny, light-emitting creatures created this effect, their brightness intensifying as they slid across the ship’s steel exterior. I felt as if I were being struck by lightning amidst these shimmering layers, which resembled streams of molten lead in a fiery kiln or metal objects heated to a white glow; consequently, the stark contrast made some areas of illumination seem to throw shadows into the surrounding blaze, where darkness should have been entirely absent. No; this lacked the steady glow of typical lightning. It possessed an extraordinary vitality and energy: this was genuinely living light!

Actually, it consisted of a boundless collection of tinted infusoria, true jelly globules, equipped with a filamentous tentacle, and of which a count of twenty-five thousand has been reached within a volume of water smaller than two cubic half-inches.

For a span of multiple hours, the Meridian drifted through those radiant swells, and our wonder grew while observing the sea creatures frolicking akin to salamanders. Amidst that flame which does not consume, I beheld the agile and graceful porpoise—the tireless jester of the deep—alongside swordfish measuring ten feet, those ominous precursors to tempests whose fearsome blades occasionally impacted the saloon’s windows. Next, tinier specimens emerged, including the balista, the jumping mackerel, wolf-thorn-tails, and a century of additional species that streaked through the glowing medium as they moved. This brilliant display was spellbinding! It is possible that a specific meteorological state heightened the power of this occurrence. It is possible that a gale disturbed the tops of the billows. Yet, at this submersion of several yards, the Meridian remained untouched by such violence, resting serenely in tranquil depths.

Thus we continued, constantly delighted by a fresh wonder. Time slipped by quickly, and I kept no track of it. Tom, following his custom, attempted to diversify the food on the vessel. We remained attached to our hulls just as snails are, and I maintain that living a snail’s life is simple.

In this way, our existence felt effortless and innate, and we ceased to dwell upon the days we spent ashore; however, an occurrence took place that reminded us of how peculiar our circumstances truly were.

The Meridian sat at 105° long. and 15° S. lat. on the 18th of January. A tempestuous atmosphere hung over the churning, turbulent waters, driven by a powerful wind from the east. Because the barometer had been dropping for a number of days, a gale was clearly approaching. I ascended to the platform at the precise moment the second lieutenant was calculating the horary angles, and I lingered, as was my custom, for the daily phrase to be uttered. However, it was replaced that day by a different expression that was equally difficult to understand. Nearly at once, I observed Captain Sorel emerge holding a glass, his gaze fixed upon the horizon.

He remained motionless for several minutes, his gaze fixed steadily upon the observation point. Afterwards, he dropped his telescope and spoke briefly with his lieutenant. The subordinate appeared to be struggling with an agitation he could not successfully hide. Captain Sorel, possessing greater self-control, remained composed. He also appeared to be raising points of disagreement, to which the lieutenant responded with official declarations. I inferred this from the contrast in their manners and voices. As for me, I had scanned the specified area thoroughly but observed nothing. The boundary where the sky met the sea had vanished into the sharp line of the horizon.

Captain Sorel, meanwhile, paced the length of the platform, ignoring my presence, or possibly failing to notice me at all. Although his stride remained steady, it lacked its customary rhythm. From time to time, he halted, folded his arms, and gazed out at the ocean. What might he be searching for across that vast stretch of water?
At that time, the Meridian was positioned several hundred miles away from the closest shoreline.

The lieutenant held the telescope, peering intently at the skyline as he paced back and forth, thumping his heel and displaying greater anxiety than his commanding officer. Furthermore, this enigma demanded an immediate resolution; consequently, following a directive from Captain Sorel, the engine boosted its thrust, causing the screw to rotate with greater speed.

At that moment, the lieutenant once more signaled to the Captain. The man ceased his pacing and pointed his spyglass in the direction specified. He stared for a significant duration. Feeling quite bewildered, I went down into the drawing-room to retrieve a superior telescope I habitually employed. Afterwards, resting against the watch-light housing that protruded from the platform’s edge, I began scanning the entire horizon where the heavens met the water.
However, no sooner had I pressed my eye to the lens than it was abruptly pulled from my grasp.

I spun about. Standing in my presence was Captain Sorel, though he was unrecognizable to me. His countenance had been transformed. A sullen glare emanated from his eyes; his jaw was locked; the rigidity of his form, his balled fists, and his head pulled down toward his shoulders revealed the intense turbulence consuming his entire being. He remained motionless. The glass I had dropped from his grasp lay at his feet.

Could I have unintentionally stirred up this outburst of rage? Was it possible that this baffling individual suspected me of unearthing a prohibited mystery? No; I was not the target of his animosity, as he was not gazing in my direction; his stare remained locked upon the unreachable line of the horizon. Eventually, Captain Sorel regained his composure. His restlessness faded. He spoke a few phrases in an alien tongue to his lieutenant, before facing me. “M. Delorme,” he said, in a somewhat commanding manner, “I require you to keep one of the conditions that bind you to me.”
“Captain, what is that?”
“You are to be held in confinement, along with your associates, until such time as I deem it appropriate to set you free,” I said.
“You hold the authority,” I answered, my gaze fixed firmly upon him. “However, is it permitted for me to pose a single inquiry?”
“Zero, sir.”

It was impossible to defy such an authoritative order, as any attempt would have been futile. I descended to the quarters where Tom Harlan and Baptiste resided, informing them of the Captain’s decision. You can imagine the manner in which the Canadian reacted to this news.
However, there was no opportunity for a dispute. A quartet of the shipmates stood by the entrance, escorting us toward the chamber in which we had spent our initial evening aboard the Meridian.
The door was closed against Tom Harlan, who otherwise might have voiced his protest.
“Is master going to explain the meaning of this?” asked Baptiste.
I related the events that had occurred to my associates. They shared my profound surprise, and they were just as unable to explain the situation.

In the interim, I remained preoccupied with my personal musings, unable to focus on anything other than the peculiar dread visible upon the Captain’s face. I found myself completely incapable of explaining it, until my thoughts were interrupted by this statement from Tom Harlan:
“Greetings! the morning meal is prepared.”
The table had, in fact, been set. It was clear that Captain Sorel had issued this instruction while simultaneously increasing the velocity of the Meridian.
“May I offer a suggestion, master?” inquired Baptiste.
“Indeed, my lad.”
“It is that master breakfasts, well. Since we are uncertain of what might occur, it is wise.”
“You’re correct, Baptiste.”
“They have merely provided the ship’s fare, unfortunately,” Tom Harlan said.
“What would you have remarked if the morning meal had been completely overlooked, Friend Tom?” inquired Baptiste.
The harpooner’s reproaches were terminated by this dispute.
We took our places at the table. The food was consumed without a word.

At that moment, the glowing sphere illuminating our chamber extinguished, plunging us into absolute blackness. Tom Harlan quickly drifted off, and I was amazed to see Baptiste succumb to a deep sleep. I was pondering the cause of his sudden, overwhelming lethargy when I felt my own mind grow clouded. My attempts to remain awake were futile; my eyes insisted on closing. A distressing theory occurred to me. Clearly, sedatives had been added to our recent meal. Captain Sorel found confinement insufficient to hide his plans from us; he required us to be unconscious. I then listened as the shutters closed. The rhythmic swaying of the ocean, which had provided a gentle rocking, stopped. Had the Meridian departed the sea’s surface? Had it returned to the still depths? I fought against the slumber, but it was hopeless. My respiration weakened. A deadly chill numbed my rigid, semi-paralyzed body. My eyelids dropped like heavy weights. I was unable to lift them; a sickly sleep, crowded with delusions, stripped me of my consciousness. Eventually, the phantoms faded, abandoning me to total unconsciousness.

I awoke the following morning to find my mind remarkably lucid. It was a profound shock to discover myself back in my private quarters. My associates had surely been returned to their own cabin, just as unaware of the transition as I had been. They possessed no more knowledge than I regarding the events of the night, and I relied solely on the possibilities of what was to come to unravel this enigma.

It occurred to me then to leave my quarters. Had I regained my liberty, or was I still confined? Entirely at liberty. I unlatched the door, proceeded to the half-deck, and ascended the central staircase. The panels, which had been fastened the previous night, stood open. I continued out onto the platform.

Baptiste and Tom Harlan stood waiting for my arrival. Upon being asked by me, they claimed to have no information. Having been trapped in a deep slumber that left them completely unaware, they were surprised to discover their presence in their cabin.
The Meridian appeared as enigmatic and still as it always had. Moving at a measured speed, the vessel drifted across the water’s surface. Everything on the ship looked exactly the same.
The second lieutenant stepped onto the platform and issued the customary command to those beneath.
Captain Sorel, meanwhile, remained absent.
Among those aboard, the only individual I observed was the stoic steward, who attended to me with his customary silent consistency.

At approximately two o’clock, while I was occupied with organizing my records in the drawing-room, the Captain entered through the doorway. I offered a bow. He responded with a brief nod, remaining silent. I returned to my task, anticipating that he might offer some clarification regarding the occurrences of the previous night. He provided none. I observed him. He appeared exhausted; his weary eyes lacked the restoration of slumber; his countenance was deeply mournful. He paced back and forth, sat and stood repeatedly, picked up a random book only to set it aside, checked his instruments while neglecting to record his usual data, and appeared agitated and troubled. Finally, he approached me and said:
“Is M. Delorme a physician?”
Because I anticipated such an inquiry so slightly, I gazed at him for a duration before I replied.
“Do you practice medicine?” he asked again. “A number of your peers have pursued medical studies.”
“I am a physician and the hospital’s resident surgeon,” I remarked. “Before I joined the museum, I spent a number of years in practice.”
“All right, sir.”

The Captain was clearly content with my response. However, as I was uncertain of his subsequent remarks, I remained in anticipation of further inquiries, prepared to tailor my replies based on the situation.
“Will you agree to treat one of my crew members, M. Delorme?” he inquired.
“Does he feel unwell?”
“Indeed.”
“I am prepared to accompany you.”
“Approach, therefore.”

My heart’s rhythm belongs to me, though the reason remains unclear. I perceived a link involving a crew member’s ailment and the happenings of the previous day; this enigma captivated me every bit as much as the invalid himself.
Captain Sorel led me toward the poop deck of the Meridian, where he brought me inside a cabin positioned close to the crew’s living area.
Upon a bed rested a male of roughly forty years, his features set in a determined look, representing a genuine example of an Anglo-Saxon.

I bent down above him. Beyond being sick, he had sustained injuries. Resting upon a cushion was his head, wrapped in blood-stained gauze. As I loosened the dressings, the injured individual gazed at me with wide eyes, showing no indication of suffering throughout the process. It was a ghastly injury. The cranium, crushed by a lethal implement, revealed the damaged brain beneath. Within the fractured and contused tissue, lumps of blood had gathered, resembling the sediment of wine in hue.

The brain exhibited signs of both bruising and congestion. His respiration had slowed, while involuntary muscular twitches disturbed his features. Upon checking his pulse, I found it to be irregular. Because his limbs were cooling rapidly, I realized that his passing was certain. Once I had tended to the poor man’s injuries and secured the head dressings again, I faced Captain Sorel.
“How did this injury happen?” I inquired.
“What is the meaning of this?” he answered, dodging the question. “A jolt snapped a lever on the engine, and it hit me. But what is your assessment of his condition?”
I paused prior to handing it over.
“You have permission to talk,” the Captain stated. “This individual lacks comprehension of French.”
I cast one final glance toward the injured individual.
“In two hours, he shall be deceased.”
“Is there no way to rescue him?”
“Zero.”
Captain Sorel’s fingers tightened, and moisture sparkled within his eyes, though I had believed them unable to weep.

I continued to observe the expiring individual for a short time, as his vitality gradually faded. His complexion grew paler beneath the illumination cast upon his death-bed. I examined his thoughtful brow, marked by early lines, likely caused by grief and adversity. I attempted to discover the mystery of his existence through the final utterances that fell from his mouth.
“You are free to leave, M. Delorme,” the Captain stated.

I abandoned him inside the cabin of the expiring individual and went back to my quarters, deeply moved by what I had witnessed. Throughout the entire day, unsettling doubts plagued me, and my rest was poor during the night, as I imagined hearing faint moans resembling the melody of a burial hymn amidst my fragmented slumber. Could those have been the orisons of the deceased, whispered in a tongue beyond my comprehension?
I arrived at the bridge the following morning. Captain Sorel had already reached it. Upon noticing my presence, he approached me.
“Is it going to be suitable for you, Professor, to go on an underwater trip today?”
“Along with my associates?” I inquired.
“Should they choose to.”
“Your commands are followed, Captain.”
“Would you mind wearing your cork jackets?” I asked.

The issue was not one of life or death. I returned to Tom Harlan and Baptiste to relay the offer made by Captain Sorel. Baptiste moved quickly to agree, and on this occasion, the Canadian appeared entirely prepared to emulate our actions.

The time was eight in the morning. By eight-thirty, we had prepared for this fresh outing, carrying two devices for illumination and respiration. With the double door unlatched, and in the company of Captain Sorel, trailed by twelve members of the crew, we stepped out at a depth of roughly thirty feet onto the firm seabed where the Meridian lay.

The terrain sloped downward until it reached a jagged floor, situated fifteen fathoms below the surface. This seabed was completely unlike the one I had explored during my initial journey beneath the Pacific Ocean. There was an absence of soft sand, underwater meadows, or kelp forests here. I instantly identified that extraordinary territory where, on that occasion, the Captain acted as our host. It was the realm of coral.

A thousand delightful diversities were generated by the illumination, dancing amongst the brightly hued boughs. It appeared to me that the cylindrical, membraneous tubes quivered under the rippling currents. I felt an urge to pluck their crisp petals, which were adorned with fine tentacles—some in full bloom, others merely sprouting—as a tiny fish darted past, brushing against them in a manner reminiscent of a flock of birds. Yet, whenever I reached toward these sentient blossoms, these responsive, living plants, the entire group grew startled. The pale petals retreated into their crimson sheaths, the blooms withered before my eyes, and the shrub transformed into a cluster of rocky protrusions.

Fate had placed me directly beside the most exquisite zoophyte samples. This coral possessed greater worth than the varieties discovered within the Mediterranean, along the shores of France, Italy, and Barbary. Its hues validated the lyrical titles of “Flower of Blood” and “Froth of Blood” bestowed by commerce upon its finest yields. Coral fetches £20 per ounce; here, the submerged layers could establish the wealth of a coral-diving syndicate. This valuable substance, frequently mistaken for alternative polypi, comprised the tangled thickets known as “macciota,” where I observed various stunning examples of pink coral.

Before long, the shrubbery drew inward, and the branch-like formations grew more numerous. Genuine stone copses, lengthy beams of whimsical design, were revealed to our sight. Captain Sorel positioned himself beneath a shadowed passage, through which we descended a gentle slope to a level of one hundred yards. The illumination from our lanterns occasionally created enchanting displays, tracing the jagged contours of the organic vaults and hanging structures arranged like chandeliers, which glowed with fiery tips.

Following a two-hour trek, we finally reached a depth of roughly three hundred yards, which marks the absolute boundary where coral starts to develop. Yet, there were no solitary shrubs or humble thickets beneath the towering trees. Instead, a vast woodland of massive mineral flora stretched out, with giant fossilized trunks linked by wreaths of graceful sea-bindweed, all embellished by shifting lights and shadows. We moved without obstruction beneath those elevated boughs, wandering through the dimness of the currents.

Captain Sorel came to a standstill. As I and my companions paused, I looked back to see his crew arranging themselves in a half-moon pattern about their leader. Keeping a close watch, I noted that a quartet of them were bearing a rectangular item upon their shoulders.

Positioned within the heart of an expansive clearing, we were enclosed by the towering leaves of the underwater woods. The illumination from our lanterns cast a pale, dusk-like glow across the area, stretching the shadows upon the earth in an unusual fashion. Beyond the edge of the glade, the gloom deepened, broken only by faint glimmers caught by the tips of the coral.

Near me stood Tom Harlan and Baptiste. As we observed, I anticipated the unfolding of an unusual event. Upon examining the earth, I noticed it was elevated in specific spots by minor outgrowths covered in calcareous crusts, arranged with a symmetry that revealed human intervention.

At the center of the clearing, resting atop a mound of crudely stacked stones, rose a coral crucifix, its elongated limbs appearing as if fashioned from hardened gore. Following a gesture from Captain Sorel, a crewman stepped forward; he commenced excavating a pit a few paces from the cross using a pickaxe retrieved from his waist. Everything became clear to me! This woodland opening served as a graveyard, the excavation was a grave, and that rectangular shape was the corpse of the individual who perished during the night hours! The Captain and his subordinates had arrived to inter their associate within this communal burial ground, situated at the base of this unreachable sea!

The burial site was excavated at a sluggish pace; aquatic creatures darted away in every direction as their sanctuary was interrupted; I listened to the rhythmic impacts of the pickaxe, which emitted flashes of light upon striking flint buried deep beneath the surface. Before long, the pit was sufficiently wide and profound to accommodate the remains. Following this, the pallbearers drew near; the corpse, swaddled in white linen fabric, was deposited into the moist sepulcher. Captain Sorel, his arms folded across his chest, joined the companions of the deceased in kneeling to offer prayers.
Everyone dropped to their knees, assuming a posture of prayer.

Debris excavated from the earth was shoveled back into the pit, creating a modest elevation. Once finished, Captain Sorel and his crew stood up; they drew near the burial site, knelt once more, and reached out their hands as a final gesture of farewell. The burial party then made their way back to the Meridian, moving beneath the forest’s vaulted branches, through dense brush, past coral shrubs, and continuing upward. Eventually, the vessel’s glow came into view, and its radiant path led us toward the Meridian. We arrived back at one o’clock.
Once I had swapped my attire, I ascended to the platform and, overcome by a turmoil of feelings, took a seat by the binnacle. Captain Sorel came over to me. Standing up, I addressed him:
“So, just as I predicted, did this man pass away during the night?”
“Indeed, M. Delorme.”
“So he is at peace currently, beside his peers, within the reef graveyard?”

“Indeed, ignored by everyone else, yet remembered by us. We excavated the burial site, and the polypi assume the task of sealing our departed forever.” And, hiding his visage rapidly within his palms, he attempted unsuccessfully to stifle a cry. He then continued: “Our tranquil graveyard lies there, approximately one hundred feet beneath the ocean’s surface.”
“At the very least, Captain, your deceased rest in peace, beyond the grasp of any sharks.”
“Indeed, sir, regarding both sharks and men,” the Captain answered solemnly.
